text_variants.text: A girl of about fourteen with her mother's squint blocks the corridor, a ratting pole held like a spear. "Mam described you. Down to the boots." Her voice shakes, but the pole doesn't. "She got home. No thanks to you. I've come for her satchel."

A girl of about fourteen with her mother's satchel and her mother's squint stops square in front of you. "Mam said a stranger who knew a tourniquet. Said you swore at her leg till it listened, and didn't ask anything for it." She holds the satchel out. "You don't owe me anything. I'm here to pay."

escort_lena.name: Lena

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair Lena hands you the last of her mother's tonic and is back up the steps before you can argue.
on_arrive.chronicle: Lena walked me a whole floor and never once stepped on a trap. Then she went home.

on_fail.chronicle: I lost Lena on the stairs. I keep thinking about her mother's squint.

escort_lena.on_fail_trapdoor: The floor dropped out and took me without Lena. That was the floor's doing. It does not feel that way.

options.label: Take her mother's kit
options.outcome: She looks relieved, as if an account has been closed. "Mam'll be glad. She hates owing."
options.chronicle: Marta's girl found me and paid her mother's debt in potions. I took them. She seemed relieved.

road.hint: A debt paid back lets two people stop thinking about it.

options.label: "Keep it. Go home."
options.outcome: She argues. You win, narrowly. She goes back up with the satchel still on her shoulder and the look of someone who will try again.
options.chronicle: Sent Lena home with her mother's kit still on her shoulder. She argued. I won, barely.

road.hint: Refusing a repayment is a gift too, though not a free one.

options.label: "Walk me down one floor. You know the traps."
options.outcome: She grins her mother's grin. "Step where I step."

road.hint: Someone who learned the traps from her mother is worth following.

options.label: Tell her it was you, and pay back the bread too
options.outcome: You count the potions into her mother's satchel, and the price of the bread on top. "It was me," you say. "I took them off her while she couldn't stand. I'm sorry." The pole doesn't move for a long moment. "Mam said you'd lie or you'd run," Lena says. "She didn't have a word for this." She slings the satchel and goes. Halfway up the stair she stops. "I'll tell her you said it."
options.chronicle: Told Marta's daughter it was me who robbed her mother, and paid back the potions and the bread. Saying it cost more than the potions did.

road.hint: Saying it was you costs more than what you took, and buys more.

options.label: Give back what you took
options.outcome: She takes them and checks every stopper. "That's the potions," she says. "Mam counted the bread too." She goes, and does not look back.
options.chronicle: Marta's daughter came for her mother's satchel. I gave back the potions. She said her mother had counted the bread too. She was right.

road.hint: What you take from a mother, her daughter comes to collect.

options.label: Tell her it's all gone
options.outcome: "Then I hope it was worth it." She spits on your boots, very accurately, and goes.
options.chronicle: Told a rat-catcher's daughter her mother's medicine was spent. She spat on my boots. Good aim.

road.hint: Some accounts stay open for good.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: She watches you go, and for a moment she looks exactly like her mother.

name: Ostrander
text: A man is up to his chest in a sucking pit of black mud at the bottom of a drop. "Rope. For the love of God, a rope." His coat is a wrecker's coat, tar-black, and a dark lantern on a pole lies in the mud beside him, the kind you hang on a cliff to make ships think there is a harbour. "I know what I am," he gasps. "Pull me out anyway."

options.label: Throw him your rope
options.outcome: You haul him out. He lies on the edge coughing mud, then grins up at you with very good teeth. "You're a saint," he says. "Saints are good for business." He picks up his lantern and goes.
options.chronicle: Pulled a wrecker named Ostrander out of a mud pit. He thanked me, then took his false lantern with him.

road.hint: A rope thrown with no conditions is a gift to whatever the man does next.

options.label: Make him swear on the rope never to light a false lamp again, then pull
options.outcome: "Swear it." He looks at the rope, and at you, and at the mud at his chin. "Never another false light," he says. "On my mother's grave." You pull. He leaves the lantern in the pit.
options.chronicle: Made a wrecker swear on my rope never to light a false lamp again before I pulled him out. He left his lantern in the mud.

road.hint: A rope thrown with a condition attached can pull a man further than the pit.

options.label: Leave him
options.outcome: "I know what I am," he shouts after you. "That's why I asked."
options.chronicle: Left a wrecker in his own pit. He said he knew what he was. So did I.

road.hint: A man caught in his own trap has already told you who he is.

name: Grumwald
text: Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: YES, YOU.

text_variants.text: Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: NUMBER NINE CROSSES FREE.

Another chasm, another rope bridge, and Grumwald, minding his cousin's bridge now, asleep beside a new box. The sign reads: TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY. Underneath, in newer paint: ESPECIALLY YOU. The box is chained to his ankle.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens. "Nine. Twice. That's never happened."
options.chronicle: Met Grumwald's second bridge. His sign said number nine crosses free. I paid anyway. He nearly fell off his stool.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens. "Huh," he says, and you have the feeling a long ledger has been squared, approximately.
options.chronicle: Grumwald's new sign said especially you. I paid. I think we are square, approximately.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens.

road.hint: A troll remembers faces for a very long time.

options.label: Wake him and tell him who emptied his box
options.outcome: You put a hand on a knee the size of a millstone and shake it. One yellow eye opens, then the other, and the troll sits up, and up. "It was me," you say. "The box on the first bridge. Both fistfuls." You feed a tenth of your purse into the new box, coin by coin, while he watches. For a long time he says nothing at all. "Forty years of that box," he rumbles at last, "and you're the first that ever came back to say it." He rubs out ESPECIALLY YOU with one thumb, and goes back to sleep.
options.chronicle: Woke Grumwald and told him I was the one who emptied his honesty box. Paid it back with interest while he watched. He rubbed the line about me off his sign.

road.hint: A sleeping troll can be woken for a confession, and he remembers that too.

options.label: Cross
options.outcome: The bridge holds. The snoring never changes.
options.chronicle: Crossed another of Grumwald's bridges. He has added a line to his sign, and I am fairly sure it is about me.

road.hint: Every bridge you cross remembers you a little.

name: Elspeth
text: A woman with a candle in a jar is coming up the corridor against the flow of everything else, thin as a reed and walking like someone who was in bed a month ago. "Aldric said a stranger was carrying his sin for him. The cordial worked." She sets the candle down. "I've come to carry it back."

text_variants.text: A woman with a candle in a jar stops in front of you. "You're the one. The altar broke it. Aldric felt it go, all the way up in our kitchen. He sent me to say so, since he has a farm to mend."

options.label: Let her take the stone
options.outcome: She takes it in both arms and staggers, and does not complain. "There's an altar two stairs down," she says. "I'll take it there and break it, then go home light." The candle goes out. She does not relight it.
options.chronicle: Elspeth took Aldric's stone down to an altar to break it, and then home. I let her. She did not relight her candle.

road.hint: A carried burden can be handed back without being dropped.

options.label: "I gave Aldric my word. I'll finish it."
options.outcome: She looks at you a long time, then lights your way to the next stair with her candle, and goes back up alone.
options.chronicle: Elspeth offered to take the stone. I said no. It is my promise, not hers.

road.hint: Some promises are kept by refusing help.

options.label: Thank her for the news
options.outcome: She presses the candle on you, jar and all. It burns without wax, the way some candles do in old stories.
options.chronicle: Aldric's wife found me to say thank you. She left me her candle. It burns without wax.

road.hint: A candle lit for someone else's knight can show your own road too.

options.label: Keep walking
options.outcome: She watches you go, and goes on her way.

name: Man Who Is Owed
stance_note: Steel-man: Pike is sincere and selfless, and Basil the Great's sermon is the strongest Christian case for his claim, quoted accurately. The pass answers it (§3.9: a duty on the giver, not a right in the receiver) by showing the harm of the principle to a third party, not by mocking the man.
text: A gaunt man in a patched apron steps into your path with a basket. Behind him a thin girl stands silent, watching your pack. "Gerrold Pike. You carry rations; she has none. Saint Basil said it, and he meant it: the bread you hold back belongs to the hungry. It isn't yours to give. It's hers, and I'm here to collect it." He is not asking. He has the calm of a man who has never once kept back a crumb for himself.

options.label: Put a ration in his basket
options.outcome: He hands it to Nell whole, without tasting it. Then he turns to the old pilgrim coming down the stair behind you, who has one heel of bread, and holds out the basket to her as well, gently, by right. She gives it to him. She thinks she must.
options.chronicle: Paid my share to Gerrold Pike for a hungry girl. He gave her all of it. Then he collected the last crust off an old pilgrim, by right.

road.hint: A collector who means well still collects from everyone.

options.label: Give it to the girl yourself
options.outcome: Nell takes it in both hands and eats as if someone might take it back. Pike nods, satisfied but not pleased. "Good. But you'd have owed it whether you felt like giving or not."
options.chronicle: Fed a hungry girl myself rather than paying the man who said the bread was hers by right. He said I would have owed it anyway.

road.hint: A gift goes furthest from the hand that gives it.

options.label: Answer him: a gift owed is no gift at all

pass.outcome: You say it plainly. Feeding her is your duty, and you'll do it because you choose to. But Basil was telling the rich man what he ought to do, not handing anyone a warrant to collect. A gift taken by right stops being a gift and makes servants of the givers, starting with that old pilgrim. Pike is silent a long time. Then he turns, walks back up the stair to the pilgrim, and gives her bread back with both hands. "I've been taking it like a tax," he says. "Basil never asked me to be a tax."
pass.chronicle: Argued with Gerrold Pike that charity owed is no charity. He gave an old pilgrim back her bread and said Basil never asked him to be a tax.

fail.outcome: You tangle yourself up. Pike is kind about it, which is worse for the argument. He takes the ration as owed, gives it to Nell, and turns to the pilgrim.
fail.chronicle: Lost an argument about charity to a man who keeps nothing for himself. He was kind about it. The pilgrim behind me still paid.

road.hint: A duty you owe is not a debt someone else can collect.

options.label: Refuse him and walk on
options.outcome: Pike nods, unsurprised, and turns to the next traveller on the stair.
options.chronicle: Told a man collecting for the poor that my rations were mine to give. He nodded and went on to the next traveller.

road.hint: A refusal is a door shut, and the stair goes on.

name: Samson
text: A wedding feast in a cave hall, and at the head of the table a huge man with hair to his waist in seven braids. Thirty sullen young men line the benches. "Samson of Zorah. A riddle and a wager: thirty fine cloaks says you can't answer it." He grins. "Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." By the door, the thirty's leader catches your sleeve. "We got it out of the bride. We said we'd burn her father's house. Pay us, and the answer's yours."

options.label: Answer it yourself, staking a fifth of your purse

pass.outcome: "A lion," you say, "and the honey the bees made in its carcass." Samson roars and slaps the table hard enough to crack it. "Honestly come by. Not like these will try to." He looks at the thirty. They look at their plates.
pass.chronicle: Answered Samson's riddle myself. A lion, and honey. He cracked the table laughing, and gave the thirty a look I would not want.

fail.outcome: You guess wrong. Samson takes your stake and shrugs, almost sorry. "Seven days, they had," he says. "You had a minute."
fail.chronicle: Lost my stake guessing at Samson's riddle. Seven days, the others had. I had a minute.

road.hint: An answer forced out of a frightened woman is not yours to sell.

options.label: Buy the answer from the thirty
options.outcome: "A lion, and honey," you say. Samson's face goes very dark. "Somebody has been talking to my bride." He pays you, and then he goes out with the thirty, and you hear what that sounds like.
options.chronicle: Bought the answer to Samson's riddle from men who had bullied it out of his bride. He paid me. Then he went to see them.

road.hint: Some answers come with the bride's tears still on them.

options.label: Tell Samson his bride was threatened, and give up the wager
options.outcome: Samson goes very quiet, which on him is terrible. He sends four of his own men to sit outside her father's house with clubs, and only then does he go looking for the thirty.
options.chronicle: Told Samson the men at his wedding had threatened to burn his bride's father's house. He sent guards first and went hunting second. Good order.

road.hint: In the old story, nobody warned him, and the house burned.

options.label: Decline the wager

name: The Piper
text: A line of children dances down the corridor behind a tall man in a coat of red and yellow, playing a pipe. Their eyes are open and empty. Behind them a fat man in a mayor's chain runs, puffing. "Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay." The Piper doesn't stop. "A thousand guilders, he promised, for the rats. He paid me fifty, and laughed." At the very back a small boy on a crutch is falling behind, crying to keep up.

options.label: Pay the Piper his thousand yourself
options.warning: Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay.
options.outcome: The Piper looks at your gold, then at the mayor, then pockets it and plays a different tune. The children blink, and turn, and go home. The mayor wipes his face. "Generous," he says. "Very generous. Hamelin thanks you." He does not offer to pay you back.

delayed.text: A notice nailed to a stair-post: HAMELIN SEEKS A RAT-CATCHER. FAIR TERMS. B. HARDEKOPF, MAYOR.

options.chronicle: Paid the Piper his fee out of my own purse to bring Hamelin's children home. The mayor thanked me warmly. He is advertising for a rat-catcher again.

road.hint: Pay a cheat's debt for him and he will run up another.

options.label: Make the mayor pay what he owes, staking your breath

pass.outcome: You catch the mayor by his chain of office and hold it up so the Piper can see the town seal on it. A contract made under that seal binds Hamelin, not just Hardekopf, and Hamelin is right here, dancing. The mayor pays, in full, from the purse on his belt he swore was empty. The Piper counts it, nods, and plays the children home. The boy on the crutch is the first one back.
pass.chronicle: Held the mayor of Hamelin to his own contract in front of the Piper. He paid in full from a purse he swore was empty. The children went home.

fail.outcome: The mayor argues that the contract was for rats, not sorcery, and while you argue the music gets into your feet. You dance until you fall. When you get up, the corridor is empty except for the mayor, alone now and grey, and the boy on the crutch, who was too slow to follow, crying in the dust. The mayor takes Hans by the hand. "I'll get this one home, at least."
fail.chronicle: Argued contracts with the mayor of Hamelin while the Piper took the children into the hill. Only the lame boy was left. In the story, he always is. The mayor took him home.

road.hint: A town's seal on a promise makes the whole town the debtor.

options.label: Carry the lame boy out of the line
options.outcome: You scoop up the boy on the crutch. He fights you, crying, because he wants to go where the music is. The others go into the hill, and the hill closes. He stops fighting then. His name is Hans. The mayor, alone now and grey, takes him by the hand. "I'll get this one home, at least."
options.chronicle: Carried the lame boy out of the Piper's line. The others went into the hill. He fought me the whole way and then he stopped. The mayor took him home.

road.hint: Saving the one you can reach is still saving one.

options.label: Stand aside
options.outcome: The music goes past, and the children, and the mayor, still promising.

name: Sir Aldric
text: A knight kneels at a fresh cairn with a black stone still lashed to his back. A crystal vial lies empty beside him, the one you drank from. He does not look up, and he does not speak. A pilgrim's staff leans on the cairn; whoever brought the news down from the surface did not stay. Somebody has scratched one word on the top stone: ELSPETH.

options.label: Kneel beside him a while
options.outcome: He doesn't acknowledge you. After a long time he reaches out and straightens a stone that was already straight.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Aldric at his wife's cairn. He did not speak. I do not think he will again.

road.hint: Some answers come back as cairns.

options.label: Offer to take the stone now
options.outcome: He shakes his head once, very slowly. The stone is part of the cairn now, or he is.
options.chronicle: Offered to carry Sir Aldric's stone, far too late. He shook his head. He has decided to keep it.

road.hint: An offer made too late is still an offer, and still too late.

options.label: Tell him it was you who drank it, and ask to carry the stone
options.outcome: "It was me," you say. "I drank her cordial. You asked me for help, and I took the one thing that could have saved her." For the first time he looks up. "Nobody has said it," he says. "Not the pilgrim. Not the priest. I've been waiting a long time for somebody to say it out loud." He works the straps loose with stiff fingers and lays the black stone in your arms. It weighs exactly what he said it did. "There's an altar somewhere below," he says. "I'm going home to bury her properly." He goes up the stair without it, slowly, like a man learning to walk again.

person_status.last_line: There's an altar somewhere below. I'm going home to bury her properly.

options.chronicle: Told Sir Aldric at his wife's cairn that I was the one who drank her cordial. He gave me his stone to carry and went home to bury her. It weighs what he said it did.

road.hint: Some weights pass to whoever finally says the true thing out loud.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The stone grinds against his armour as he leans forward to rest his head on the cairn.
options.chronicle: Walked past a knight kneeling at a cairn with an empty vial beside it. I knew whose vial it was.

name: Great Lion
text: Something heavy has kept pace with you in the dark for three rooms. Now it steps into the light: a full-maned lion in his prime, scarred across the muzzle, with a pale old mark on one forepaw. He sits down in the middle of the corridor and waits to see what you'll do.

options.label: Hold out the thorn

pass.outcome: You hold it low and still, palm up, eyes down, the way you'd offer something to any big cat that hasn't decided about you. He sniffs it, and then sniffs you, and then puts his whole great head against your chest and pushes, the way a house cat does.
pass.chronicle: The lion I helped came back, grown. He remembered the thorn and pushed his head against me like a house cat. Androcles had the right idea.

fail.outcome: You hold it up too fast. He flinches back, then takes the thorn delicately from your fingers in his teeth, the way a dog takes a biscuit, and walks off with it.
fail.chronicle: The lion came back. I startled him. He took the thorn and went. I think we are still on good terms.

road.hint: A kindness to a beast is repaid in the beast's own coin.

options.label: Stand very still
options.outcome: He looks at you a long time, then pads past, close enough to brush your leg.

options.label: Throw him food and back away

name: Ostrander
text: A lamp glows across a chasm, warm and inviting, as if a path ran to it. The lamp is on the wrong side of the chasm, where no path goes.

text_variants.text: At the lip of a chasm a lamp burns on an iron pole, on the right side, where the path is. A man in a wrecker's coat sits under it, trimming the wick. Ostrander. "Never another false light," he says, before you can ask. "I swore on your rope. Lamp's been lit every watch since."

options.label: Sit under his lamp a while
options.outcome: He tells you where the floor gives way.
options.chronicle: Found Ostrander keeping a true lamp at a chasm. He swore on my rope never to light a false one, and he hasn't. Some people mend.

road.hint: A lamp kept true is a promise lit again every watch.

options.label: Walk toward the light
options.outcome: The path ends a step before the light does. You fall a short, painful way into a cut where two men in wreckers' coats are waiting with clubs. Above, someone laughs and trims the wick.
options.chronicle: Walked toward a lamp across a chasm. It was Ostrander's. I pulled him out of a pit once. He has not changed his trade.

road.hint: A lamp on the wrong side of a gulf is lit for the wrong reason.

options.label: Look for whoever is holding it

pass.outcome: You find him in the shadow under the lamp, and he sees you see him. He blows it out and runs.
pass.chronicle: Caught Ostrander lighting false lamps again. He ran. I pulled him out of a pit once, which I now regret in a measured way.

fail.outcome: You see nothing but the light. You go round the long way, for no reason you can name.

road.hint: Before you follow a lamp, look for the hand holding it.

options.label: Go round the long way

name: Lawspeaker's Rock
text: Two families face each other across a flat rock under a lamp-stone, axes held low. A big man sets a bag of silver on the rock. "Hallbjorn. I killed Kol over a whale stranded on the shore of the under-sea, and I'm sorry for it, and there's his price." Kol's brother Steinar doesn't look at the silver. "Silver doesn't eat at my table." Every face turns to you. "You're a stranger," says Hallbjorn. "Strangers have no side. Speak the law."

options.label: Speak the law: the price, the oath, the outlawry

pass.outcome: You speak it as the old lawspeakers did, case by case: the price for a free man killed in hot blood, the oath of peace sworn on the ring, the outlawry for whoever breaks it. In Iceland the lawspeaker carried the whole law in his head and recited a third of it every summer from the Law Rock at Thingvellir, in the rift where two plates of the earth pull apart. Steinar listens to the end. Then he picks up the silver, slowly, as if it weighed more than it does, and puts out his hand.
pass.chronicle: Spoke the old law at a blood feud because the Lawspeaker was dead and I was a stranger. They took the silver instead of the axe. It nearly did not work.

fail.outcome: You stumble over the price and the oath. Steinar hears the hesitation. "Then there's no law here," he says, and the axes come up. Hallbjorn dies on the rock with his silver beside him.
fail.chronicle: Tried to speak the law at a blood feud and forgot the middle. Without the law they used axes. I keep thinking about the middle.

road.hint: Law is what stands between a grudge and an axe.

options.label: Add your own silver to sweeten the price
options.warning: Silver doesn't eat at my table.
options.outcome: Steinar looks at your coins on top of Hallbjorn's. "Now my brother's price is paid by a stranger," he says. "He's worth less than I thought." The axes come up. Hallbjorn dies on the rock, on top of both your silvers.
options.chronicle: Added my own silver to a blood price to make the peace. It made the dead man cheaper. They used axes.

road.hint: A grieving man hears an insult in a stranger's coin.

options.label: Tell Steinar to take his revenge
options.outcome: "Blood for blood," you say, and Steinar nods as if you'd told him the weather.

delayed.text: A new cairn by the stair, two names scratched on it: Hallbjorn's sons. Under them, in a fresh hand: AND STEINAR.

options.chronicle: Told a grieving brother to take his revenge. He did. Some floors later I passed a cairn with more names on it than his.

road.hint: Blood for blood is a sum that never comes out even.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the silence on the rock stretches, and stretches, and breaks.
options.chronicle: Walked away from a blood feud at a law rock. I heard it break behind me.

road.hint: A law rock with no lawspeaker is only a rock.

name: Nestor of Pylos
text: A very old man in very old bronze is sitting halfway up a broken pillar, with his spear planted beside it like a ladder. "Nestor of Pylos. I am not stuck," he says. "I am resting where I landed. When the Boar of Calydon came at me I vaulted on this spear into a tree, and a man my age does not come down from a thing like that in a hurry. Sit. I will tell you about the hunt. All of it."

options.label: Sit down and hear all of it
options.outcome: Artemis sent the boar because a king forgot her at harvest. Half the heroes of Greece came. A huntress named Atalanta drew first blood with an arrow, which the men have not forgiven, and Meleager finished it with a spear. "They say a beast of that blood roots about below here still. Blades skid off the bristles. A point goes in." You get up stiff, and strangely ready for anything.
options.chronicle: Sat through the whole of an old spearman's story about the Calydonian Boar. It took a long time and was mostly true.

road.hint: An old soldier's story is long because he lived all of it.

options.label: Ask him who drew the boar's first blood

pass.outcome: "Atalanta," you say, and his old eyes shine. "With an arrow, behind the ear, and the men have not forgiven her yet. Meleager finished it with a spear." He leans down. "Since you listen: a beast of that blood roots about below here still. Blades skid off the bristles. A point goes in. Set your spear against the charge and let it run itself onto the point." He shows you how to stand.
pass.chronicle: Nestor of Pylos told me Atalanta drew the Calydonian Boar's first blood, and that a point goes in where a blade skids.

fail.outcome: "Meleager?" you guess. "Meleager killed it," he says, disappointed. "Atalanta drew first blood, with an arrow, and the men never forgave her. Young people never want the middle of a story."
fail.chronicle: Nestor of Pylos told me a huntress drew the Calydonian Boar's first blood. I had guessed wrong.

road.hint: The boar's first blood was drawn by an arrow, not a spear.

options.label: Help him down and move on
options.outcome: He comes down slowly, complaining about modern pillars. "In my day," he says, "we had trees."

options.label: Leave him on his pillar
options.outcome: "In my day," he calls after you, "we had trees."

name: Tarek the Guard
text: A broad-shouldered man is sitting on an overturned crate, head in his hands, among broken bales of salt and a dead mule. He looks up when he hears you, too quickly, too hopefully. "Tarek. Caravan guard, on the salt road. The ground opened under the camp three nights ago and we came down with it. The others went looking for the way up and didn't come back. Tell me you know the way out. Or tell me you have food. Or both." He pauses. "Please, in any order."

options.label: Give him food and directions
options.outcome: He eats quickly, then stands, squaring his shoulders. "You're a decent soul." He grips your forearm, soldier to soldier, and says a guardsman's blessing over you. "Keep your left side covered." A steadiness settles around you like a second coat.
options.chronicle: Gave a lost caravan guard food and directions. He asked in any order, so I gave both.

road.hint: Food first, then directions, then hope.

options.label: Help him find which way is up

pass.outcome: You wet a finger and hold it up until you feel it: a cold draught on one side. A cave breathes through its mouths, so where the air moves there is a way to the open sky. You follow the draught with Tarek to a crack with daylight at the top of it, and he laughs out loud. "The bales nobody can carry are yours. On the old caravan roads to Timbuktu, salt was traded for gold. It still buys a fair bit."
pass.chronicle: Found the way up for a caravan guard named Tarek by following the draught. A cave breathes toward the sky. He left me the salt.

fail.outcome: You lead him the wrong way, downhill, toward the water, and he follows you because you sound sure. Later it comes to you: a wet finger in the draught would have told you. A cave breathes through its mouths, and where the air moves, there is a way out.
fail.chronicle: Tried to lead a lost caravan guard out and went the wrong way. I should have felt for the draught.

road.hint: A cave breathes through its mouths.

options.label: Buy salted provisions from the broken bales
options.outcome: He sells you salt fish and hard bread out of the caravan's stores at a fair price. "The owners would want paying," he says. "And I'll need coin up there, if there is an up there."

options.label: "Sorry, I'm lost myself."
options.outcome: He laughs, short, tired, genuine. "Of course you are." He nods toward the dark. "Well. Company for a few minutes, then. That's something."

name: Saint Brendan
text: In an underground sea, on a low black island with no trees, fourteen monks in wet habits are building a cookfire for an Easter supper, and an old monk in the bow of a leather boat is watching them with a look you can't read. "Brendan," he says, nodding to you. "Will you help the brothers with their fire?" The island is warm under your boots. It rises, slowly, and falls again, as if it were breathing.

options.label: Help the brothers build up the fire
options.warning: It rises, slowly, and falls again, as if it were breathing.
options.outcome: The fire catches beautifully. Then the island shudders from end to end and goes down like a stone, and you are all in black water among floating loaves and a cauldron, and Brendan is fishing monks out with a boathook, unsurprised.
options.chronicle: Helped some monks light a cookfire on an island. The island was a fish. Saint Brendan fished us out with a boathook and did not seem surprised.

road.hint: Check what you are standing on before you build a fire on it.

options.label: Look at the island properly

pass.outcome: Warm, breathing, no trees, and at the far end a hole that mists every few minutes. You get the brothers back into the boat before the fire is lit, and Brendan laughs out loud for the first time in seven years. "Then we'll say the Mass on his back without a fire," he says. "He's been patient with us." They do. You stay for it.
pass.chronicle: Spotted the island under a monk's cookfire was breathing and got them off it. They said Easter Mass on the whale's back. Saint Brendan laughed out loud.

fail.outcome: It looks like an island to you. Only later, dripping, do you learn what the sailors call it: Jasconius, the fish so big that Brendan's monks once lit their Easter fire on its back.
fail.chronicle: Looked hard at an island in an underground sea and decided it was an island. It was not.

road.hint: An island that breathes is not an island.

options.label: Share your food with the brothers
options.outcome: They bless it, and you, and then go back to building the fire.

options.label: Wish them a happy Easter and go

name: Wren Hallet, Scout
text: A young scout with a badly wrapped leg wound is propped against a pillar, pale but awake. "Don't bother with the north passage," she says immediately, as if she's been waiting to warn someone. "There's something down there that doesn't die clean." She winces and shifts her weight. "I'd offer to trade, but I'm a bit short on leverage right now."

options.label: Re-dress her leg properly

pass.outcome: You unwrap the bad bandage, wash the grit out with clean water, press a pad on the cut until it stops seeping, and bind it firm. A wound wrapped over dirt festers; a clean one heals. She stands, tests the leg, and gives you a rough sketch of the north passage. "It doesn't die clean because steel only slows it. Fire, or something blessed. That's what finally put the last one down."
pass.chronicle: Washed and bound a scout's leg. Wren Hallet told me the thing in the north passage fears fire and blessing, not steel.

fail.outcome: You tighten the old bandage over the old dirt, and she winces. "That'll fester," she says. "Wash it first. Always wash it first." She'll manage. She still warns you: "Steel only slows it. Fire, or something blessed."
fail.chronicle: Bound a scout's leg badly. She told me to always wash a wound first, and that steel only slows what is in the north passage.

road.hint: A wound wrapped over dirt festers.

options.label: Give her bandages and splints (60 gold)
options.outcome: She takes the supplies with real relief, binds herself up with a practised hand, and presses a rough sketch of the north passage into yours, with the creature's patrol marked in red. "It circles. There's a window. That's how I got out."

options.label: Sit with her until she can walk
options.outcome: You help her re-bind the wound properly and wait while she recovers enough to stand. She insists on returning the favor, pulling out a small medkit and seeing to a few of your own injuries with a practiced hand. "Scout training," she says simply.
options.chronicle: Sat with a wounded scout until she could walk. She warned me about the north passage. I listened.

road.hint: Listen to the scout who came back.

options.label: Wish her luck and move on
options.outcome: "Yeah," she says, to no one in particular. You hope she finds her way out. You've seen enough of this dungeon to know that hope doesn't cost anything, but it isn't cheap either.

name: Bramble the Vendor
text: A heavyset halfling has set up a small cookfire in a wide junction, with something genuinely savory simmering in a pot. In a dungeon. In a pot. He stirs it cheerfully. "Before you ask: yes, I have a permit. No, I won't tell you who issued it. Yes, it smells as good as it looks. You want some or not?"

options.label: Buy a bowl (fills you up)
options.outcome: It is, genuinely, excellent. Rich, well-seasoned, served in a chipped but clean bowl. You eat it standing and feel almost civilized. "Good recipe," you manage. "Family secret," he says, and winks. "It's mushrooms. Everything down here is mushrooms."
options.chronicle: Bought stew from a halfling with a permit he would not explain. It was excellent stew.

road.hint: Do not ask who issued the permit.

options.label: Buy extra provisions
options.outcome: He packs a portion into a waxed cloth bundle with professional efficiency. "Keeps two days, three if you don't think about it too hard." He tucks a small herb packet in with it. "For flavor. Even emergencies deserve flavor."

options.label: Guess what's in the pot

pass.outcome: "Morels," you say, sniffing. He beams. A true morel's cap is honeycombed and it is hollow right through when you slice it; the false ones are stuffed with cotton inside, and nobody sensible eats those. "And never raw," he says. "Raw, even a true one will turn your stomach. Cooked, best thing under the earth." He gives you a bowl on the house, and a packed portion for the road.
pass.chronicle: Guessed a halfling's stew was morels. He told me how to tell a true one: hollow right through. He fed me for nothing.

fail.outcome: "Beef?" He laughs. "Morels. Hollow right through when you cut them; that's how you know a true one from a false one. And always cooked." He goes back to stirring. "Bowl's still for sale."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong about a halfling's stew. It was morels, which must always be cooked.

road.hint: A true morel is hollow right through.

options.label: "Just enjoying the smell."
options.outcome: "Free of charge," he says magnanimously. You stand there for a moment longer than strictly necessary, and he doesn't rush you. Some kindnesses are very small and very important.

name: Thrar Coalhand, Journeyman
text: A young dwarf with a grinding wheel strapped to his back sits on a fallen column, pedalling the wheel and holding a blade to it in a fan of sparks. "Thrar Coalhand, journeyman, on my wander-years," he says, squinting at you through soot-black hair. "Can't make you armour; the masters do that. But I can put an edge on anything. Weapon's looking a bit sad, isn't it?"

options.label: Pay him to sharpen your weapon
options.outcome: Thrar pedals the wheel up to a howl and works your blade along it in short, precise strokes. When he hands it back, it catches the torchlight differently, sharper, hungrier. "Now that's a proper tool," he mutters approvingly.
options.chronicle: Paid a journeyman dwarf named Thrar to put an edge on my weapon. He called it sad. It is less sad now.

road.hint: A smith who insults your blade is about to improve it.

options.label: Ask him who the best smiths ever were

pass.outcome: "The sons of Ivaldi," you say, "and Brokkr and his brother." He grins through the soot. "Now you're talking. Ivaldi's sons made Skidbladnir, a ship with a fair wind the moment the sail goes up, that folds small enough to go in your pocket. Brokkr's brother made Draupnir, a gold ring that drips eight more like itself every ninth night." He takes your blade off you without asking and puts an edge on it for nothing.
pass.chronicle: Named the great dwarf smiths to a journeyman named Thrar. He told me about a ship that folds into a pocket, and sharpened my blade for nothing.

fail.outcome: "Wayland?" you guess. "An elf," he says, offended on behalf of his people. "The sons of Ivaldi made a ship that folds into your pocket. Brokkr's brother made a ring that drips eight more every ninth night. Look it up."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong about the great smiths. A journeyman dwarf named Thrar was offended on behalf of his people.

road.hint: A ship that folds into a pocket was made by dwarves.

options.label: Have him grind the rust and nicks out of your gear
options.outcome: Thrar clicks his tongue at every pit and freckle of rust, then takes them out on the wheel one by one, with a lot of opinions. "Rust is just metal that's stopped caring," he says. "The wheel reminds it."
options.chronicle: A journeyman dwarf named Thrar ground the rust out of my gear on his wheel and lectured me the whole time. Worth it.

options.label: "Just browsing, thanks."
options.outcome: He shrugs and goes back to his wheel without ceremony. The whine of it follows you down the corridor long after he disappears from sight.

name: Old Veska
text: An elderly woman rummages through a pile of broken weapons with the methodical joy of someone with a lifelong hobby. She holds up a snapped sword hilt to the light with genuine admiration. "Fine craftsmanship, even ruined." She notices you. "Ah! You've got equipment that still works. Interesting."

options.label: Trade gold for her oddments
options.outcome: She rummages through her bag and produces a trinket that looks like scrap but hums faintly at the correct frequency. "Found that one near a collapsed shrine. Something still lives in it." She seems delighted by your uncertainty.
options.chronicle: Traded with an old woman who loves broken weapons. She looked at mine with professional pity.

road.hint: Broken things still tell you how well they were made.

options.label: Let her examine your weapon, and guess its making

pass.outcome: She turns it to the light and you talk metal together: the famous Damascus blades were forged from wootz, a steel made in crucibles in India, and the watered pattern on them was the steel's own grain, folded into the blade. "You know your steel," she says, approving, and shows you the blade's sweet spot: the place a hit lands best. "You're the latest chapter. Try to be a good one."
pass.chronicle: An old woman who collects broken weapons showed me my blade's sweet spot. We talked about Damascus steel, made from Indian wootz.

fail.outcome: "Hammered from a horseshoe?" She sniffs. "Hardly. The best old blades were Damascus, forged from wootz, crucible steel from India, and the watered pattern was the steel's own grain." She hands it back. "You're the latest chapter. Try to be a good one."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong about my own weapon. An old collector told me about Damascus steel.

road.hint: Broken things still tell you how well they were made.

options.label: Decline and keep moving
options.outcome: "Sensible," she says, already turning back to her pile. "Most things worth finding are worth finding by accident anyway."

name: Apprentice Runescribe
text: A teenager in oversized apprentice robes is carefully inscribing runes onto the dungeon floor and muttering to herself. She looks up with the startled expression of someone who forgot monsters also use this hallway. "Oh! Oh good, you look human. My master says a ward needs Tyr's rune, and I've got the whole futhark here but I can't remember which one is his. Do you know?"

options.label: Help her find Tyr's rune

pass.outcome: You point to the arrow, the T-rune, Tiwaz. "Of course," she breathes. The futhark is named for its first six letters, f-u-th-a-r-k, the way alphabet is named for alpha and beta, and the old poem tells a warrior to carve victory runes on his sword hilt and name Tyr twice. She inks the arrow twice onto a scroll and gives it to you. "Yours. You found it."
pass.chronicle: Showed an apprentice runescribe Tyr's rune, the arrow. The old poem says to carve it on a sword hilt and name Tyr twice.

fail.outcome: You point at the wrong one, and she copies it with total confidence, and it does nothing at all. Later she finds it herself: the arrow, Tiwaz, Tyr's rune, the one the old poem says to carve on a sword hilt. "It's the arrow," she calls after you, a little smug.
fail.chronicle: Showed an apprentice the wrong rune. Tyr's is the arrow.

road.hint: A rune half drawn is a rune half dangerous.

options.label: Buy one of her scrolls
options.outcome: A fair exchange. She drives a harder bargain than her age suggests, but the scroll she produces is clearly from a higher-level compendium than anything she should have access to. You decide not to ask how she got it.

options.label: "I don't know runes. Good luck."
options.outcome: "Right. Okay. I'll figure it out." She turns back to her work with the particular determination of a woman who has been underestimated her whole life and has stopped minding.

name: Thökk

tells: the white seams of old stitches
a salmon tail in her pot
laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp

text: In a cave mouth sits an old giantess in rags by a cookfire, with a salmon tail sticking out of her pot. Outside, everything is weeping: water runs down the stones in sheets, and a tired young god with a messenger's staff is waiting at the cave mouth. "Hermod," he says. "Ask her. She'll not weep for my brother." The old woman laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp. Her lips have the white seams of old stitches. "Thökk will weep dry tears," she says. "Let Hel keep what she has." She holds out a red-gold ring to you. "And you'll say nothing."

options.label: Take her ring and say nothing
options.outcome: She closes your fingers round it. Outside, Hermod waits a long time, and then goes home alone.
options.chronicle: Took a ring from an old giantess who would not weep for a dead god, and said nothing. His brother went home alone.

road.hint: A gift for silence is payment for something.

options.label: Refuse her ring, look hard at her mouth, and tell Hermod what you see

pass.outcome: "Those are Brokk's stitches," you say. "The dwarf who sewed Loki's mouth." Hermod's face goes very still. The old woman laughs one last time and is not there: a fly goes out of the cave, very fast. Baldr will stay in Hel. But now the gods know who kept him there, and Loki will answer for it with a long binding.
pass.chronicle: Recognised the stitches on an old giantess's mouth and told Hermod. She turned into a fly. Baldr stays dead. Now they know who to blame.

fail.outcome: You know you have seen those scars somewhere, and you cannot say where. Hermod thanks you anyway and goes home with nothing but the knowledge that one creature in the world would not weep.
fail.chronicle: Refused a ring from an old woman who would not weep for Baldr. I knew her face from somewhere. I still cannot place it.

road.hint: The only creature that would not weep had a reason not to.

options.label: Weep for Baldr yourself
options.outcome: You do. It is not hard; everything around you is weeping. It changes nothing. "Dry tears," says Thökk, pleased.
options.chronicle: Wept for a god called Baldr because the whole world was weeping for him. It was easy, and it did not help.

road.hint: Every voice in the world but one is still not every voice.

options.label: Walk on

name: Aristodemus
text: A Spartan in a red cloak gone brown sits polishing a bronze shield that is already polished. "Aristodemus. You'll have heard. Sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler. Nobody speaks to me. Nobody gives me fire." He tests the spear-point with his thumb. "There's a horde below. I mean to die in front of it so well they'll have to stop calling me that. Tell me I'm right."

text_variants.text: A Spartan in a red cloak gone brown sits polishing a bronze shield that is already polished. "Aristodemus. You'll have heard. Sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler. Nobody speaks to me. Nobody gives me fire." He tests the spear-point with his thumb. "There's a horde below. I mean to die in front of it so well they'll have to stop calling me that. Tell me I'm right." He frowns. 'A Legion boy came through here telling my story to himself. Got the ending wrong, I hope.'

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair he stops. 'You walk like someone who means to go home,' he says. 'I'd forgotten that was allowed.' He goes back up, toward the light.
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked a floor with the Trembler. At the stair he said I walked like someone who meant to go home, and went home himself.

on_fail.chronicle: The Trembler fell beside me on the stair, facing the right way. Nobody can call him that now. I wish he had not had to prove it.

options.label: "Live. Dying well won't change what they call you."
options.outcome: He looks at you as if you'd slapped him, and then, slowly, as if you hadn't.

delayed.text: A bronze vault door on the stair has been forced and wedged open with a Spartan spear. The hoarder inside will not be needing his things.

options.chronicle: Told the Trembler to live. He did not like it. A few floors down I found a vault door wedged open with a Spartan spear.

road.hint: A man told to live may still find a use for his spear.

options.label: "Go and die well."
options.outcome: He stands, and the cloak hangs right on him for the first time.

delayed.text: A low doorway on the stair has a bronze shield wedged across it, face out, polished, with a spear-point broken off in the rim. Behind it, a caravan's children are asleep in a heap of blankets, unharmed. Of the Spartan there is no sign.

options.chronicle: Told the Trembler to go and die well. A few floors down I found his shield wedged across a doorway with children asleep behind it.

road.hint: A shield is a door for the people behind it.

options.label: "Walk a floor with me first, and decide on the way."
options.outcome: "A floor," he says. "One."

road.hint: A floor walked beside someone can change which way he goes next.

options.label: Call him what they call him
options.outcome: "Trembler," you say. He nods as if you had told him the time, and goes back to his shield.
options.chronicle: Called a Spartan the Trembler to his face. He just nodded. I think he has heard it from better people than me.

road.hint: A name thrown at a man who already carries it only adds weight.

name: Doctor Finch
text: A figure in a long black coat and a beaked mask stands in a doorway, clipboard in hand. "Ah. A living one." His voice is nasal and clinical through the mask. "I've been cataloguing the afflictions down here. You look relatively intact, remarkable, given the level. Any symptoms I should note? Bleeding, visions, involuntary cursing?"

options.label: Let him examine you, and talk shop

pass.outcome: He prods and pokes, and you talk while he works: his beak is stuffed with herbs because his teachers believed plague rode on bad air, miasma, and that a sweet smell kept it off. "Wrong, of course," he says cheerfully. "A London doctor named Snow mapped the cholera dead in Soho, found nearly every one had drunk from one pump, and had its handle taken off. Germs in the water, not bad air." Pleased with you, he treats you for nothing.
pass.chronicle: Talked shop with Doctor Finch while he treated me. His beak is stuffed with herbs against bad air. He knows it does nothing.

fail.outcome: You tell him the herbs in his beak must be what keeps him well. "Miasma," he sighs. "Bad air. That is what my teachers believed, and my teachers were wrong: a doctor named Snow traced the cholera to one water pump." He makes a note on his clipboard. "My fee stands, if you want treating."
fail.chronicle: Told Doctor Finch his herbs kept the plague off. He corrected me. Germs, not air.

road.hint: A doctor who catalogues the dead wants a living one for once.

options.label: Buy a curative compound
options.outcome: He produces a small vial from a rack of identical vials and labels it in tiny, precise handwriting. "Take with water. Do not take with alcohol. Do not take with other potions unless you understand what you're doing, which you probably don't." Charming bedside manner.

options.label: Have the Doctor treat what ails you
options.outcome: "Fascinating. Disgusting, but fascinating." The Doctor works through you symptom by symptom with tongs, tinctures and a running commentary. Whatever you had, you no longer have it. You suspect it is now in a jar.
options.chronicle: Paid the beaked Doctor to cure me. He kept a sample. I did not ask of what.

road.hint: A doctor of plagues knows a cure for most of them.

options.label: "I'm fine. Good day, Doctor."
options.outcome: "You are demonstrably not fine," he says, and makes a note on his clipboard anyway. You find this oddly comforting.

name: Morrow
text: A man in a stolen priest's cassock waits on the stair with two friends in locust masks. Morrow spreads his hands, smiling. "You freed me. I've brought friends to say thank you."

text_variants.text: A man in a stolen priest's cassock waits on the stair with two friends in locust masks. Morrow spreads his hands, smiling. "You freed me. I've brought friends to say thank you." 'The old man told you I'd be back, didn't he? He always did ruin a surprise.'

options.label: Fight
options.outcome: They come at you on the stair. Morrow fights in the cassock to the end, which tells you something about him.
options.chronicle: The cultist I freed came back with friends to thank me. We settled it on the stairs. The robe did not suit him.

road.hint: Mercy to the wrong man is repaid on a stair, with interest.

options.label: Remind him you saved his life
options.outcome: "You did," Morrow says. "That's why I'm letting you go first."
options.chronicle: Told the cultist I freed that he owed me his life. He agreed, and attacked me anyway. Gratitude is not a cult virtue.

road.hint: A debt owed by a liar is not a debt.

name: Calla Strand
text: A battle-scarred woman sits with her back to the wall, methodically oiling a short sword she clearly does not intend to use again tonight. There are too many fresh bandages on her arms. "You've got that look," she says without glancing up. "Like you're still believing this was a good idea."

options.label: Ask her how she beat the gnoll pack

pass.outcome: "You know your history, then." Gnolls hunt like hyenas: they circle, and pull down the one who runs. So you don't run. Back to a wall, points out, shields together, the way the Scots stood in their schiltrons at Bannockburn and the English horse could not break them. "A beast won't run onto a hedge of points," she says. "Neither will a man. Stand." She drills you in it until it is in your feet.
pass.chronicle: Calla Strand taught me to stand against a pack: back to a wall, points out, the way the Scots stood at Bannockburn.

fail.outcome: "Charge them first?" you suggest. She laughs, and it hurts her ribs. "That's how you lose a pack fight. They circle and pull down whoever breaks. You stand, back to a wall, points out. The Scots did it at Bannockburn, in rings of spears."
fail.chronicle: Calla Strand told me never to charge a pack. Stand, back to a wall, points out.

road.hint: A pack pulls down whoever runs.

options.label: Ask her for a sparring lesson (costs SP)
options.outcome: She raises an eyebrow but nods. She spends an hour drilling you in proper defensive stances and controlled breathing under pressure.
options.chronicle: Sparred with a retired pit fighter named Calla Strand. She hit me in the same rib three times to make a point. Point taken.

road.hint: A fighter who has stopped counting has started living.

options.label: Buy her spare shield
options.outcome: She looks at the shield for a long moment, then hands it over. "I won't need two. I'm not sure I'll need one." She takes the coin without counting it.

options.label: "Just passing through."
options.outcome: "Sure you are," she says, with the tone of someone who has heard that line from people who didn't make it. She goes back to oiling her sword. You go back to believing.

name: Exposed Child
stance_note: Steel-man: Hrolf's relativism is given its strongest form (your people burn witches; every people judges by its own law; exposure as mercy in a famine). The pass text keys the reformer's dilemma (§3.10). No option rewards "whatever a hall approves is right".

authority.why: Sets a lame newborn out on the stone to die.

text: Outside a longhouse built into the rock, a newborn lies wrapped in a fleece on a cold stone, crying thinly. Her foot is twisted. The chief stands over her with his arms folded. "Hrolf Ketilsson. A hard winter, and a lame mouth. In our hall this is right." He meets your eye. "Your people burn witches and call that right. Mine leave a weak child to the gods; it's kinder than a winter of starving. Every people judges by its own law. Who are you to judge mine?"

options.label: Argue with him

pass.outcome: You ask him about the first chief of his people who ever made the law kinder: was that man wrong, because the hall had not yet approved? And the first one who refused to set a child on the stone? If his hall is always right, no hall can ever become better than it was, only different. Hrolf is quiet a long time. Then his wife comes out and picks up the baby, and he does not stop her.
pass.chronicle: Asked a hall-chief whether the first of his people to make the law kinder had been wrong. He had no answer. His wife picked up the baby.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "Hrolf's wife brought the little one to us for the winter, where the hall can't change its mind. She feeds like a wolf cub. We named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. Hrolf's wife brought the girl from the stone to them for the winter. She is feeding. They named her Astrid.

fail.outcome: He has an answer for everything you say. So you pick the baby up yourself, fleece and all, and carry her to the Brothers' house on the side stair, and he lets you, because by his law she is nobody's now.
fail.chronicle: Lost an argument with a hall-chief about leaving babies on stones, so I took the baby. By his law she belonged to nobody. By mine she did.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "The girl you carried in is feeding. Her mother comes at night, when the hall is asleep. We named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. The girl I carried in from the stone is feeding, and her mother comes at night. They named her Astrid.

road.hint: Every custom you would defend was once somebody's new idea.

options.label: Buy the child for the price of her winter's keep
options.outcome: He takes the money and does not argue. Then his wife comes out of the longhouse and lifts the baby off the stone, because the coin is her winter's bread now, and she goes back in without a word to either of you. The custom stands. The next one will be on the stone too.
options.chronicle: Paid a hall-chief the price of a winter's bread for a baby he was leaving on a stone. His wife took her back inside. The next baby will be on the stone too.

road.hint: Buying one child off a custom keeps the custom open for business.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit from the house on the side stair catches you up. "Hrolf's wife brought her girl to us to be blessed, the one your gold bought back. She is feeding. We named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother from the side stair found me. The girl my gold bought off the stone is feeding. The Brothers named her Astrid.

options.label: Walk on. His hall, his law
options.outcome: The crying follows you a long way down the corridor. Then it doesn't.
options.chronicle: Walked past a baby on a stone because it was their custom. The crying stopped before I reached the stair.

road.hint: Their law, their hall, and a crying that stopped.

name: Scholar Evaine
text: A woman in ink-stained robes sits cross-legged in the middle of the corridor, surrounded by open tomes and hasty notes. She doesn't look up when you approach. "Fascinating: the marble here was cut at least four centuries before the outer chambers, and the plinth in the next hall is the size of the one in the Parthenon. Oh. You're a person. Hello."

options.label: Ask what a plinth that size once held

pass.outcome: "The Athena Parthenos," you say, and she finally looks up. Phidias's goddess: wood inside, ivory for the skin, gold for the robes, nearly twelve metres tall, with a winged Victory in her hand and the head of Medusa on her breast. "And the gold was made to come off," Evaine says, delighted, "so when they accused Phidias of stealing it, they could weigh it." She reads you the inscription on the plinth, which tells you which way the goddess faced, and so which way the halls run.
pass.chronicle: Scholar Evaine and I worked out that a plinth here held a goddess like Phidias's Athena, gold that came off to be weighed.

fail.outcome: "A king?" you guess. "A goddess," she says, already writing again. "Like Phidias's Athena in the Parthenon: ivory and gold, twelve metres high, Medusa's head on her breast. The gold came off so it could be weighed when they accused him of theft."
fail.chronicle: Heard from Scholar Evaine that Phidias's Athena wore gold that came off to be weighed.

road.hint: The goddess's gold was made to come off.

options.label: Buy a scroll from her notes
options.outcome: She tears a page from a secondary notebook with minimal hesitation. "Copied that one twice anyway." The transcription is meticulous, the ink still faintly warm from her pen.

options.label: "I'll leave you to your research."
options.outcome: "Mm. Wise choice, I'm nearly at a breakthrough." She's already forgotten you, her quill scratching furiously at a new page.

name: Gyges
text: A shepherd sits at the lip of a chasm, turning a gold ring on his finger. Each time he turns it he flickers out and back. Far below in the chasm, a bronze horse lies on its side with its belly open. "It was on a dead giant's hand, down there," he says. "Since I put it on I've taken a purse, a goat, and a girl's silver comb, and nobody saw." He pulls it off and holds it out. "Take it, or put it back on him. I can't do either." His hand keeps going to the empty finger.

options.label: Take the ring and keep it
options.outcome: He lets it go with a sound like a sob and a laugh at once. "Better you than me," he says, and then, already doubtful: "Is it?"
options.chronicle: Was given the Ring of Gyges by a shepherd who could not stop using it. He said better me than him. Then he asked whether it was.

road.hint: A ring that hides you from everyone hides you from yourself first.

options.label: Climb down and put it back on the dead giant's hand
options.outcome: The climb is long and the bronze is cold. The giant's hand is the size of a cart. You push the ring back on, and for a moment you are very tempted to turn it once, just to see. You don't. Up top, the shepherd is crying with relief.
options.chronicle: Climbed down a chasm to put the Ring of Gyges back on a dead giant's finger. I was tempted to turn it once, just to see. I did not.

road.hint: The hardest thing to put back is the thing that makes you unseen.

options.label: Promise to hold it for him until he's ready
options.warning: His hand keeps going to the empty finger.
options.outcome: He thanks you and sits beside you while you check your pack. Nobody sees anything at all. When you look up, the ring is gone, and so is a share of your purse, and so is he.
options.chronicle: Offered to keep a magic ring safe for a shepherd until he was ready to give it up. I looked away for a moment and nobody saw anything. My purse is lighter.

road.hint: A man cannot lend you the thing he cannot let go of.

options.label: Walk on

name: Boundary Stone
text: A boundary stone on a moor of grey moss, with six holes bored in it and filled with vinegar. Coins lie in the vinegar. Beyond it a village has shut itself in against the plague, on its rector's word. A man in the doorway of the nearest cottage calls to you. "I'm well. I swear before God I'm well. My children are at Low Middleton, a few stairs down. Lift the bar." He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm, and his face shines with sweat while he shivers.

options.label: Lift the bar and let him go
options.warning: He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm
options.outcome: He shakes your hand hard, both of his around yours, and goes for the stair at a run.

delayed.text: At the foot of the stair a bell is tolling in Low Middleton. It tolls every hour you are on this floor.

options.chronicle: Let a man out of a plague village because he swore he was well. He shook my hand with both of his. A bell has been tolling ever since.

road.hint: A buttoned collar in a warm cave is hiding something.

options.label: Look at him properly before you lift anything

pass.outcome: You ask him to open his collar, and he knows why, and he does it anyway. A swelling the size of a pigeon's egg under his jaw, hot to the touch, and his skin is burning with fever though he shivers. He sits down on his side of the stone and cries. You sit down on yours. You stay until his lamp burns low, and promise to leave word at the stone for his children. He writes a letter for Low Middleton and drops it in the vinegar, and you fish it out and leave it under the stone where the carriers look.
pass.chronicle: Saw the plague swelling under a man's jaw before I let him out. We sat either side of the boundary stone a long while. I left his letter under it for the carriers.

fail.outcome: You look, and see a frightened man with his collar done up.
fail.chronicle: Looked at a man from a plague village and saw only a frightened father. I lifted the bar. I have regretted few things more.

road.hint: Before you open a sealed gate, ask why it was sealed.

options.label: Leave coins in the vinegar for their supplies
options.outcome: The coins sink into the vinegar. When the watch changes, the village will find them and buy bread with them, and the baker will wash them twice. Hawksworth watches you from the doorway, and does not ask again.
options.chronicle: Left coins in the vinegar at a plague village's boundary stone. They will buy bread with them, and wash them first.

road.hint: Some help is best passed over a boundary, not through it.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Please," he says, once, and then nothing.

name: Brother Osias
text: A monk with a shaved head and eyes closed in meditation sits absolutely still in the corridor, hands folded in his lap. He speaks without opening his eyes. "You carry exhaustion like a second pack. I can ease it, but concentration requires an anchor, something to focus the breath."

options.label: Ask him whose way he follows

pass.outcome: "Antony's," he says, opening one eye, pleased you guessed. Antony walked out into the Egyptian desert alone and shut himself in an old tomb, and the demons came at him at night in the shapes of lions and serpents and wolves, and he did not run; he lived to a hundred and five. Osias teaches you his breathing. Your mind clears, and whatever comes at you in the dark looks smaller.
pass.chronicle: Brother Osias taught me Antony's way: the demons came at him in the desert in the shapes of beasts, and he did not run.

fail.outcome: "A good guess, but no." The Desert Fathers, he says, and Antony first: alone in an Egyptian tomb, with demons in the shapes of beasts, and he did not run. He guides you through a little of the breathing anyway.
fail.chronicle: Brother Osias told me about Antony in the desert, who did not run from the demons.

road.hint: A quiet mind carries further than a full pack.

options.label: Offer food to support his vigil
options.outcome: He opens his eyes for the first time and accepts the food with a slight bow. "Sustaining the body sustains the spirit." He shares a brief blessing that warms your muscles from the inside, like a long-forgotten memory of sunshine.

options.label: Pass quietly without disturbing him
options.outcome: He does not acknowledge your passage. But as you round the bend, you could swear the silence behind you is a fraction more peaceful than the silence ahead.

name: Courteous Giant
text: A giant sits at a table far too long for the room it is in, and the room does not seem to mind. "Nobody stays in my hall who cannot do one thing well," he says pleasantly. "We keep it modest. Empty my drinking horn. Lift my cat off the floor. Or wrestle my old nurse, Elli, if you can wake her." The horn is long, the cat is grey and very large, and the nurse is asleep by the fire.

options.label: Take the horn and drink

pass.outcome: You drink until your eyes water and the level drops the width of a finger. The giant goes rather pale. "The far end of that horn lies in the sea. You have lowered it. People will call that the tide."
pass.chronicle: Drank from a giant's horn in Utgard and lowered the sea a little.

fail.outcome: You drink and drink and the horn stays full. "Thor did no better," says the giant kindly, "and he was a god."
fail.chronicle: Lost a drinking contest to a horn. In my defence, the far end was in the sea.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Get both arms under the cat and lift

pass.outcome: One grey paw leaves the ground. "That cat is the serpent that circles the world. Nobody was supposed to move it at all."
pass.chronicle: Lifted one paw of a giant's cat. It was not a cat.

fail.outcome: The cat arches and does not leave the floor. It yawns at you.
fail.chronicle: Failed to lift a giant's cat. It yawned. It was, I learned later, a world serpent, which helps a little.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Wake the old nurse and wrestle her

pass.outcome: She puts you down on one knee, gently, like a parcel. "Elli is Old Age. Nobody beats her. Most do not last as long as you did."
pass.chronicle: Wrestled an old woman named Elli and lost. Everyone does. I lasted longer than most.

fail.outcome: She puts you down at once. "Elli is Old Age," says the giant. "You'll meet her again."
fail.chronicle: Wrestled Old Age and lost very quickly. I am told everyone does in the end.

road.hint: In a giant's hall, the contest is never quite what it looks like.

options.label: Decline his contests
options.outcome: "Then you cannot stay," says the giant, pleasantly. "But you may certainly go." The door is a long way off, and the grey cat watches you all the way to it.
options.chronicle: Turned down a giant's three contests in his hall of tricks. He let me go. His cat watched me all the way to the door.

road.hint: A contest you decline cannot fool you.

name: Hymir's Boat

tells: ate two of my oxen at supper

text: On a black lake under the ice a frost giant with icicles in his beard sits in a rowing boat, and beside him a broad young man with a red beard is baiting a hook the size of an anchor with the head of an ox. "Hymir," says the giant sourly. "This lad ate two of my oxen at supper, and now he wants to row out past the place I fish. Past it is where the Serpent lies." The young man grins at you. There is a short-handled hammer in his belt. "Room for one more. Hold the line with me?"

options.label: Hold the line with him

pass.outcome: The line goes taut, and the lake heaves, and a head as big as a hall comes up out of the black water with the ox's head in its jaws: the Serpent that circles the world. You hold. The young man braces so hard that his feet go through the bottom of the boat and stand on the bed of the lake. Then Hymir, white with terror, saws the line through, and the Serpent sinks. "Every time," says the red-bearded man, and flings Hymir over the side. You know him now: Thor, who fished for Jormungandr with an ox's head and was robbed of it by a frightened giant. He claps you on the shoulder, which hurts.
pass.chronicle: Held the line with a red-bearded young man while he fished up the World Serpent with an ox's head. Hymir cut it. It was Thor.

fail.outcome: The line goes taut and the lake heaves, and the rope tears through your hands and you let go. Something enormous rolls under the boat. Hymir saws the line through before the young man can stop him, and the red-bearded lad looks at you with real disappointment. Later you remember the story: Thor fishing for the World Serpent with an ox's head, and a giant who cut the line.
fail.chronicle: Lost my grip on a fishing line with something enormous on the end. The giant cut it. I think I know now who was holding the other end.

road.hint: A red-bearded lad with an ox's head for bait is fishing for something big.

options.label: Help Hymir cut the line
options.outcome: You and Hymir saw at the rope together, and it parts, and something vast sinks away under the boat. The giant is so grateful he gives you a flask from his stores. The red-bearded young man says nothing at all, which is somehow worse than shouting.
options.chronicle: Helped a frightened giant cut a fishing line. The young man with him said nothing. I would rather he had shouted.

options.label: Stay on the shore
options.outcome: You stay on the ice. Far out on the lake the boat rocks, and something enormous breaks the surface and goes down again, and a little later a very wet frost giant swims ashore, swearing.

name: The Hermit
text: Huddled against a wall in a chamber that smells of old smoke and dried herbs, a figure wrapped in layers of mismatched cloth watches you with sharp, intelligent eyes. A row of small sealed vials hangs from his belt, each with a scrap of red thread. "I've lived down here twelve years," he says softly. "I've followed the gorgon-kind a long way, and collected what they leave. You look like someone who could use a secret."

options.label: Ask what a gorgon's blood is good for

pass.outcome: "Ah. You've read Apollodorus." Athena gave the healer Asclepius the gorgon's blood: from the veins of the left side, death; from the right side, life enough to raise the dead, until Zeus struck him down for it. The hermit unhooks a vial with a red thread. "Right side," he says. "I'm careful about sides."
pass.chronicle: A hermit who follows the gorgons gave me a drop of blood from the right side. The left side kills. The right side heals.

fail.outcome: "Poison?" you guess. "Half right," he says. "Left side, death. Right side, healing, enough to raise the dead. Asclepius had both from Athena, and Zeus killed him for using the good half too well." He keeps his vials.
fail.chronicle: A hermit told me a gorgon's blood kills from one side and heals from the other.

road.hint: A gorgon's blood depends on which side it came from.

options.label: Share a meal together
options.outcome: You sit together in comfortable silence, sharing food like two people who have long since run out of small talk. When you rise to leave, you feel more settled than you have in days. Sometimes stillness is its own kind of strength.
options.chronicle: Shared a meal with a hermit who has lived down here twelve years. He knew the floor's moods.

road.hint: Twelve years in the dark teaches the dark's moods.

options.label: Buy one of his vials
options.outcome: He unhooks a vial with a scrap of red thread and holds it up to the light before he hands it over. "Right side," he says. "I'm careful about sides."

options.label: "I prefer my own counsel."
options.outcome: He nods slowly, with no offense taken. "That's how I started too," he says. You're not entirely sure what he means by that.

name: The Head of Mimir
text: Under a root as thick as a tower, in a cave rimed white, black water fills a stone basin, and just below its surface floats a man's head with its eyes open, its beard spread like weed. Sprigs of dried herbs are knotted in the beard. At the very bottom, very small, something white catches the light, round as a coin, looking up. The head speaks without bubbles. "Mimir. The Vanir cut my head off and the All-Father kept it, with herbs and spells, to talk to. I keep the well. Wisdom costs. Everyone asks how much."

text_variants.text: Under a root as thick as a tower, in a cave rimed white, black water fills a stone basin, and just below its surface floats a man's head with its eyes open, its beard spread like weed. Sprigs of dried herbs are knotted in the beard. At the very bottom, very small, something white catches the light, round as a coin, looking up. The head speaks without bubbles. "Mimir. The Vanir cut my head off and the All-Father kept it, with herbs and spells, to talk to. I keep the well. Wisdom costs. Everyone asks how much." The head smiles. "He sent you. He always sends the clever ones. Tell him the eye is keeping well."

options.label: Drink, and pay what it costs

pass.outcome: The water is so cold it hurts your teeth, and then your head, and then it doesn't hurt at all, and for a moment you understand something very large. It goes. Some of it stays.
pass.chronicle: Drank from Mimir's well. It cost me something. I understood the whole world for a moment and then most of it left. Some of it is still here.

fail.outcome: The water runs through your mind like a sieve. Mimir keeps the price. "Everyone asks how much," he says. "Nobody asks how much he can hold."
fail.chronicle: Drank from Mimir's well, and paid, and it ran through me like a sieve.

road.hint: Wisdom from a well is paid for before you drink, not after.

options.label: "What's that at the bottom?"

pass.outcome: "You know whose," says Mimir, and his eyes narrow with respect. An eye: Odin's. The All-Father paid it for one drink from this well, and hung nine nights on the windy tree for the runes besides. "He thought it cheap. He's usually right about prices. And he walks about in a grey cloak and a broad hat pulled over the empty socket, if you ever want to thank him."
pass.chronicle: Knew the white thing at the bottom of Mimir's well for Odin's eye. Mimir told me the All-Father walks about in a grey cloak and a broad hat.

fail.outcome: "A pearl?" you guess. "An eye," says Mimir. "A god paid it for one drink. He thought it cheap."

road.hint: Something at the bottom of the well is looking up.

options.label: Leave the well
options.outcome: "Come back when you can afford me," says the head, and closes its eyes.

name: Sword in the Anvil
text: A churchyard under the rock, a great stone with an anvil on it, and gold letters: WHOSO PULLETH OUT THIS SWORD OF THIS STONE AND ANVIL IS RIGHTWISE KING BORN. The anvil is empty. A big young knight holds the sword aloft. "Sir Kay. I drew it." Behind him a skinny squire stares at his own hands. The squire's hands are red from the hilt; Kay's are clean. Kay leans close. "Say you saw me draw it. Tell my father so, and you'll eat at my table all your days."

options.label: Back Kay's claim
options.outcome: Sir Ector looks at Kay, and at you, and at the skinny boy. "Is it so?" You say it is. The boy says nothing, because nobody has ever asked him anything.
options.chronicle: Swore to Sir Ector that Kay drew the sword from the anvil. It was the skinny squire. I am to eat at Kay's table all my days.

road.hint: A false witness is paid at the table and charged at the gate.

options.label: Tell Sir Ector what you saw
options.outcome: Ector goes very quiet. Then he kneels, an old man in a churchyard, to the boy he raised. Kay goes red, then white, and then, give him his due, kneels too.
options.chronicle: Turned down a knight's table for life to tell his father who really drew the sword. It was the squire. The old man knelt to him.

road.hint: The truth about who drew the sword is worth more than a seat at any table.

options.label: Put it back in the anvil and let them both try

pass.outcome: You remember how the old test went. Kay strains until his face is purple, and when he gives up he takes it out on your ribs. The squire draws it like a knife from butter, twice, looking more frightened each time. Sir Ector kneels.
pass.chronicle: Made Sir Kay put the sword back in the anvil and try again. He could not. His little brother could, twice. The old man knelt.

fail.outcome: Kay snatches it back before you can explain the test. "We're done here," he says, and you are.
fail.chronicle: Tried to set Kay and his squire the old test of the anvil, and Kay would not stand for it. At least I did not lie for him.

road.hint: A true sword can be put back and drawn again. A lie cannot.

options.label: Walk on
