options.outcome: "Good," says Kay. "Friend." Behind you, an old man's voice: "Kay? Who drew it?"

name: Damocles
text: A long table laid for a king under a crystal ceiling, and at its head a gold couch, and on the couch a courtier in a crown, very pale, not eating. "I said kings were lucky," he tells you, without moving his head. "I would like to take it back now." Above him, point down, on a single horsehair, hangs a sword. The horsehair runs up to a hook, and from the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door. A tired, clever man at the table's foot waves at you. "Dionysius. My friend Damocles envied kings. Take his place, if you like, and eat like one."

options.label: Cut the horsehair down and pull him clear
options.warning: from the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door.
options.outcome: The hair parts, the sword falls into the soup, and the bell above the door rings like the end of the world. Damocles is clear. The guards come through the door, and they are not interested in the lesson.
options.chronicle: Cut the horsehair over Damocles and pulled him clear. The cord rang a bell. The guards did not care about the lesson. Damocles hid under the table.

road.hint: A thread that holds a sword may hold a bell as well.

options.label: Tell Dionysius the lesson has been learned, and show him you know it too

pass.outcome: You tell him what the sword is for: so his guest feels what the king feels at every meal, which is the whole of the lesson, and Damocles has felt it for three courses. A tyrant who goes on teaching it after it is learned is only showing how much he enjoys the sword. Dionysius looks at you for a long moment, then laughs, and nods to Damocles. "Get up, then." Damocles gets up very carefully, and sits down on the floor, and cries.
pass.chronicle: Talked a tyrant into letting Damocles off his couch by telling him the lesson was already learned. Damocles sat on the floor and cried.

fail.outcome: You explain the lesson back to him, and get the point of it wrong, and Dionysius smiles in a way you do not like. "Then perhaps you should sit there and learn it."
fail.chronicle: Tried to explain the sword of Damocles to the tyrant who hung it. He sat me under it until I understood. I understand.

road.hint: The lesson of the sword is short. Only a tyrant keeps teaching it.

options.label: Take his place for an hour, and eat like a king

pass.outcome: Damocles gets up and nearly falls over thanking you. You eat like a king and never once stop watching the hair, and you get up before you can forget to.
pass.chronicle: Took Damocles's place under the sword and ate a king's dinner, watching the hair the whole time. I left before dessert.

fail.outcome: You relax. The hair doesn't. You throw yourself sideways as it falls and it opens your shoulder instead of your skull. Damocles is free, at least.
fail.chronicle: Took Damocles's place under the sword and forgot about it for one moment. My shoulder remembers it for me.

road.hint: The feast is the same. It is the sword that tells you what a crown costs.

options.label: Leave him there
options.outcome: Dionysius shrugs. "He'll be there at breakfast." Damocles does not look away from the hair.
options.chronicle: Left Damocles on his couch under the sword. The king said he would still be there at breakfast. I believe him.

name: The Witch-Finder

authority.why: A rigged test, and twenty shillings a witch.

text: A mill pond, a crowd with pitchforks, and a woman tied thumb to toe on the bank. A man in a tall black hat reads from a paper. "Matthew Hopkins. At Manningtree a witch killed a child with a look and nobody did anything. I did something." He nods at the woman. "If she sinks she's innocent. If she floats, God's water has refused her." He mentions, as a man mentions the weather, that the town pays him twenty shillings a witch. The crowd behind him has pitchforks and is very large. Alys looks at you. "I set their bones," she says. "That's all."

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Hopkins does not look up from his paper. Behind you the crowd begins to count, slowly, and somewhere past twelve it goes quiet.
options.chronicle: Walked away from a witch-finder's ducking. Behind me the crowd counted, and then went quiet. I did not turn round.

road.hint: A crowd that has made up its mind does not need you to watch.

options.label: Cut her loose and run with her
options.outcome: You get her free and three steps up the bank before the crowd closes. You come out of it bloody, with Alys over your shoulder, and the whole village now sure of two witches instead of one. At the stair she slides down and runs. "I know the back ways. You'd only slow me."
options.chronicle: Cut an herbalist loose from the witch-finder's ducking and ran. The whole village came after us. Now they think there are two witches. They may be onto something.

road.hint: A crowd convinced by a trick is not unconvinced by a sword.

options.label: Take his test apart in front of the crowd, staking your own name

pass.outcome: You ask the miller what floats. Wood, he says. And ducks, says a boy. And a woman tied in a ball with air in her lungs, you say, any woman, and you offer to tie Hopkins the same way and see. Somebody laughs. Then a lot of people do. Hopkins leaves with his paper and his hat, quickly, and Alys gives you a kit of her cures with shaking hands.
pass.chronicle: Showed a crowd that anyone tied in a ball floats, and offered to swim the witch-finder to prove it. He left quickly. The herbalist gave me her cures.

fail.outcome: You get tangled in it, and Hopkins is quicker. "Mark how the witch's friend speaks for her," he says, and the crowd turns.
fail.chronicle: Tried to argue a witch-finder down in front of a crowd and lost them. They swam her. Then they came for me.

road.hint: A test that every innocent fails is not a test.

options.label: Pay Hopkins his fee to let her go
options.warning: the town pays him twenty shillings a witch.
options.outcome: He takes your gold with a little bow and cuts her bonds himself. "The Lord is merciful, and so am I, for a consideration." Alys runs.

delayed.text: A broadsheet nailed to a stair-post: WITCH-FINDER GENERAL SWIMS TWO AT HOLLOWAY MILL. FEES AS USUAL.

options.chronicle: Paid a witch-finder his fee to let an herbalist go. He bowed and let her go. A few floors on, I read he had swum two more the next week.

road.hint: Pay a man for a kindness and he will sell the next one too.

name: The Moth Woman
text: A woman stands perfectly still in the center of the room, arms slightly extended, skin dusted with iridescent powder that catches the torchlight like wings. Her eyes are entirely silver. "You are drawn here the way all things are drawn to light," she says. "Let me look at you. I will tell you what I see."

options.label: Let her read you (costs mana)
options.outcome: She circles you slowly, trailing a finger through the air near your face, reading something invisible. When she stops, she presses one dusty fingertip to your temple. "There. I have opened a window." The world snaps into sharper focus, colors brighter, distances clearer. You perceive more than you did before.
options.chronicle: Let a woman with silver eyes read me. She knew things. I did not ask how.

road.hint: Things drawn to a flame are not always moths.

options.label: Ask why her kind circles a lamp

pass.outcome: "Because the sky is up," you say, and the silver eyes widen. A moth flies by keeping its back to the brightest thing it sees, and for as long as there have been moths the brightest thing was the sky. A lamp below the sky tilts its whole world, so it circles, and circles, correcting forever. "Yes," she says softly. "We are not drawn. We are lost." She touches your temple with a dusty fingertip and the world snaps into focus.
pass.chronicle: Told the Moth Woman why her kind circles a lamp: a moth keeps its back to the sky, and a lamp below the sky tilts its world.

fail.outcome: "Because they love the light?" She laughs, a dry dusty sound, and unfolds herself, and the light off her wings is too bright to look at. When you can see again she says: "We keep our backs to the sky. A lamp tilts the sky. We are not drawn. We are lost."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong about moths and lamps. The Moth Woman dazzled me, and then told me: a moth keeps its back to the sky.

road.hint: A moth at a lamp is not drawn but lost.

options.label: Back away from her
options.outcome: She does not follow. She watches you retreat with those silver eyes and does not blink once. Around the corner, you check your reflection in your blade. Your own eyes look briefly, impossibly, silver. Then they don't.

name: The Shade
text: Something that might be a shadow, but isn't, peels itself from the wall. It has the rough shape of a person and the approximate manners of one. "I collect things that people don't know they're carrying," it says, in a voice that seems to come from slightly behind where it's standing. "Are you interested in a transaction?"

options.label: Offer stamina for invisibility
options.outcome: It reaches forward and takes something from you that you cannot name, a weight you hadn't noticed until its absence. In exchange, it drapes something else over you: a quality of unseeing, of negative presence. For a time, the dungeon will look through you.
options.chronicle: Traded some of my stamina to a shadow for a little invisibility. It said I would not miss it. I miss it.

road.hint: A shadow collects what you did not know you were carrying.

options.label: Ask what it needs to speak plainly

pass.outcome: "Blood," you say, and it goes very still. In the Odyssey the dead flocked to the trench Odysseus filled with blood, and only those who drank could speak truly; he held them back with his sword until the prophet Tiresias had drunk. You let it drink a few drops from a nick in your arm. It speaks plainly then, and tells you where every living thing on this floor is lying in wait.
pass.chronicle: Let a shade drink a little of my blood, as the dead drank from Odysseus's trench. It spoke plainly and told me where everything on the floor was waiting.

fail.outcome: "Gold?" It murmurs something that sounds like a voice through a wall, and you cannot make out the words. Only blood gives the dead a voice; Odysseus knew it, and filled a trench for them.
fail.chronicle: A shade tried to tell me something. Without blood the dead only murmur.

road.hint: The dead speak plainly only after they drink.

options.label: Refuse and walk away
options.outcome: "As you wish." It does not move to stop you. It simply returns to the wall, and the wall accepts it without argument. You do not look back, but you are certain, completely certain, that nothing follows you.

name: Watch Sergeant
text: Four soldiers of the City Watch hold a barricade of overturned tables, a long way below any city. The sergeant has the look of a woman who was told to wait for orders and waited. "We were promised a courier," she says. "Iron scroll case, Watch seal. Without it we don't know which gate to fall back on, and nor do the companies above."

options.label: Hand over Edric's dispatch
options.outcome: She breaks the seal, reads it once, and starts giving orders before she has finished reading. Two runners go up the stairs at a sprint. "He didn't make it, then," she says. You tell her he made it almost all the way. She writes that down. Somewhere far overhead, a city has a better night than it was going to have.
options.chronicle: Delivered Edric's dispatch to Sergeant Holt. I told her he made it almost all the way. She wrote it down in the Watch book.

road.hint: A message carried the whole way is worth more than the man who carried it.

options.label: Ask how the siege stands
options.outcome: "Badly, last we heard, and the last we heard was a long time ago." She looks at the stair. "If you've seen a courier, or a scroll case with our seal, it's worth more to us than to you."

options.label: Leave food for the post
options.outcome: The soldiers share it out to the crumb, by rank and then by hunger. The sergeant gives you a proper salute. Nobody has given you one in a while.
options.chronicle: Left food at a Watch post that has been waiting weeks for orders. The sergeant saluted me. It was a good salute.

road.hint: Soldiers waiting for orders eat like anyone else.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Courier'll come," says one of the soldiers. Nobody answers him.
options.chronicle: Walked past a Watch post that is still waiting for its courier. I had his case in my pack.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Courier'll come," says one of the soldiers. Nobody answers him.
options.chronicle: Walked past a Watch post that is still waiting for its courier.

name: The Brass Warden
text: An enormous construct of tarnished brass blocks the corridor, its chest glowing with banked furnace light. Etched on its torso: NONE SHALL PASS WITHOUT PROVING WORTH. A slot in its palm holds a counting board. "CHALLENGER," it says, in a voice like a bell in a cellar. "THE EXCHANGE REQUIRES PROOF OF ARITHMETIC. STAKE A QUARTER OF YOUR PURSE. LOSE, AND IT IS FORFEIT TO THE GUILD. WIN, AND THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." The Guild has not existed for four hundred years.

options.label: Answer the Warden's sums, staking a quarter of your purse

pass.outcome: The furnace in its chest flares white. "WORTH PROVEN. THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." A drawer slides out of its belly with a cog in it, warm and heavy and perfectly cut. Then, quietly, almost in a different voice: "IS THE GUILD STILL THERE?"
pass.chronicle: Out-counted the Brass Warden. It paid me in a cog, then asked whether its guild still existed. I said I did not know. I did know.

fail.outcome: It counts your coins into its chest without comment, one by one, and steps aside anyway. "THE GUILD THANKS YOU FOR YOUR CUSTOM."
fail.chronicle: Lost a quarter of my purse to a brass guard counting for a guild that died four hundred years ago. It thanked me for my custom.

road.hint: A guard that counts never forgets the sum.

options.label: Tell it the Guild is gone
options.outcome: It is still for a long time. "THEN WHO DO I GUARD FOR?" it asks. You have no answer. It steps aside. The furnace in its chest is a little dimmer as you pass.
options.chronicle: Told the Brass Warden its guild died four hundred years ago. It asked who it guards for now. I did not have an answer. It let me pass.

road.hint: Some guards are kinder left unknowing.

options.label: Walk past by another way

name: Brothers of the Deep Watch
text: Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your neck before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" The reliquary is warm against your chest.

options.label: Lay the reliquary in the niche
options.outcome: The brothers kneel. The niche takes the reliquary as if it had been cut for it, which it was. "Iona to here," the eldest says. "A brother and a sister, and then one stranger." He blesses you slowly and thoroughly, like a man paying a debt in full.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Columba's relic in the chapel it was meant for. I carried it all the way down. Letting it go was harder than I expected.

road.hint: A thing carried to the end weighs nothing once it is set down.

options.label: "I lost him on the way."
options.outcome: The eldest closes his eyes. "Then he is somewhere on the stair," he says, "and the stair is ours to search." He gives you no blessing and no reproach, and goes back to his watch.
options.chronicle: Reached the chapel of the Deep Watch without Saint Columba. I had lost him on the way down. The brothers did not reproach me. The niche is still empty.

road.hint: A thing carried for others is still owed when it is lost.

options.label: Keep the reliquary
options.outcome: The brothers say nothing. The eldest looks at the empty niche, then at you, and turns his face to the wall to pray. The reliquary stays warm. It does not feel like the same warmth.
options.chronicle: Reached the chapel with Saint Columba on me and kept him there. The brothers did not argue. That was worse.

road.hint: A promise broken at the very door is the most expensive kind.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing
options.outcome: He gives it, and asks nothing. If there is a saint in your keeping, he is too polite to mention it.
options.chronicle: Asked the brothers of the Deep Watch for a blessing and did not mention what I was carrying. They were too polite to.

road.hint: A blessing asked for under false pretences still has to be lived up to.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The brothers watch you to the stair. The eldest is still looking at the empty niche.

text_variants.text: Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your empty hands before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" You have nothing to lay in it.

Three brothers in mail under their habits keep a chapel at the head of a black stair, spears leaning by the door. Over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your pack before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks. Then he sees the answer. "Did Saint Columba come down?" The reliquary is warm through your pack.

name: Last Bearer
text: A monk sits against a long oak box, his feet bound in rags. "Seven of us carried him out of Lindisfarne when the longships came," he says. "Seven years on the road. I am the one left, and I cannot manage the stairs." He takes a small red book from his habit. "This lay in the coffin with him. There is a chapel below where the brothers wait. The saint can rest here. The book should not."

options.label: Take the book and give your word

oath.what: Lay Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the reading desk of the chapel below.

options.outcome: He puts it in your hands as if it weighed more than the coffin. "It is John's Gospel. Small enough for a pocket. People will offer you money for it on the way down. They always do." He closes his eyes, relieved of the last thing he was carrying.

thread.hint: A reading desk below is still empty.

options.chronicle: A monk of Lindisfarne trusted me with Saint Cuthbert's Gospel. I gave my word to carry it down.

road.hint: A book small enough for a pocket can still be too heavy to sell.

options.label: Share a meal with him, but refuse the errand
options.outcome: He blesses the food and then you, in that order. "No shame in knowing your load," he says. "Somebody will come." He does not sound sure.
options.chronicle: Shared a meal with the last of Saint Cuthbert's bearers, and would not carry his book. He said there was no shame in it.

options.label: Wish him well and go on
options.outcome: He nods and tucks the book back inside his habit, next to his heart, where it has been for seven years.

name: "Legitimate" Merchant
text: A goblin in an oversized merchant's coat has set up a stall using two skeletons as display racks. His wares are labeled in large, confident handwriting: "DEFINITELY NOT CURSED RING," "POTION (PROBABLY GOOD)," and "HAT (BELONGED TO SOMEONE ELSE, NOW YOURS)." "Welcome to Grix's Emporium of Totally Fine Items!" he announces. "Everything one hundred percent legal!"

options.label: Buy the ring at the honest price
options.outcome: Grix sells it to you at what it is worth, which pains him visibly. "Customer reads too well," he mutters. "Bad for business. Good for customer."
options.chronicle: Read a goblin's ring before I paid for it, and Grix sold it to me at what it was worth.

options.label: Buy the "Definitely Not Cursed" item
options.outcome: Grix takes your gold with suspicious speed. The item turns out to be... fine, actually. Genuinely fine. You inspect it carefully for curses and find none. Grix watches your confusion with poorly concealed amusement. "Is being honest about dishonesty," he says philosophically, "still dishonest?"
options.chronicle: Bought a ring labelled DEFINITELY NOT CURSED. I am choosing to trust the label.

road.hint: A label that protests too much is a label.

options.label: Buy the Probably Good Potion
options.outcome: "Excellent choice," Grix says. "I tasted it myself. Three times. The last two times were to check." The potion sloshes with something enthusiastic. You pocket it, fairly confident that "probably good" is better odds than most things in this dungeon.

options.label: Inspect the ring before you pay

pass.outcome: You turn the ring in the light, read the maker's mark, feel for the cold that a curse leaves in metal, and find none. It is a perfectly ordinary ring, priced as a treasure. "Caveat emptor," you tell him: let the buyer beware, the oldest rule of any market. Grix sighs and names a real price.

fail.outcome: You squint at it and can't tell a thing. Grix watches you squint with deep contentment. Caveat emptor, the old Romans said: let the buyer beware. It is your eye or his price.

road.hint: Let the buyer beware.

options.label: "I don't trust you."
options.outcome: Grix puts a hand to his chest, wounded. "Nobody trusts Grix," he says sadly. "And yet Grix is here. Every day. With his mostly fine items. For the ungrateful." He resumes polishing a skull with his sleeve as you leave.

text_variants.text: A goblin in an oversized merchant's coat has set up a stall using two skeletons as display racks. His wares are labeled in large, confident handwriting: "DEFINITELY NOT CURSED RING," "POTION (PROBABLY GOOD)," and "HAT (BELONGED TO SOMEONE ELSE, NOW YOURS)." "Welcome to Grix's Emporium of Totally Fine Items!" he announces. "Everything one hundred percent legal!" Then he squints at you. "Cousin Brix wrote about you. Hard customer. Grix is warned."

name: Grieving Cyclops
text: The corridor widens dramatically to accommodate a giant sitting with its knees pulled to its chest, weeping from one great eye into enormous hands. The tears pool on the floor and small silver sea-fish swim in them, fish that should not exist here. "She said she'd come back," the giant says, without looking up. "The sea-girl. Galatea. I sang to her. I'd have given her my sheep."

options.label: Sit with it in silence (spend SP)
options.outcome: You sit on the floor beside it, in the shallow water of its grief, and say nothing. It cries for a while longer, then grows quiet. "You're still here," it says, surprised. "Most things run." It looks at you with enormous, wet eyes and breathes out something that feels like peace, and some of that peace settles into you like a cool wind.
options.chronicle: Sat with a weeping giant in a pool of his own tears. There were fish in it. I did not ask.

road.hint: Some grief makes a lake, and things live in it.

options.label: Give it something from your pack (food)
options.outcome: You offer the food upward like a small, absurd gift. The giant stares at it, then at you, then cups it in one hand and eats it with enormous, careful delicacy. "Thank you," it says. "She would have done that." It tucks one of the glowing fish into your pocket, gently. The fish dissolves into protective light.

options.label: Tell him why she will not come back

pass.outcome: You tell him what Ovid tells: Galatea loved a shepherd boy named Acis, and Polyphemus caught them together and crushed Acis under a piece of the mountain, and Galatea turned her lover's blood into a river, running to the sea. The giant goes very still. "I did that," he says at last. "I forgot that I did that." He gets up, slowly, and rolls aside the boulder that has blocked a side cave for longer than the dungeon has stood. "Take what's in there. I want to sit by the water."
pass.chronicle: Told a weeping Cyclops why Galatea will not come back: he crushed Acis, and she made her lover a river. He opened a cave for me.

fail.outcome: You tell him she may come back yet. He nods, and cries harder, because he knows better. In Ovid the Cyclops crushed her lover Acis under a rock, and Galatea turned Acis into a river. A thing like that, a sea-nymph does not forgive.
fail.chronicle: Told a weeping Cyclops his sea-nymph might come back. She will not. He killed the boy she loved.

road.hint: A one-eyed giant crushed the boy the sea-nymph loved.

options.label: Carefully wade past
options.outcome: You pick your way through the shallow tears, the small glowing fish parting around your boots. The giant doesn't notice, or doesn't mind. You carry the image of it for the rest of the level, all that grief, in the dark, with no one left to witness it.

name: Echo
text: A girl stands at the end of the corridor, thin as mist, so faint at the edges that the wall shows through. When you say "Hello?" she says "Hello?" When you ask who she is, she says "Who she is." She cannot say anything of her own; she can only give back the last of your words. She holds something out in one hand, and looks at you as if everything depends on what you say next.

options.label: Say something she can answer with

pass.outcome: You know her: Echo, whom Hera cursed for talking too much, so that she could only repeat; who loved Narcissus and faded for him until only her voice was left. So you ask the way Narcissus did in Ovid, "Is anyone here?", and she answers, glowing, "Here!" You say "Come to me," and she says "Come to me!" and comes, and puts what she was holding in your hand, and is gone, and is happy.
pass.chronicle: Met Echo, who can only repeat. I asked as Narcissus did, so that her echo was an answer. She gave me something and was glad.

fail.outcome: You ask her name. "Her name," she says sadly. You ask what she wants. "She wants." She fades into the wall. Later you remember Echo, cursed by Hera to repeat the last of others' words, and how in Ovid one boy's "Is anyone here?" let her answer "Here!"
fail.chronicle: Met a girl who could only repeat my last words. I never found the question she could answer.

road.hint: A girl who can only repeat needs a question she can answer with.

options.label: Echo her back
options.outcome: You repeat her repeating you, softly. She tilts her head, and for a moment the two of you are only voices in the stone. When it passes, you are a little harder to see, as if part of you went into the wall with her.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: "Slowly," she says, as you go. "Slowly."

name: The Thinking Mushroom
text: You nearly step on it before you realize it's thinking. The mushroom, enormous, bioluminescent, pulsing gently with green light, projects words directly into your mind in a calm, measured voice. "I have been considering the nature of courage for forty-three years," it tells you. "You appear to be practicing it. I find this interesting. Shall we discuss the matter?"

options.label: Engage in philosophical debate (spend SP)

pass.outcome: You sit. You argue. You put Aristotle's case: courage is a mean, standing between two vices, cowardice that fears too much and rashness that fears too little, and the brave man fears the right things, at the right time, for the right reason. The mushroom pushes back for three hours, patient and precise, and concedes one point. When you stand, your mind feels sharper, more precise, more dangerous to itself.
pass.chronicle: Argued about courage with a mushroom that has been thinking about it for forty-three years. It conceded one point.

fail.outcome: You argue that courage means fearing nothing. "Then a man who leaps into a fire for no reason is the bravest of all," the mushroom says gently. "Aristotle would call that rashness, the vice on the far side of courage from cowardice. The brave man fears what is worth fearing." You have no answer.
fail.chronicle: Argued with a mushroom that courage means fearing nothing. It said Aristotle would call that rashness. I had no answer.

road.hint: Forty-three years of thought is still open to a good argument.

options.label: Ask it about the dungeon
options.outcome: "The dungeon is a question," it says. "The answer is whoever survives it."

options.label: Nod politely and keep moving
options.outcome: "Understandable," the mushroom projects, without resentment. "Courage without reflection is still courage. I wish you well." The green glow fades behind you as you walk on, and you find yourself slightly regretting the conversation you didn't have.

name: Two Mothers
text: Two women stand in the mud of a mining camp, each with a hand on the same baby. "He's mine," says one, and cries. "He's mine," says the other, and cries louder. The camp's men stand back with their arms folded, looking at you, because you carry a weapon and they don't want this. One of the women never once looks at the baby. She looks at you.

options.label: Give him to the one who weeps loudest
options.warning: One of the women never once looks at the baby. She looks at you.
options.outcome: The loud one takes him and stops crying at once, which you notice too late. The other woman sits down in the mud and does not get up.
options.chronicle: Gave a baby to whichever mother cried loudest. She stopped crying the moment she had him. The other one sat down in the mud.

road.hint: One of them never looked at the baby.

options.label: Call for a sword and offer to divide him

pass.outcome: "Cut him in two, then. Half each." One woman says, "Fair. Divide him." The other screams, "No, give him to her, only let him live." You hand the baby to the one who screamed. Somewhere above, they say, a tribunal of the old king still sits in stone, waiting for the next case like this one.
pass.chronicle: Settled whose baby it was by offering to cut him in half. The right one screamed. I did not enjoy the minute before she did.

fail.outcome: You draw the sword, and the whole camp shouts, and in the noise you can't tell which cry was which. The men take the baby away to "decide among themselves".
fail.chronicle: Tried the old trick with the sword and lost my nerve and my answer at once. The camp took the baby away to decide. They will get it wrong.

road.hint: A sword in the room changes what people say.

options.label: Leave it to the camp
options.outcome: The men argue for an hour and give him to the one with the louder friends.
options.chronicle: Left two mothers and one baby to a mining camp's justice. They gave him to the woman with the louder friends.

road.hint: A camp with no judge has a crowd instead.

name: Weeping Mason
text: A translucent figure kneels beside a crumbling wall, pressing ghostly hands against the stone as if trying to repair it. He doesn't notice you at first. "Forty years," he murmurs. "Forty years and the mortar still won't hold." He built this section of the dungeon in life and cannot leave until it's perfect.

options.label: Help him find peace (offer mana)
options.outcome: You channel a little magic into the ancient stones. They glow briefly, warm and gold. The mason stares at his repaired section with trembling hands, then slowly dissolves into the air, weeping with relief. As he goes, he wraps something protective around you, the pride of a craftsman, made into a ward.
options.chronicle: Helped a ghost mason find peace after forty years of mortar that would not hold.

road.hint: Forty years of mortar is a long apology.

options.label: Tell him what his mortar is missing

pass.outcome: "Ash," you say. "Volcanic ash." He stops. The Romans mixed their lime with ash from the hills at Pozzuoli, and their harbour walls have stood in the sea for two thousand years. The cinders here are the same stuff. He mixes, sets the last stone, and steps back, and the wall holds. "Forty years," he says, and smiles, and is gone. Where his wall meets the old one, a sealed door has come unstuck.
pass.chronicle: Told a mason's ghost to mix volcanic ash into his lime, as the Romans did. His wall held, and he could rest.

fail.outcome: "More water?" He shakes his head. "Forty years." Long after, you think of the Roman harbours: lime mixed with volcanic ash from Pozzuoli, standing in the sea two thousand years. The cinders here would have done it.
fail.chronicle: Could not help a mason's ghost finish his wall. Roman mortar used volcanic ash. I thought of it too late.

road.hint: The Romans' harbour mortar had ash in it.

options.label: Leave him to his grief
options.outcome: You walk past quietly. Behind you, the sound of his murmuring fades, "forty years, forty years", until the dungeon swallows it whole.

name: Relic Broker
text: A neat little man has set up a folding table of bones, each labelled in a confident hand. He looks you over once, and his eyes stop at your pack. "If you should happen to be carrying something old and small and red," he says, "the brothers below would give you a blessing for it. I will give you a heavy purse for it. Blessings don't buy bread."

options.label: Sell him the red book
options.outcome: He wraps it in silk with genuine love. "A wise choice," he says. "Saints don't eat."
options.chronicle: Sold Saint Cuthbert's Gospel to a relic broker for a heavy purse. The monk who gave it to me said people would offer. He was right.

road.hint: Every relic carried down will be priced by someone on the way.

options.label: Tell him the book is promised
options.outcome: "Everything is promised to somebody," he says pleasantly, and lets you go.
options.chronicle: Told a relic broker the red book was promised. He said everything is. Not this.

road.hint: A promise refused for a price is a promise twice made.

options.label: Buy one of his vials instead

name: The Bone Diviner
text: A woman sits behind a low table bearing dozens of small bones, each carved with symbols, and the cinders show through her as if she were smoke. She doesn't look up when you approach. "Shang oracle bones," she says. "I read them for a king three thousand years ago, and I have not stopped. I ask a question, I touch the bone with hot metal, the crack gives the answer. You want to know something? The bones charge their own price."

options.label: Ask where this floor keeps its secrets

pass.outcome: You know how it is done, and she hears it in your question. The diviners of Shang pressed hot metal into pits drilled in ox shoulder-blades and turtle shells, read the cracks, and carved the question and the answer onto the bone: the oldest Chinese writing anyone has found. She cracks a bone for you. The crack runs like a map, and she reads you the floor from it, room by room.
pass.chronicle: A diviner's ghost cracked an oracle bone and read me the whole floor from it. Her bones carry the oldest Chinese writing there is.

fail.outcome: She cracks a bone and reads it, but your question was the wrong shape and so is the answer. "Turtle shell and ox bone," she says, "hot metal, and the question carved on the bone with its answer. That is how my king asked. Ask like a king next time."
fail.chronicle: Asked a diviner's ghost a question the wrong way. The oracle bones only answer a question asked properly.

road.hint: The oldest Chinese writing was carved on bones that answered questions.

options.label: Pay the bones' price for a long reading (130 gold)
options.outcome: She takes your coin, heats an old dark bone, and reads its cracks aloud for a long time: where each danger on this floor is waiting, and which of them is waiting for you. You feel, for the rest of the floor, as if someone is reading over your shoulder.

options.label: Ask about danger ahead (pay MP)
options.outcome: She heats a different bone, older, darker. The crack branches twice. "Two dangers. One you can see, one beneath it. Don't fight the visible one first." The smoke from the bone curls into your eyes, and for a while you see the dungeon with the particular clarity of having been warned properly.

options.label: Leave the bones unasked
options.outcome: She finally looks up as you turn to go. "The bones don't mind," she says. "They've been patient for three thousand years."

name: The Lost Soldier
text: A soldier in armour two centuries out of fashion stands at attention in the middle of the corridor, facing a direction that is neither toward nor away from anything. His breath does not fog, though yours does, and the frost on his shoulders has not melted in a long time. "Halt," he says, without heat. "These halls are under the protection of King Edric the Fourth." He searches your face. "You don't know that name. How long have I been standing here?"

options.label: Tell him the truth gently
options.outcome: You tell him, as carefully as you can, that King Edric the Fourth died two hundred years ago, that his kingdom has a different name now, that the war he was guarding against ended long before his grandchildren were born. He is quiet for a long time. "Then I have kept my post well," he finally says. He salutes you with tremendous dignity and walks away into the dark.
options.chronicle: Told a soldier two centuries out of date that the war is over. He thanked me and kept standing guard.

road.hint: A soldier who never got the order to stand down is still on duty.

options.label: Pay him the soldier's tribute
options.outcome: You press coins into his gauntleted hand, the gesture of an officer paying a soldier's due. He straightens further, somehow. "King's blessing upon you, traveler." He draws a symbol in the air, and you feel it settle around you like plate armor that weighs nothing.

options.label: Relieve him of his post, properly

pass.outcome: You know a soldier like this will not stand down on a stranger's word. A Japanese officer, Onoda, held his post in a Philippine jungle for twenty-nine years after his war ended, and came out only when his old commanding officer flew there to relieve him in person. So you do it the old way: name his post, his king, his orders, and give the order to stand down. He salutes. "At last," he says, and lays his shield at your feet, and is gone.
pass.chronicle: Relieved a dead soldier of his post the proper way, as an old officer once relieved Onoda in the jungle. He left me his shield.

fail.outcome: You tell him the war is over. He nods politely and does not move: orders come from officers, not strangers. Onoda held his post in the jungle for twenty-nine years after his war, until his own old commander came to relieve him in person.
fail.chronicle: Told a dead soldier his war was over. He did not believe a stranger. He is still standing there.

road.hint: A soldier stands down for an order, not a rumour.

options.label: Walk around him quietly
options.outcome: He doesn't stop you. He seems to have already returned to whatever internal world he occupies between visitors. You glance back from the corner. He is still there, still at attention, still facing nothing.

name: Cartographer Issek
text: A compact, intensely focused woman is pinning hand-drawn maps to the wall using a knife she does not look up from. "Don't talk to me for thirty seconds," she says. Twenty-nine seconds later, she exhales and turns. "Right. Issek. I map the deep floors. I have information. You look like you have things I could use."

options.label: Trade food for her maps
options.outcome: She takes the food without ceremony and eats it standing up, already rolling a map cylinder for you. "The next few floors, approximate. Key features marked. Monsters marked where I survived long enough to mark them." The map's knowledge settles into your spatial memory like a gift.

options.label: Buy her composite survey (250 gold)
options.outcome: "The premium edition," she says without irony, and produces a map annotated by six different people with six different opinions about which rooms were dangerous. The synthesis of all six floods your mind.

options.label: Help her reconcile her six surveys

pass.outcome: Six surveyors, six maps, six opinions. You sort them by their bearings: two were taken with a compass that read north wrong near the iron in these rocks, so you correct their bearings against the one surveyor who measured stair to stair between fixed points, and the rooms snap together. Issek stares, then pins the finished survey up and gives you the first fair copy.
pass.chronicle: Helped a cartographer named Issek reconcile six surveys. Two had a compass thrown off by iron in the rock. She gave me the first fair copy.

fail.outcome: You try, and the rooms will not close. Issek finds it herself in the end: two surveyors' compasses were thrown off by the iron in these rocks, and every bearing they took is a few degrees out. "A compass lies near iron," she says. "Write that down."
fail.chronicle: Could not reconcile a cartographer's surveys. A compass lies near iron.

road.hint: A compass lies near iron.

options.label: "I prefer to discover things myself."
options.outcome: She shrugs with the equanimity of someone who has heard this before. "Most of the 'discover things myself' types don't make it back to update my maps." She turns back to her wall and pulls out another pin. "Good luck, though. I mean that."

name: Ormond's Granary
text: A stone granary with a barred door, scratched deep on the inside. Nobody answers when you knock. Nobody has answered for a while. The bar inside has rotted through; the door would give to a shoulder.

text_variants.text: A stone granary with a barred door, and on the step Corporal Pell, his tabard filthy now and his sword nicked, grinning like an idiot. Behind him the door is open and a grey sergeant is counting men: eleven, and Pell. "He came back," says Sergeant Ormond, as if he still can't believe it. "Stood in the door and told us he'd run, first thing, before anyone could ask. Then he showed us the way out."

options.label: Shake Pell's hand
options.outcome: "Trembler," Pell says, "that's what they called him, that Spartan. Right?" He's still grinning. "Not me. Not any more."
options.chronicle: Found Pell at the granary with eleven living men behind him. He went back. They are calling him something better than Trembler now.

road.hint: A man who came back is more use than a man who never ran.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Pell waves you on with his nicked sword, still grinning.

options.label: Open the door
options.outcome: It gives to your shoulder, and the rotten bar with it. Inside, a journal on a sack of grain, in a sergeant's square hand. The last line: "Day nine. No runner. I hope Pell got out." You find the pencil beside it and write under it: He did.
options.chronicle: Opened a granary that had waited nine days for a runner. The sergeant's last line hoped Pell got out. I wrote under it that he did.

road.hint: The runner you send away is the runner someone else was waiting for.

options.label: Leave it barred
options.outcome: You leave the door as it is, rotten bar and all.
options.chronicle: Did not open the granary door. Some doors answer questions I did not want to ask.

name: Star Merchant
text: A small, delicate figure sits behind a fold-out table displaying glass bottles, each one containing a swirling cluster of light, constellations, captured and miniaturized. "Genuine Ursae Majoris, never used," the figure says in a voice like wind chimes. "The Pleiades, slightly incomplete. And this one, I don't know what it is. It followed me home."

options.label: Buy the unknown constellation
options.outcome: The moment the bottle leaves the merchant's hands, it uncorks itself. Light pours out and coalesces into something solid, a wand of starlight, pulsing with a frequency that matches no known school of magic. The merchant watches it go with what might be relief.
options.chronicle: Bought a constellation in a bottle. I have not opened it. I do not know what it would do.

road.hint: A sky in a bottle is still a sky.

options.label: Ask for the true Pleiades

pass.outcome: You pass over the bottle with seven bright points and pick the one with six, a little hazy, blue-white. The merchant chimes with pleasure. The Seven Sisters, a young cluster of hot blue stars some four hundred and forty light-years off, and most eyes count six of them; the Greeks said one sister hid herself. "An honest eye gets an honest price," it says, and the bottle uncorks itself into a wand of starlight.
pass.chronicle: Chose the true Pleiades from a star merchant's bottles: six stars, not seven, as most eyes see them. It sold me a wand of starlight at an honest price.

fail.outcome: You pick the bottle with seven bright stars. "Ah," says the merchant gently. "That is a forgery. The Seven Sisters show six to most eyes; the Greeks said one hides herself." It puts the false one under the table.
fail.chronicle: Picked a forged Pleiades with seven stars. Most eyes only ever see six.

road.hint: The Seven Sisters show six to most eyes.

options.label: Just browse. Move on.
options.outcome: "No pressure," the merchant says warmly. "The stars have waited this long." One of the bottles glows a little brighter as you walk away, as if wishing you luck.

name: Charon
text: A black river runs where no river should, and a flat ferry waits at a stone step, and an old man with an oar looks you up and down. "The girl you paid for," he says. "Melitta. She asked me to carry you once, free, when you came to deep water." He spits in the river. "I don't do free. I'm doing it."

options.label: Step aboard
options.outcome: The crossing is very quiet. On the far side he pushes off without a word, and then, from the middle of the river: "She says thank you. She's fine. She's better than fine."
options.chronicle: Charon ferried me across a black river for free because a drowned girl asked him to. He says she is better than fine.

road.hint: A coin paid for a stranger's crossing can buy back your own.

options.label: Decline
options.outcome: "Suit yourself," he says. "She'll be disappointed. They hate that, the dead."

name: The Cataloguing Spirit
text: A spectral figure is affixing tiny labels to the dungeon walls, to sconces, to cracks in stone, to a confused rat that sits very still under the attention. The labels read things like: "WALL (LOAD-BEARING)", "TORCH SCONCE, EMPTY, CIRCA UNKNOWN", "RAT (ALIVE, CURRENTLY)." "Oh!" the spirit says, producing a quill. "Adventurer! Encountered! Are you available to be catalogued?"

options.label: Help it label things properly

pass.outcome: You fix three of its labels and it nearly weeps with joy. "RAT (ALIVE, CURRENTLY)" becomes Rattus rattus, genus capitalised, species not, both in italics, the way Linnaeus wrote every living thing's name: two words, the kind and then the sort. He named himself Homo sapiens, wise man. The spirit lends you its eye for names, and for a while everything you pick up tells you what it is.
pass.chronicle: Helped the Cataloguing Spirit label a rat the way Linnaeus would: Rattus rattus. It lent me its eye for names.

fail.outcome: You write RAT (BLACK) and it shudders. "Rattus rattus," it corrects, "genus capitalised, species not. Linnaeus gave everything two names, the kind and then the sort. Even himself: Homo sapiens." It labels you UNHELPFUL, kindly.
fail.chronicle: The Cataloguing Spirit taught me how Linnaeus named things: two words, the kind and then the sort.

road.hint: Every living thing has two names: the kind, then the sort.

options.label: Bribe it for information
options.outcome: It takes your gold, labels it immediately ("COIN, GOLD, PROVENANCE: ADVENTURER, WARM"), and then shares its catalogued knowledge of the surrounding floors with you, a comprehensive mental map that gives you brief but useful foresight about what lies ahead.

options.label: "I don't want to be catalogued."
options.outcome: "Noted!" it says, writing furiously. You leave. Behind you, you can hear the faint sound of labeling continuing. Somewhere on these walls there is now a small sign that reads: "ADVENTURER, UNCATALOGUED, UNCOOPERATIVE."

name: Antigone

authority.why: Creon forbids the burial of Antigone's brother on pain of death. An edict against the unwritten law of the dead binds no one: informing on her is betrayal, and burying him or walking on is never penalised.

text: A young woman is scraping dirt over a dead man with her bare hands, beside a broken gate. Her nails are torn. "My brother. Creon says the dogs can have him." She doesn't stop. "Creon's edict isn't older than the unwritten laws. Nothing he writes can make it right to leave my brother to the dogs." Down the road a captain's voice carries: "A city where every sister chooses which laws to keep is no city at all. He burned our houses. Leave him."

options.label: Help her finish the burial
options.outcome: You dig together until the body is under. She says the words. Then the captain's men are at the gate, and she does not hide. "Let him do it in daylight, in front of the whole city," she says. "If I hide, I'm agreeing with him. Go."
options.chronicle: Helped Antigone bury her brother against the captain's edict. When the soldiers came she would not hide. She said hiding would be agreeing with Creon.

road.hint: Refusing to hide makes the law do its work in daylight.

options.label: Go and speak for her to Creon

pass.outcome: You meet Creon on the road and put it to him: a law against burying the dead fights a law older than his city, and a ruler who wins that fight loses something worth more. He hears you out. He goes back to the gate himself, in time, and orders the burial finished with honours, and Antigone looks at him as if he were a stranger.
pass.chronicle: Talked King Creon round about burying a traitor. He went back in time. In the old story he was too late. I am glad of the difference.

fail.outcome: Creon hears you out, and is unmoved, and courteous about it. "The law is the city," he says, and walks on to the gate.
fail.chronicle: Argued with King Creon about the law of the dead. He was courteous and unmoved, and he walked on to the gate.

road.hint: A law against the dead is a quarrel with something older than the city.

options.label: Tell Creon's men where she is
options.outcome: The soldiers thank you. They do not look at you while they do it. They find her at the grave, finished, waiting.
options.chronicle: Reported Antigone to Creon's men for burying a traitor. It was the law. They did not look at me when they paid me.

road.hint: Gold for a sister at her brother's grave. Even the soldiers looked away.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you she goes on scraping at the dirt with her bare hands.

name: Lantern of Regret
text: A lantern hangs at chest height in the middle of an empty corridor, hanging from nothing. Inside it, instead of flame, burns a small golden person the size of your thumb, walking in tight circles and occasionally sitting down with its head in its hands. Everything it touches inside the glass has turned to gold. "Are you going to free me," it asks, muffled by glass, "or just stare like the others?"

options.label: Free it (pay HP, unknown consequence)
options.outcome: You break the glass with your palm, the cut is sharp and the tiny figure pours out like warm light, expanding as it goes until it's gone, dissolved into the air of the dungeon. "Thank you," says the air, softly, from everywhere at once. Something like gratitude settles around you, and the dungeon feels, briefly, like it is rooting for you.
options.chronicle: Freed a small regret from a lantern. It thanked me and walked off into the dark looking lighter.

road.hint: A regret set free is lighter for both of you.

options.label: Tell it how the first wish like it was undone

pass.outcome: You know what it is: a wish like the one Dionysus granted King Midas, that everything he touched turn to gold, until his bread and his wine turned to gold in his mouth. Midas was told to wash in the river Pactolus, and the gold went out of him into the river, and its sands have glittered ever since. You tip the lantern's water over the little figure, and the gold runs out of it in a glittering stream, and it goes up like warm light, laughing. A few flakes of gold are left in the bottom of the glass.
pass.chronicle: Freed a wish like Midas's from a lantern by washing the gold out of it, as Midas washed in the Pactolus. A few flakes stayed behind.

fail.outcome: "Wish harder?" It sighs. "I am a wish. That is the trouble." Later you remember Midas, who wished that all he touched turn to gold and nearly starved, and who was freed by washing in the river Pactolus.
fail.chronicle: Could not free a sad golden wish in a lantern. Midas was freed by water. I remembered too late.

road.hint: A golden wish was once washed away in a river.

options.label: Leave the lantern where it hangs
options.outcome: "Understandable," it says, without bitterness. "This is usually how it goes." It resumes its small, sad circles. The lantern grows fainter as you walk away, until you can no longer tell whether the darkness behind you is shadow or simply the absence of light.

name: Neferkaptah
text: A door of black stone that was never meant to open, and opens. Inside, the air smells of river mud and myrrh. A book lies open on a bier, and where its light falls, things name themselves: your own pack murmurs the true names of the things in it, and the bones of something you killed on the way down tell you, quite clearly, what they were. Two ghosts sit at a senet board beside it: a prince in a gold collar, and a woman whose hair is still wet. A small wet footprint leads from the bier to the wall and stops. "You've come for the Book of Thoth," says the prince, and sets out the pieces. "Setne came for it too, and he was a prince." The woman does not look at the board. She looks at you.

options.label: Listen to Ahwere
options.outcome: "I am Ahwere. That is Merib's footprint; he was six." She says it quietly, the way you say a thing you have said to yourself every night for three thousand years. "My husband read one page on the boat, and he understood the birds and the fishes, and he laughed. Then Merib leaned out to see the fishes he understood, and the river took him. I went in after my son. I did not come up." She looks at the book. "Neferkaptah tied it to his chest and walked in after us. He had it. He had it all the way to the bottom." She turns back to you. "It is a true book. Every word in it is true. It costs everyone you love. Please don't take it."
options.chronicle: A drowned woman named Ahwere told me what the Book of Thoth cost her. Her son was six. There is still one small wet footprint by the wall.

road.hint: A true book can still cost more than it is worth.

options.label: Play Neferkaptah at senet for the book, staking yourself

per_miss.text: Your feet go into the stone as if it were mud. It is cold, and it is the Nile.
You are in to the waist. Your legs are a long way away, in very cold water.
The stone closes round your throat.

pass.outcome: The last piece lands and Neferkaptah stares at the board as if it had cheated him. "So." He lifts the book off the bier and holds it out, and does not let go when you take it. "Then swear it, as Setne swore to me once. Read it, and bring it back. The gods will not leave you alone with it for long." Ahwere has turned her face to the wall, toward the footprint.

oath.what: Read the Book of Thoth once, then lay it on an altar so it can go home.

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a drowned woman is counting floors.

pass.chronicle: Beat a dead prince at senet for the Book of Thoth. He made me swear to bring it back once I had read it. His wife would not look at me.

fail.outcome: Neferkaptah sweeps the pieces into his hand. "Not you, then." You are waist-deep in the floor, and it lets you go only slowly, like a river letting go of a boot. The book stays on its bier.
fail.chronicle: Lost at senet to a dead prince with the Book of Thoth as the stake. The floor kept me to the waist for a while. The book stayed where it was.

road.hint: In a dead man's game the stake is always more than you put down.

0.outcome: The stone closes over your mouth. Then a wet hand takes yours and pulls, and you come up gasping on the floor above, a long way from the tomb. You will not find that black door again.
0.chronicle: Lost every round of senet for the Book of Thoth and went into the floor up to my mouth. Ahwere pulled me out. I woke higher up.

thread.closed_line: I never saw the tomb of Neferkaptah again. I think Ahwere made sure of it.

options.label: Leave the book, because she asked
options.outcome: You put your hands behind your back. Neferkaptah laughs, unbelieving, and then stops laughing. Ahwere gets up from the board for the first time in three thousand years and crosses to you, and puts her wet hand flat on your chest, over your heart, the way you would to feel whether someone was still alive. "Thank you," she says. "No one has ever left it." When you look back from the door, she is sitting by the small footprint on the wall, and for once she is not looking at the book.

person_status.last_line: No one has ever left it.

options.chronicle: Walked away from the Book of Thoth because a drowned mother asked me to. It is the best thing I have ever not owned.

road.hint: The greatest book in the world was guarded by a mother, and that was the true lock.

options.label: Leave the tomb
options.outcome: "Setne left too, the first time," says Neferkaptah, setting the pieces out again. Ahwere says nothing. The door closes behind you, and is a wall.
options.chronicle: Found the tomb of a prince who drowned for a book, and left. I did not decide anything. I just left.

road.hint: Leaving without choosing is still a kind of choosing.

name: Snerk Ledgerscale
text: A kobold in tiny spectacles sits at a desk made from a dragon's toenail, scratching in two ledgers at once. Beyond the arch something enormous breathes in its sleep, and gold shifts. "Snerk Ledgerscale, accountant to the Great Glaurveth. Shh." He taps the first ledger. "Her hoard." He taps the smaller one. "The villages she took it from. A coin at a time, back where it came from. Help me carry?" The second ledger has a third column, labelled, in tiny letters, ME.

options.label: Pick up a sack and help him carry
options.warning: The second ledger has a third column, labelled, in tiny letters, ME.
options.outcome: Halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. When you get up, Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, and you are holding the one marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening. You drop it and run.
options.chronicle: Helped a kobold carry gold out of a dragon's hoard without reading his books. He left me holding the sack. The dragon opened one eye.

road.hint: Always read the columns before you carry the sacks.

options.label: Audit his books first

pass.outcome: Two columns add up and the third doesn't. A third of every coin "returned" has gone into ME. You point at it. Snerk goes a deeper shade of green. "Handling fees," he says. You stare at him. He crosses the column out, coin by coin, and the villages get all of it.
pass.chronicle: Audited a dragon's accountant. He was robbing the dragon for the villages, and robbing the villages for himself. Now he is only doing the first one.

fail.outcome: The columns swim. "All in order," says Snerk, closing the books a little fast. You help him carry. Halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. When you get up, Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, and you are holding the one marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening. You drop it and run.
fail.chronicle: Tried to audit a kobold's books and could not find the trick. Found the dragon's tail instead.

road.hint: An honest cause can still hide a dishonest column.

options.label: Take a cut to keep quiet
options.outcome: Snerk opens a fourth column, labelled YOU. "Pleasure doing business."
options.chronicle: Took a cut from a kobold who was skimming a dragon who had robbed some villages. There is a column in his book with my name on it.

road.hint: There is always room for one more column.

options.label: Leave him to his sums
options.outcome: "Shh," he says, without looking up.

name: The Merry Wanderer
text: A man in grape-leaf garlands sits on a barrel of something that definitely wasn't here before, laughing at nothing, his eyes bright as wine held up to sunlight. The dungeon around him seems fractionally more joyful, even the torches burn warmer. "Excellent timing!" he announces. "I've been waiting for someone cheerless enough to need cheering. Sit down. Drink. It's fine. It's all fine, actually."

options.label: Share food and drink with him
options.outcome: The drink tastes like three different seasons happening at once. He watches you drink it with a smile of enormous satisfaction. "There. You see? The dungeon is still terrible but you are now full of warmth. These are not unrelated facts." Your body begins knitting itself together with strange, vinous enthusiasm.
options.chronicle: Drank with a laughing stranger in a garland of grape leaves. The torches burned warmer. I think I know who he was.

road.hint: A stranger whose barrel was not there before is no stranger.

options.label: Accept his toast (free, but risky)
options.outcome: He raises his cup to you and simply says "To surviving," with complete sincerity. You don't drink anything but somehow you feel better anyway. He seems unsurprised. "Some blessings," he says, "don't need your cooperation."

options.label: Ask him about the pirates who kidnapped him

pass.outcome: His laugh stops. "Who told you about that?" The old hymn tells it: Tyrrhenian pirates seized a young man in a purple cloak to sell him, and the ropes fell off him, and wine ran over the deck, and a vine grew up the mast, and he became a lion, and the pirates leapt overboard and came up as dolphins. All but the helmsman, who had said from the start: that is a god. "Clever," says Dionysus, and lifts his cup to you as the helmsman's heir.
pass.chronicle: Asked a merry wanderer about the pirates who tried to sell Dionysus. He stopped laughing, then raised his cup to me as to the helmsman who knew him.

fail.outcome: You ask about pirates and he looks blank, then delighted. "Pirates! I love pirates. They make such good dolphins." He does not explain.
fail.chronicle: Asked a merry wanderer about pirates. He said they make good dolphins.

road.hint: Pirates once seized a young man in purple and came up as dolphins.

options.label: "I don't drink with strangers."
options.outcome: He sighs the sigh of someone who has been hearing this since the world was young. "Every stranger," he says, "was a friend you hadn't met yet. And every friend was once a stranger you decided to trust anyway. But." He waves graciously. "Go. Be careful. Drink water at minimum."

name: Ysra Deepsong
text: You hear the music before you see her, a deep resonant hum that makes the walls vibrate. A dwarf with stone-grey skin and eyes like polished obsidian sits in a carved niche, singing into the rock and tapping it with a little iron bar, listening between notes. The stones seem to lean in to listen. She pauses when she sees you. "Ysra. A living one; it's been so long. My people sing to the stone and the stone sings back. Do you want to hear what it says?"

options.label: Ask for a song of strength
options.outcome: She sings in a frequency you feel in your bones rather than hear with your ears. The sound knits something inside you, not wounds exactly, but weariness, old damage, the slow erosion of the dungeon's weight. You walk away standing slightly straighter, your body quietly repairing itself.

options.label: Ask her what the stone sings back

pass.outcome: "You know already, I think." Sound runs through granite more than ten times faster than through air, and it rings true through sound rock and dull through rock that is cracked or hollow. Miners have always sounded a roof with a bar before they trusted it: a ring is safe, a drummy thud is loose. She taps, and listens, and teaches you to hear it, and for a while every hollow wall and hidden gap near you speaks up.
pass.chronicle: A dwarf named Ysra taught me to sound the rock: a ring is solid, a dull thud is hollow. For a while the walls told me their secrets.

fail.outcome: "Echoes?" She shakes her head. "It rings or it thuds. Solid rock rings, and hollow or cracked rock thuds; that is how a miner sounds a roof before he walks under it." She sings you a short song anyway, and you feel less tired.
fail.chronicle: A dwarf singer told me solid rock rings and hollow rock thuds. She sang me a song anyway.

road.hint: Solid rock rings; hollow rock thuds.

options.label: Keep moving
options.outcome: She doesn't call after you. But her song follows you down three corridors, fading so slowly you aren't sure when it stops.

name: Dream Weaver
text: The figure ahead of you is weaving something from threads of silver light that seem to come from nowhere. "Dreams," she explains before you ask. "They float down here when people sleep above. I collect them, make things. Would you like to trade one of yours? You won't miss it. Probably."

options.label: Trade a dream (pay MP)
options.outcome: She reaches into your mind with two fingers, the sensation is cold and not unpleasant, and extracts something shimmering. She holds it up to her eyes. "Oh, this is a good one. You dreamed of flying." She adds it to her loom and hands you a scroll woven from finished dream-thread. You don't feel the loss, but you notice later that you can't quite remember what flight felt like.
options.chronicle: Traded a dream to a woman who weaves them. I do not remember which one. That is probably the point.

road.hint: A dream given away leaves a gap shaped like it.

options.label: Commission a dream of strength
options.outcome: She weaves quickly, her fingers blurring, and presses the finished piece against your forehead. You experience three seconds of a dream: you are whole, healed, standing in sunlight. When you open your eyes, some of that wholeness has stayed behind in your body. She smiles. "I do good work."

options.label: Ask her which gate your dream came through

pass.outcome: "You know the gates?" she says, delighted. Penelope tells it in the Odyssey: dreams come to us through two gates, and those that pass through the gate of ivory deceive, and those that pass through the gate of polished horn come true. She holds your dream up to the light. "Horn," she says. "This one is true." It shows you, for a while, everything that waits near you in the dark.
pass.chronicle: A dream weaver held my dream up to the light: horn, not ivory, so it was a true one. It showed me what waited near me.

fail.outcome: "The front door?" She laughs. "Two gates, Penelope said: ivory for the dreams that lie, horn for the dreams that come true. Yours came through ivory, I'm afraid. Pretty, and no use at all."
fail.chronicle: A dream weaver told me my dream came through the gate of ivory, where the false ones come in.

road.hint: True dreams come through the gate of horn.

options.label: Keep your dreams to yourself
options.outcome: "Wise," she says, without irony. "Dreams are worth more than most people realize. Hold onto yours." She turns back to her loom, and the threads of light continue their slow, luminous dance.

name: Brother Sacristan
text: A side chapel, swept clean, with a lamp burning and an empty reading desk. A monk gets up from his knees so fast he knocks over the stool. "Is he coming? Is the saint coming down?" He sees your face and steadies himself. "No. Of course. The stairs. Did the bearers send anything at all?"

options.label: Lay the red book on the reading desk
options.outcome: He does not touch it at first. Then he opens it to the first line, In the beginning was the Word, and the lamp burns steadier. "You were offered money for this," he says. It is not a question.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the desk it was meant for. The monk knew I had been offered money for it. He did not ask how much.

road.hint: A book carried to its desk is read for a thousand years.

options.label: Read the first lines aloud with him

pass.outcome: You read it together, his Latin and your stumbling, and somewhere in the third line you stop stumbling.
pass.chronicle: Read the first lines of Cuthbert's Gospel aloud with Brother Sacristan. By the third line I had stopped tripping over it.

fail.outcome: You lose your place. He finds it for you, and keeps reading.

options.label: Tell him a bearer still lives, on the floors above
options.outcome: He is out of the door before you finish, with the lamp in one hand and a blanket in the other. The chapel is dark without him, and the desk is still empty.
options.chronicle: Told Brother Sacristan the last bearer was still alive above. He ran. I still have the book.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing about any book
options.outcome: He gives it gladly and asks nothing. If there is a small red book in your pack, it grows no lighter.

name: The Pardoner
text: A man with long yellow hair and a voice like a goat sits on a pack of relics outside a pilgrims' camp: a glass of pig's bones, a pillowcase he swears is Our Lady's veil, a sheaf of pardons sealed hot from Rome. He winks at you. "My text is always the same, friend. The love of money is the root of all evil. Never fails." He nods at the pilgrims. "Tell them you saw a miracle by my bones, and I'll split the take with you."

options.label: Tell the pilgrims you saw a miracle
options.outcome: The pilgrims empty their purses into his cap, weeping with joy. He splits it with you very fairly, which is the only honest thing he does all day.
options.chronicle: Swore to a camp of pilgrims that a pig's bones worked a miracle. The Pardoner split the take fairly. He preached against greed while he did it.

road.hint: Every fraud needs a witness, and the witness is paid in the same coin.

options.label: Refuse him
options.outcome: "Pity," he says. "You have an honest face. It would have been worth a fortune." He goes to preach anyway, and does fairly well without you.
options.chronicle: Refused to lend my face to a pardoner. He said it would have been worth a fortune. He did fairly well without it.

road.hint: An honest face is worth a fortune to exactly the wrong people.

options.label: Show the pilgrims his pardons are forged

pass.outcome: Every pardon is "given at Rome" and dated in the reign of a Pope who had been dead for a hundred years when the seal was cut. You read out the date and the name, and the Pope's dates, and an old pilgrim who once walked to Rome starts to laugh, and then they all do. The Pardoner packs his pig's bones with great dignity and leaves.
pass.chronicle: Showed a camp of pilgrims that their pardons were dated in the reign of a dead Pope. They laughed the Pardoner out. His minders hit me first.

fail.outcome: You get the Pope wrong, and he corrects you, beautifully, in front of everyone. The pilgrims buy twice as much.
fail.chronicle: Tried to catch a pardoner out on the date of his pardons and got the Pope wrong myself. His minders hit me, and the pilgrims bought double.

road.hint: A pardon dated in a dead man's reign is pardoning nobody.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the Pardoner starts his sermon. The love of money is the root of all evil. It never fails.

name: Weeping Mother
text: She appears slowly, the outline first, then the tears that fall like silver and vanish before they reach the stone. A glowing locket circles her like a small moon. "My boy, Pip. He was nine. He went in after the dog, and the dog came back without him." Her voice breaks. "Will you pray with me? Not for him. For me. I'm so tired. I just want to stop looking."

options.label: Kneel and pray with her until she can rest

pass.outcome: You find the right prayer: Simeon's, the one the old man said in the Temple when he held the child he had waited his whole life to see: now let your servant go in peace. The prayer goes on and on. Her tiredness presses down on you like a stone, twelve years of walking. When you finish, her tears have slowed. "I can feel it," she breathes. "Peace. After so long." She goes into warm light, smiling, and the locket goes with her.
pass.chronicle: Prayed Simeon's prayer with a ghost named Maud until she could rest. Her boy went in after a dog twelve years ago. She has stopped looking now.

schedule.lost_line: I never did find Maud Ferrers's boy. I hope he found the light she went into.

fail.outcome: You pray, but the words will not come right, and her tiredness is heavier than your prayer. "Thank you," she says. "Most walk right through." She keeps searching.
fail.chronicle: Tried to pray a ghost named Maud to rest. The words would not come right. She is still searching.

road.hint: Some searches end not in finding, but in being allowed to stop.

options.label: Tell her that her love has outlasted death
options.outcome: She flickers. "Thank you for seeing me. Most walk right through." She keeps searching. She will always keep searching.

options.label: Walk on

name: Pip Ferrers
text: A boy of about nine sits on a step with a frayed dog's lead in his hand, see-through as breath on glass. "Have you seen my mum?" he asks. "I went in after Bracken, and I couldn't find the way back, and then I couldn't find her. Bracken went home. I heard him barking up there. I've been waiting for someone to come and get me."

options.label: Tell him where his mother went
options.outcome: You tell him: she looked for him for twelve years, and then she was allowed to stop, and she went into the light smiling, with her locket. He stands up. "Then that's where I'll look," he says, very sensibly, and winds the dog's lead round his hand, and walks up into a light you cannot see, and does not look back.
options.chronicle: Told Pip Ferrers where his mother went. He wound up his dog's lead and walked into the light after her.

options.label: Leave him on his step
options.outcome: "That's all right," he says. "Someone will come."

name: Andvari
text: A pool under a waterfall, and in it a great pike that watches you with an old man's eyes. On the rock beside the pool lies a net of grey silk, the kind Ran uses to drown sailors. Someone has carved a sign on the rock in neat runes: ANDVARI'S POOL. THE GOLD IS UNDER HIM. THE NET IS HOW. The pike does not swim away. It looks very tired of this.

options.label: Net him and take all his gold, ring and all
options.outcome: He comes up as a dwarf, dripping and furious, and gives you everything, as he once gave Loki everything. Then, very quietly: "The ring will be the death of whoever holds it. It has never failed yet."
options.chronicle: Netted a dwarf in a pool and took his gold and his little ring. He told me it would be the death of whoever held it. It is a very good ring.

road.hint: A curse that killed a dragon is not afraid of you.

options.label: Take the net and leave him be
options.outcome: You roll up the grey silk. It is lighter than it looks and colder than water. The pike watches it go into your pack and sinks a little lower, the way a man sits down when he knows the next visitor will come with it.
options.chronicle: Took Ran's net off the rock by Andvari's pool and left the dwarf alone. Nobody can net him with it now, except whoever I give it to.

road.hint: A net taken from the rock is still a net.

options.label: Throw the net into the waterfall, so nobody can use it again
options.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is gone. The pike comes up as a dwarf, slowly, and sits on the rock and looks at you for a long time. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he tells you something about Fafnir: that a dragon's armour is all on top, and that he crawls to the water every evening along the same groove in the rock.
options.chronicle: Threw Ran's net into the waterfall so nobody could rob Andvari again. He came up as a dwarf and told me where Fafnir is soft.

road.hint: The net is how. Without the net, there is no how.

outcome_variants.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is gone. The pike comes up as a dwarf, slowly, and sits on the rock and looks at you for a long time. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he sniffs, and smells the dragon on you. "And Fafnir's dead, isn't he? Then there's nobody left on my gold but me." He laughs, a little, for the first time in a long time.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Threw Ran's net into the waterfall so nobody could rob Andvari again. He came up as a dwarf, smelled Fafnir's blood on me, and laughed.

options.label: Walk on

name: Swift Stranger

tells: two small pinions tucked in the band
a staff with two snakes carved round it

text: A young man leans against the wall with his arms crossed, grinning like he knows a joke that hasn't been told yet. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band. He carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, and one of them blinks. A tortoise shell with strings hangs on his back. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says. "Probably. Or I will have. Want to make a trade?"

text_variants.text: A young man leans against the wall with his arms crossed, grinning like he knows a joke that hasn't been told yet. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band. He carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, and one of them blinks. A tortoise shell with strings hangs on his back. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says. "Probably. Or I will have. Want to make a trade?" 'We've met. You watched my father's pitcher. He's still talking about it.'

options.label: Trade food for his gift
options.outcome: He sniffs it approvingly and flicks a feather from his hat at your boots. It dissolves into the leather. Each step lands further than it should.
options.chronicle: Traded my lunch to a grinning stranger for a feather that went into my boots. I have been walking too fast ever since.

options.label: Ask whether Apollo ever got his cattle back

pass.outcome: He laughs so hard he has to hold the wall. "I was one day old. I walked them backwards so the tracks pointed the wrong way, then made the lyre to pay him off." He taps the tortoise shell. "Clever mortal."

delayed.text: Where two corridors cross, a wand lies on the flagstones, tied with a ribbon in the shape of a winged sandal.

pass.chronicle: Asked a grinning stranger about some stolen cattle. He laughed so hard he had to hold the wall. Then he left me a present at a crossroads.

fail.outcome: "Cattle?" He looks innocent, which on him is a warning. When he's gone, you count your purse twice. It is all there, which is somehow worse.

road.hint: A thief who invented music will always tell you how he did it.

options.label: "You're a long way from Olympus, Messenger."
options.outcome: He tips the hat to you with real respect. "Most of them only look at the sandals." He is gone before the hat comes back down.
options.chronicle: Called a grinning stranger by his proper title. He tipped his hat and vanished before it came back down.

options.label: Decline the trade
options.outcome: "Fair enough. You're the careful type. I respect that. Mostly." He saunters off whistling something that sounds like it has not been written yet.

name: Azarias
text: A young man with a travelling staff and a dog at his heels falls into step beside you as if you had arranged it. "Azarias, son of the great Ananias, one of your own kin." The dog wags at you as if you were an old friend. He has a fish wrapped in leaves under his arm and talks about it a great deal. He breaks a loaf of his own and offers you half.
