He holds his half while he talks, and later it is gone, though you never see him eat.

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the second stair he stops. 'This is as far as I was sent.' He gives you a pouch with the fish's gall in it, wrapped in a leaf. 'For eyes that have stopped seeing. You'll know.'
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked a long way down with a young man called Azarias and his dog. He never stepped on a trap and never ate a thing. He left me a fish's gall for someone's eyes.

on_fail.outcome: Azarias goes down under the blows. When you reach him he is simply not there any more, and nor is the dog.
on_fail.chronicle: Lost track of Azarias and his dog on the stairs. I do not think he was lost. I think I was.

on_fail_variants.outcome: Azarias is simply not there any more, and nor is the dog.

options.label: Walk with him a while
options.outcome: "Good," he says. "It's better with company. The dog agrees."

road.hint: A guide who never eats is not travelling on bread.

options.label: Ask him what the fish is for

pass.outcome: "The heart and liver, burned, drive off a demon. The gall heals eyes." He looks at you sidelong. "You know the story."
pass.chronicle: A travelling man with a dog told me what a fish's gall is good for. He seemed pleased I knew the story already.

fail.outcome: "Supper," he says, and the dog sneezes.

road.hint: Some fish are carried for reasons other than supper.

options.label: "You haven't eaten all day, Azarias."
options.outcome: He laughs, and for a moment there is more light in the corridor than there are torches. "I am Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord. All this way you only thought you saw me eat." He blesses you with two fingers, the way a priest does, and the dog wags.
options.chronicle: Told my travelling companion he had not eaten all day. He laughed and said his name was Raphael. The dog was not surprised.

options.label: "I travel alone."
options.outcome: "Then go with God," he says, "and mind the third step." There is a trap on the third step.

name: The Mast
text: In a flooded hall of the goddess's temple, a ship has run its bow onto the marble steps at your feet, black water all round its stern, and a man is lashed to its mast hand and foot. You could climb aboard. Somewhere across the lake voices are singing, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard. His crew sit at the oars with wax in their ears. The man strains at the ropes, weeping. "Cut me loose. I'm the captain. I order it. I'll die if I don't hear the end." Scratched into the mast in his own hand: WHATEVER I SAY, DON'T.

options.label: Cut him loose

pass.outcome: The ropes part and he lunges for the water, and you get an arm round him and hold on, and say his own words back to him: whatever I say, don't. Which captain gives the orders, the one who wrote that, or the one shouting now? He stops straining. He stays on the deck, shaking, until the song ends.
pass.chronicle: Cut a captain free from his mast and then held him to his own written orders. He stayed. I am not sure I would have.

fail.outcome: He goes over the side before you can say anything at all. The song stops a moment later, as if satisfied.
fail.chronicle: Cut a captain loose from his mast because he begged. He went into the water. The singing stopped, satisfied.

road.hint: When a man's two selves disagree, ask which one wrote the orders.

options.label: Keep him bound
options.outcome: He curses you, and then begs, and then curses you again, until the song stops. Then he goes limp in the ropes. "Thank you," he says. "That was the worst hour of my life, and I would not give it back."
options.chronicle: Kept a captain tied to his mast while the Sirens sang. Afterwards he said it was the worst hour of his life and he would not give it back.

road.hint: Sometimes the kindest thing is to obey the man he was an hour ago.

options.label: Listen to the end of the song yourself
options.outcome: It promises you everything, every answer, everything that has ever happened. You come to waist-deep in black water with the captain screaming your name from the mast. You remember almost none of it. Almost.
options.chronicle: Listened to the Sirens to the end. Came to in the lake up to my waist. I remember one line of it. I am not writing it down.

road.hint: A song that promises every answer charges for the hearing.

options.label: Stop your ears and walk on
options.outcome: You walk on with your fingers in your ears. The song follows you a long way, and then it doesn't.

name: Neferkaptah
text: The torches on this floor burn blue. Water is coming up through the cracks in the floor, and it smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his gold collar, and behind him come the tomb's dead, wrapped and silent, more than you want to count. "You swore," he says. "You read it. I can smell it on you." Behind them all, a long way back, a woman with wet hair is standing very still, and does not come closer.

text_variants.text: The torches on this floor burn blue. Water is coming up through the cracks in the floor, and it smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his gold collar, and behind him come the tomb's dead, wrapped and silent, more than you want to count. "You swore," he says. "You never even opened it. You carried my book all this way and never once looked inside." For a moment he sounds more hurt than angry. Behind them all, a long way back, a woman with wet hair is standing very still, and does not come closer.

options.label: Give the book back
options.outcome: He takes it and holds it against his chest, where the linen band was. The dead go back into the walls one by one. Ahwere is the last to go. She does not say anything. She does not need to.
options.chronicle: The dead came for the Book of Thoth because I was late returning it. I gave it back. Ahwere watched. I would rather she had shouted.

road.hint: A loan returned late is still returned, but the lender remembers.

options.label: "I don't have it any more."
options.outcome: "Then you will bring me to where it is," he says, "or you will come with me to where I am." The water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Told a drowned prince I no longer had his book. He did not care where it was, only that I had sworn. His dead came up out of the floor.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is owed by the promiser, not by the pocket.

options.label: Refuse. The book is yours now
options.outcome: "Then you'll keep it the way I kept it," he says, and the water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Refused to give the Book of Thoth back to the prince I swore to. His dead came up out of the floor. I kept the book. The water is still in my boots.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is collected by the dead.

name: Socrates

authority.who: the Athenian jury, on Meletus's charge
authority.why: Condemned an innocent man on a charge his accuser could not prove.

text: A cell with the door open and a jailer asleep, and inside a snub-nosed old man in a worn cloak, cheerfully barefoot. A cup sits on the sill, waiting for the watch to change. A worried friend wrings his hands. "Crito has a boat waiting," Socrates says. "He thinks I should run. I think I shouldn't. Show me I'm wrong and I'll go." He pats the bench. "But you'll have to show me. I'm very annoying about that."

options.label: Argue with him, staking your strength

pass.outcome: You put it to him straight: Meletus could not name one young man you had corrupted, and the jury voted against you anyway. A verdict built on a lie isn't the laws of Athens speaking. It's your accusers borrowing their voice, and drinking the cup lets them keep it. Twice he has to stop and think, and once he laughs out loud and says, "Oh, that's good." When the watch changes he still drinks the cup. "You nearly had me," he says. "Nearly is the most anyone has ever got. Thank you for the best argument I've had in a month."
pass.chronicle: Told Socrates a verdict built on a lie is not the law speaking. He said it was the best argument he had heard in a month, and drank the cup anyway.

fail.outcome: He takes your argument apart so gently you hardly notice until you have nothing left to stand on. "Don't be sad," he says. "That's the useful part." You are wrung out.
fail.chronicle: Argued with Socrates and lost every point, very politely. I have never been so tired or learned so much.

road.hint: An argument lost to the right person leaves you richer.

options.label: Carry him out by force
options.outcome: He doesn't fight. He just keeps talking, all the way to Crito's boat on the black water, about whether a man carried away against his will has escaped at all. "They condemned you on a lie," Crito tells him, weeping with relief. "You owe liars nothing." You watch the boat pull away. Socrates looks back at his cell until the dark takes it.
options.chronicle: Carried Socrates out of his cell to Crito's boat. He talked the whole way about whether it counted. He looked back at his cell until the dark took it.

road.hint: You can carry a man out of a cell and not out of his reasons.

options.label: Stay for the last conversation
options.outcome: You stay. He talks about the soul and asks you questions you will be answering for years. When the watch changes he drinks, and walks about until his legs are heavy, and lies down. "Crito," he says at the very end, "we owe a cock to Asclepius. Don't forget."
options.chronicle: Stayed with Socrates to the end. His last words were about a debt of a chicken. He did not want it forgotten. Neither do I.

road.hint: The last thing a wise man remembers may be a small debt.

name: Thorleif Grimsson
text: A man with a harp across his knees sits against a wall that is white with frost in the shape of a hand. The frost is on him, too, from the chest down. He is perfectly calm. "Thorleif. Skald. A draugr shook my hand; I'll not see the morning." He smiles. "My brother Eyvind went over the edge of the Long Dark. There's a stone there with room on it. I made him a verse. Will you carve it for me? I'll teach it to you. It's short. He was not a patient man."

options.label: Learn the verse and swear to carve it
options.outcome: He teaches it to you three times, beating the time on the harp. Eyvind went where the dark goes down; no mead, no fire, no brother's hand. Stone, say his name to the wind that stays. "Good," he says. "Now you're a skald. A bad one. It'll do."

oath.what: Carve his verse for his brother Eyvind on the rune-stone at the Long Dark.

thread.hint: A verse in my head is waiting for a stone.

options.chronicle: Learned a dead skald's verse for his brother by heart and swore to carve it on the stone at the Long Dark. He said I was a bad skald. It will do.

road.hint: A verse carried in your head weighs nothing and is still a load.

options.label: Give him a healing potion for the cold
options.outcome: It warms his face and hands, and does nothing at all for the frost. "That's good," he says. "Now I can feel my fingers to play."

options.label: Ask him to play while there's time
options.outcome: He plays the verse for his brother, and then a long, bad, funny song about a goat, and then he stops in the middle of a line.
options.chronicle: A dying skald played me a verse for his brother and then a terrible song about a goat. He stopped in the middle of a line.

options.label: Walk on

name: Pellok the Slightly Lost
text: A merchant in a wine merchant's apron is sitting on a crate labeled FINE VINTAGES, looking at a map upside-down with tremendous concentration. He does not hear you until you are quite close. "GAH. Oh. Sorry. Sorry. Do you, is this the 40th floor? I was told there was a marketplace on the 40th floor. I have been down a great many stairs and I am very much getting the sense I have not been down enough of them."

options.label: Buy a bottle from him
options.outcome: He is so relieved to make a sale that he nearly hugs you. The wine is, inexplicably, excellent, a deep red that tastes of a summer several decades ago and warms you to the marrow. Your wounds respond favorably to the vintage. He marks you on his route map as a 'reliable customer.'

options.label: Give him food for the last stretch
options.outcome: He accepts the food with enormous gratitude. "You are a saint. A genuine saint. Here, take this, I've been using it as a paperweight. The previous owner said it was powerful. Very confident about it, too." He presses a potion into your hands and begins the long walk upward, muttering.

options.label: Tell him why half his bottles have gone sour

pass.outcome: You pull a cork that has shrunk and gone dry. "Air got in," you tell him. "Keep the bottles on their sides so the cork stays wet and swollen; once air gets in, a little bacterium turns the wine to vinegar." He stares at his crate, which he has been carrying upright for two hundred miles. Then he gives you the best bottle he has left, which is very good indeed.
pass.chronicle: Told a wine merchant his bottles had gone sour because he carried them upright and the corks dried out. He gave me his best one.

fail.outcome: "Too much shaking?" He considers it seriously. It is only later that you think of the corks: dry and shrunk, because he carries his bottles upright, so the air got in, and the wine turned to vinegar.
fail.chronicle: Could not tell a wine merchant why his wine went sour. It was the corks.

road.hint: A dry cork lets the air in.

options.label: Tell him what is really on the fortieth floor
options.outcome: "A gorgon," you say. "In a temple. No market." He goes slowly white under his apron. "Up," he says. "Up is good. Up has customers." He hoists his crate, takes two steps in the wrong direction, corrects himself, and sets off for the stair, a good deal faster than he came down.
options.chronicle: Pointed a lost wine merchant upward. He is far below daylight. I hope he has a lot of wine.

road.hint: Some merchants are lost on purpose by their maps.

name: Mourne, Dwarf Alchemist
text: A dwarf has set up a field laboratory in what was once a guardroom, among glass that has no business surviving this far down. Her goggles glow faintly green, and her beard is singed at the ends. "Oh, a live one. Excellent. My people have brewed in the cinders since before your kings were born. I've been working on something that needs a test subject, and before you refuse, I'm offering fair compensation. I'm an alchemist, not a monster."

options.label: Volunteer, but check her working first

pass.outcome: You read her notes before you drink. She has doubled one reagent and halved another, and you point out that a compound strong enough to knit flesh needs a measured dose, not a hopeful one: the dose makes the poison, as Paracelsus said. She swears in dwarvish, fixes it, and this time the compound tastes of copper and plums and your wounds begin to knit at once.
pass.chronicle: Checked a dwarf alchemist's dose before I drank her compound. The dose makes the poison. Fixed, it knit my wounds.

fail.outcome: You drink it without reading the notes. There is a moment of alarming internal heat, and then a long sour sickness. Mourne frowns at her page. "Ah. I doubled that one. The dose makes the poison, as the old Swiss said." She writes this down with real interest.
fail.chronicle: Drank a dwarf alchemist's compound without checking her dose. The dose makes the poison.

road.hint: The dose makes the poison.

options.label: Buy her regeneration salve
options.outcome: "Tested and approved," she says, by which she means tested on herself, which you realize when she pulls up her sleeve to show old burn scars in various stages of alchemical healing. The salve is thick and smells terrible and works immediately.

options.label: Buy a sealed bottle for the road
options.outcome: She wraps a bottle in a scrap of hide and seals the cork with wax. "Dosed properly," she says, "which is more than I can say for the last batch."

options.label: "Hard pass."
options.outcome: "Noted," she says, without offense. "Healthy skepticism of unsolicited chemistry. Good instinct, actually. Come back if you change your mind, I'll be here until I run out of subjects or the dungeon runs out of patience with me." She returns to her bubbling apparatus.

name: Sir Lorvaine the Certain
text: A knight in immaculate but deeply outdated armour stands squarely in your path. The cold here fogs your breath; his does not fog at all. "I am Sir Lorvaine the Certain, and I have a riddle from the old book at Exeter. Answer it and you shall have the gift of my failed quest. I have asked it for forty-seven years. A moth ate words. A thief in the dark swallowed a man's song, and was not one whit the wiser for it. What am I?"

options.label: Answer his riddle

pass.outcome: "A bookworm," you say. "A moth that eats the page and learns nothing." Sir Lorvaine stares at you, then sits down on the floor in his armour with a great clang. "Forty-seven years," he says. "The monks at Exeter wrote it down a thousand years ago, and nobody's ever got it." He presses his quest's gift into your hands, and as he does he fades a little, like a man who can finally stop.
pass.chronicle: Answered Sir Lorvaine's riddle from the Exeter Book: a bookworm, that eats words and learns nothing. He gave me his quest's gift and faded.

fail.outcome: You guess wrong. He nods, very slowly. "A bookworm," he says. "A moth that eats the words and is none the wiser. The monks at Exeter wrote it down a thousand years ago." He keeps his gift. "Forty-eight years, then," he says, and begins again.
fail.chronicle: Got Sir Lorvaine's riddle wrong. It was a bookworm. He keeps waiting for someone to answer it.

road.hint: Some riddles are asked only to be answered at last.

options.label: Wish him well and continue
options.outcome: "Of course," he says, very slightly too loud. You hear him composing a new riddle as you walk away.

name: Ulf Haraldsson, of the Einherjar
text: A massive warrior sits on the ice polishing a mail coat that was cut to pieces this morning and is whole again tonight. "Ulf Haraldsson. One of the einherjar," he says, "Odin's chosen dead. We fight all day and the fallen stand up whole at evening, and we eat the boar that is cooked every night and whole again by morning, and we wait for the wolf." He looks up at you and something wakes behind his eyes. "Still coming down, are they? Good. The deep floors need witnesses."

options.label: Ask him to train you the old way

pass.outcome: He trains you for the holmgang, the island duel: a cloak pegged out on the ground and ropes round it, each man with his shield-bearer and three spare shields, and whoever steps off the cloak with both feet has fled and is named nithing for life. First blood on the cloak ends it. "Small ground teaches small, sure steps," he says, and corrects your grip until your blade bites truer.
pass.chronicle: Trained for the holmgang with Ulf Haraldsson of the einherjar: a cloak pegged on the ground, three spare shields, and no stepping off.

fail.outcome: He drills you hard, and you keep stepping back. "Off the cloak," he says, every time. "In a holmgang that's flight, and they call you nithing for life." You leave bruised and no better.
fail.chronicle: Trained with one of the einherjar and kept stepping back. In a holmgang that counts as running.

road.hint: In the old duel, the ground was a single cloak.

options.label: Share a meal with him
options.outcome: He receives the food with the dignity of a man who has forgotten what it means to receive anything. He eats slowly. "My first meal shared in..." He counts. Stops counting. "Thank you." He refills something in your pack, rations you didn't know you were missing. "You'll need it more than I do."

options.label: "What are you waiting for?"
options.outcome: He looks down at the armor in his hands. The question takes a long time to reach an answer. "The idea," he finally says, "that someone should still be here when the next one comes through. So the next one knows the road has been walked before." He gestures you onward. "It has been walked before."

name: Squire Tobyn
text: A squire of about sixteen sits on a broken step with a wooden practice sword across his knees, watching the stair you came down. He stands up too fast when he sees you. "Is Ser Brennan behind you? He said he'd catch up. He always catches up."

options.label: Give him the sword, and Ser Brennan's message
options.outcome: He takes the sword the way Brennan held it out, hilt first, before he understands. Then he understands. "He said I was ready?" You nod. He cries the way boys do when they're trying not to, and then he stops, and buckles it on.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's sword and told him he was not left behind. He buckled it on before he had finished crying.

road.hint: A message from the dead is the one delivery that cannot wait.

options.label: Give him Ser Brennan's message, without the sword
options.outcome: You tell him what Brennan said, and then you have to tell him the rest: the sword is gone, lost on the way down. He listens to all of it. "Ready," he says. "He said ready." He picks up the wooden sword, and holds it differently.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's last words but not his sword. I had lost it on the way down. He took the words anyway.

road.hint: A dead man's words can be delivered even when his steel cannot.

options.label: Keep the sword. Tell him Brennan fell, nothing more
options.outcome: "Fell." He nods slowly. "Then I'll wait for his body." He is still sitting on the step when you look back.
options.chronicle: Told Brennan's squire his knight fell, and kept the sword. He is still waiting on that step. I gave my word to a dying man and broke it to a boy.

road.hint: A promise to the dead is broken in front of the living.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "He'll catch up," Tobyn says, mostly to himself.

name: The Lingering Echo
text: A figure composed entirely of slowly dispersing letters flickers in the centre of the corridor, the echo of a wizard who died mid-word. The echo loops: hand raised, mouth forming the word, letter by letter, a-b-r-a-c-a-d-a-b-r, then reset, raised again. It notices you and breaks the loop with visible effort. "I require... the last letter. I have forgotten the last letter. I have knowledge yet to spend."

options.label: Let the echo channel through you
options.outcome: The sensation is like holding a lightning bolt by the wrong end. Decades of arcane study pour through your nervous system in seconds, most of it incomprehensible, but the raw magical energy saturates you. The echo completes its word at last, a single syllable of great satisfaction, and disperses. Your mana swells with the residue.
options.chronicle: Let the echo of a dead wizard finish his spell through me. It was a long word.

road.hint: A word left half spoken waits for a mouth.

options.label: Offer a scroll as a vessel instead
options.outcome: The echo examines the scroll with something like hope. It pours itself into the parchment in a cascade of luminous script. The scroll blackens and crumbles, used up, but in its place a wand assembles itself from notation and will, solid as steel, humming with the dead wizard's last intent.

options.label: Give him the last letter, and tell him what it was for

pass.outcome: "A," you say. "Abracadabra." The echo shudders with relief. The oldest record of the word is a Roman doctor's, Serenus Sammonicus: write it on parchment in a triangle, dropping a letter every line down to a single A, and wear it round the neck, and the fever shrinks as the word does. The echo finishes its spell at last, and the spell was never fire or lightning: it was to make a sickness smaller. It spends what is left of itself on you.
pass.chronicle: Gave a dead wizard's echo the last letter of abracadabra. A Roman doctor wrote it in a shrinking triangle to shrink a fever.

fail.outcome: You guess wrong, and the echo resets: hand raised, letter by letter. Later it comes to you: abracadabra, ending in A, the Roman fever-charm written in a triangle that shrinks one letter a line, so the fever would shrink with it.
fail.chronicle: Could not give a dead wizard's echo his last letter. It was A. The word was abracadabra.

road.hint: An old fever-charm shrinks one letter at a time.

options.label: Leave the echo in peace
options.outcome: You step carefully around the looping figure. Behind you, the hand raises, the mouth forms the word, and resets. Raises. Resets. Some spells take longer to finish than their casters do.

name: Rune-Stone
text: A standing stone at the edge of a great dark drop, carved with runes in a ribbon that ends in a serpent's head. Most of the ribbon is full: names, and who raised the stone for whom. The last loop is empty. Somebody has left a chisel in a crack, as if knowing someone would need it.

options.label: Carve Thorleif's verse for his brother
options.outcome: You carve it the way he said it, line by line, the serpent's head last. When you step back the stone looks finished, the way a sentence does when it has its full stop. Far below in the dark, someone laughs, the way a brother laughs.
options.chronicle: Carved Thorleif's last verse on the rune-stone for his brother, as I swore. It took an hour and all my patience. The stone looks finished now.

road.hint: A stone with an empty loop is waiting for somebody's words.

options.label: Carve your own name in the empty loop instead
options.outcome: It looks very good there. Anyone who comes this way will read it and wonder who you were. Nobody will ever read Thorleif's.
options.chronicle: Carved my own name on the rune-stone in the place I promised to a dead skald. It looks very good. I am trying not to read it.

road.hint: A stone remembers whoever cut it, and whoever was left off.

options.label: Walk on

name: Lady Bertilak
text: In a warm hall cut into the rock, a lady in green sits by a fire, winding a sash of green silk round her fingers. "My lord said whatever you win in his house, you give to him before you leave. Those are the terms." She holds out the sash. "This is a girdle no blade can cut through. You go to meet the Green Knight soon. He will swing at your neck." She smiles. "My lord need never know."

options.label: Take it and keep it secret
options.outcome: She ties it round your waist herself. At the door her husband asks what you won in his house. You tell him: nothing.

thread.hint: Somewhere below, a green knight is sharpening an axe for my neck.

schedule.lost_line: I never did find the Green Chapel. The girdle and I went on down without it.

options.chronicle: Took a lady's green girdle against the Green Knight's axe and did not tell her husband. The terms were plain. I wanted to live.

road.hint: A secret kept from your host goes with you to the chapel.

options.label: Take it, and give it to your host at the door, as agreed
options.outcome: Her husband turns the sash over in his hands, laughing, and does not give it back. "Honest," he says. "We'll see how honest the Knight finds your neck." That night you hardly sleep. As Gawain did on the night before the chapel, you hear every cock crow and know the hour.
options.chronicle: Was given a girdle that would save my neck, and handed it to my host because those were his terms. I lay awake all night. I would do it again.

road.hint: Keeping a bargain you could break unseen is the whole test.

options.label: Refuse it
options.outcome: She winds the sash back round her fingers. "Gawain took it," she says. "He was very nearly perfect." She seems disappointed in you, and impressed, at once.
options.chronicle: Refused a girdle that would have saved my neck from the Green Knight. The lady said Gawain took it. I am not Gawain.

road.hint: The gift that saves your life can cost you something you meant to keep.

name: The Green Knight

authority.who: the Green Knight, keeper of the Green Chapel
authority.why: He keeps his bargains exactly, and his judgement of the girdle is honest: a nick for a small lie, and forgiveness for the truth.

chronicle_meet: Found the Green Chapel: a hill of turf with holly growing on it, and somebody inside sharpening an axe for my neck.
text: A green mound stands in a hollow of the rock, grown over with turf and holly in full berry, like a barrow that never closed. From inside comes the shriek of an axe on a grindstone. The Green Knight ducks out, head on his shoulders and a great axe on one of them. "You came. Most don't." He looks you over slowly, the way a host looks over a guest at his door. "You owe me one blow. Kneel, and bare your neck."

text_variants.text: A green mound stands in a hollow of the rock, grown over with turf and holly in full berry, like a barrow that never closed. From inside comes the shriek of an axe on a grindstone. The Green Knight ducks out, head on his shoulders and a great axe on one of them. "You came. Most don't." He looks you over slowly, the way a host looks over a guest at his door, and his eyes stop at your waist. "You owe me one blow. Kneel, and bare your neck."

options.label: Kneel, and bare your neck
options.outcome: You kneel on the cold turf. The axe goes up, and you flinch. He stops it in the air. "Gawain never flinched," he says, almost kindly. The second time you hold still, and the blade halts a hair from your skin. The third comes down for real and bites the side of your neck: a nick, hot and running. He leans on the haft, and for a moment he is the lord of the warm hall, Bertilak, laughing by his own fire. "One swing for the bargain. One for your nerve. And a nick for what you won in my house and called nothing." He waits.
options.chronicle: Knelt at the Green Chapel and let the Green Knight swing at my neck. He stopped twice. The third time he nicked me, and named my lie without saying the word.

road.hint: A bargain kept at the block is still a bargain kept.

options.label: Tell him about the girdle before he swings
options.outcome: Before you kneel, you untie the green sash and hold it up between you. "Your lady gave me this. At your door you asked what I'd won in your house, and I said nothing. I lied, because I wanted to live." The Green Knight looks at the girdle a long moment. Then he laughs, a great green bark that knocks the snow off the holly, and takes it. He swings three times anyway, because a bargain is a bargain, and all three stop a hair from your skin. "Gawain needed the axe before he could say it," says Bertilak. "You said it first. I hold you as clean as the day you were born."
options.chronicle: Told the Green Knight about his lady's girdle before he raised the axe, and gave it back. He swung three times and never touched me. Then he laughed and said I was clean.

road.hint: Say it before the axe falls, and the axe has less to say.

options.label: Refuse his game, and draw on him
options.outcome: "No." You draw. The Green Knight sighs like a teacher with a slow pupil, and lifts the axe off his shoulder. "Then we play it the old way. Strike first, if you like. I'll have my turn after."
options.chronicle: Would not kneel at the Green Chapel. I drew on the Green Knight instead. He seemed to think that was fair, which worried me more than the axe.

road.hint: A man who has lost his head once is not afraid to lose it again.

options.label: Walk away from the chapel
options.outcome: You turn your back on the mound. Behind you the grindstone starts up again. "The girdle goes with you," he calls after you, not unkindly, "and so does the reason you carry it."
options.chronicle: Walked away from the Green Chapel with the Green Knight's girdle still on me. He called after me that the reason I carried it was coming too.

road.hint: An appointment you walk away from keeps its own calendar.

options.label: Tell him the truth about the girdle, and give it back
options.outcome: Your neck is bleeding into your collar. You untie the green sash anyway and hold it out. "Your lady gave me this. You asked what I'd won in your house, and I said nothing. I lied, because I wanted to live." Bertilak takes it, turns it over in his huge hands, and laughs until the holly shakes. "You lacked a little loyalty," he says, "and only for love of your life. That is the whole of your fault, and you have owned it." He presses a fistful of snow to your neck. "I hold you as clean as the day you were born."
options.chronicle: Told the Green Knight the truth about his lady's girdle with my own blood running into my collar, and gave it back. He laughed until the holly shook and said I was clean.

road.hint: A cut heals cleaner once you stop hiding what it was for.

options.label: Call it a fair blow, and say you're quits
options.outcome: "A fair blow," you say. "We're quits." Bertilak looks at you for as long as it takes the snow to settle. "Quits," he agrees, and does not laugh. "Keep it, then. Every time you buckle it on, you'll know what it is." He shoulders the axe and goes back into his hill, and the grindstone starts again.

outcome_variants.outcome: "A fair blow," you say. "We're quits." Bertilak looks at you, and at your empty belt, for as long as it takes the snow to settle. "Quits," he agrees, and does not laugh. "Wherever it is now, you'll know what it was." He shoulders the axe and goes back into his hill, and the grindstone starts again.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Told the Green Knight it was a fair blow and we were quits. He agreed, and did not laugh. I had not known how much I wanted him to laugh.

options.chronicle: Told the Green Knight it was a fair blow and we were quits. He agreed, let me keep the girdle, and did not laugh. I had not known how much I wanted him to laugh.

road.hint: A lie told twice to the same host weighs twice as much.

options.label: Say nothing, and go
options.outcome: You press a hand to your neck and say nothing at all. Bertilak nods slowly, as if that were an answer of a kind. "Go on, then. It's yours. So is the knowing." When you look back from the end of the hollow, he is still watching you go.

outcome_variants.outcome: You press a hand to your neck and say nothing at all. Bertilak nods slowly, as if that were an answer of a kind. "Go on, then. Wherever it is now, the knowing is yours." When you look back from the end of the hollow, he is still watching you go.

options.chronicle: Said nothing to the Green Knight about his lady's girdle, though we both knew. He let me go. He was still watching when I looked back.

road.hint: Silence is an answer too, though not the one he waited for.

name: Vafthrudnir
text: A hall of ice-black stone, and a giant on a high seat with a beard like frozen rope. A row of skulls on the shelf behind him, each labelled in runes. "Vafthrudnir. I know more than anyone who has ever sat on that bench." He points at it. "Sit, and we'll trade questions. Lose, and your head goes on the shelf. Win, and you'll carry home more than you came with."

options.label: Wager your head

pass.outcome: He sits back. He has run out of questions, and you have not. "Take your head home," he says slowly. "And some of mine."
pass.chronicle: Traded questions with Vafthrudnir for my head, and won. He gave me some of his on the way out.

fail.outcome: "Close," he says, and takes his fee. It is not your whole head. It is enough.
fail.chronicle: Lost a contest of questions to Vafthrudnir. He kept a piece of me on his shelf, labelled. I would rather not know what the label says.

road.hint: Never stake your head against someone with a shelf.

options.label: Play a short contest for coin instead

pass.outcome: You answer his one question, and he answers yours, and then he cannot answer your second. The giant laughs and pays out, as a giant of honour must. "A small contest," he says. "Odin once played me for my head."
pass.chronicle: Played the giant Vafthrudnir a short contest of questions for coin, and won. Odin once played him for his head.

fail.outcome: He asks, and you have no answer, and he keeps your stake with a courteous nod. "In my hall the wager is always head or coin," he says. "Be glad you chose coin."
fail.chronicle: Played the giant Vafthrudnir a contest of questions for coin, and lost the stake. Better than my head.

options.label: "What did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear on the pyre?"

pass.outcome: The giant's face goes grey. Nobody has ever asked him that. Nobody alive knows the answer, and he has just realised who taught you to ask. "You've been talking to a one-eyed man," he says, and gets up from his seat, and gives it to you.
pass.chronicle: Asked Vafthrudnir the one question nobody can answer. He went grey and gave me his seat. I had it from a one-eyed man at a well.

outcome_variants.outcome: The giant's face goes grey. Nobody has ever asked him that. Nobody alive knows the answer, and he has just realised where you learned to ask. "You've been drinking at Mimir's well," he says, and gets up from his seat, and gives it to you.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Asked Vafthrudnir the one question nobody can answer. He went grey and gave me his seat. I had it from the water of Mimir's well.

fail.outcome: You fumble the question you came to ask. He laughs, and lets you go anyway, and the laugh follows you out.

road.hint: Some contests are won by remembering who you met at a well.

options.label: Decline

name: The Chooser of the Slain
text: Frozen into the ice wall is a young warrior in old mail, eyes open, a spear-wound under his ribs, and beside his body his shade sits shivering. "Eyvind," he says. "I fell here, against the frost-giants. The line broke and I ran. Then I came back, and held the gap alone until they killed me." Over him stands a woman in a mail coat, with a spear and a helmet bright as frost; ravens wait on the beams. "I am Skogul, a chooser of the slain," she says. "Half go to Odin's hall, half to Freyja's field. He told you how he died, living one. Tell me, and I will choose." Eyvind catches your sleeve. "Tell her I never ran."

options.label: Tell her he never ran
options.warning: Tell her I never ran.
options.outcome: "A chooser of the slain is not lied to about the slain," she says, and turns her spear and strikes you with the butt of it, hard, across the ribs. Then she is gone with the ravens, and Eyvind's shade looks at you, and fades into the ice unchosen.
options.chronicle: Lied to a valkyrie for a dead warrior who asked me to. She struck me for it and left him in the ice unchosen.

road.hint: A chooser of the slain cannot be lied to about the slain.

options.label: Tell her all of it: he ran, and he came back

pass.outcome: You tell it the way a skald would, the whole of it: the line broke, he ran, and then he turned and came back alone into the gap and held it until they killed him. "The coming back," says the valkyrie. "Most men never have to choose twice. He chose twice." Her name for herself, valkyrja, means chooser of the slain, and half of those she chooses ride to Odin's Valhalla and half to Freyja's field. She lifts Eyvind up behind her, and as she goes she touches your shield with the point of her spear.
pass.chronicle: Told a valkyrie the whole truth about a dead warrior: he ran, and came back. She chose him for the coming back.

fail.outcome: You stumble over it, and the running comes out and the coming back does not. Her face closes. "Then I cannot choose him," she says, and is gone with the ravens, and Eyvind fades into the ice.
fail.chronicle: Tried to tell a valkyrie how a warrior died and told it badly. She did not choose him.

road.hint: The whole of a story can save what half of it damns.

options.label: Tell her only that he ran
options.outcome: "True," she says. "And not all of it. A chooser cannot choose on half a story." She looks at you a long moment, and then she is gone, and Eyvind fades into the ice without a word.
options.chronicle: Told a valkyrie a dead warrior ran. It was true, and it was not all of it.

options.label: Leave the choosing to her
options.outcome: You step back. The valkyrie watches you go, then turns to the ice. You never learn what she chose.

name: Crossroads Fiddler

tells: one of his boots is the wrong shape

text: A gentleman in a black coat sits on a milestone where four corridors meet, tuning a fiddle. He smells of good cologne and, under it, of struck matches. "Tired of being asked questions? Everyone down here is quizzing you. Sign, and the answers will come to you sooner, from here to the bottom." He holds out a paper covered in very small print, and a pen. One of his boots is the wrong shape, as if there were no toes in it. "Payment later. Much later."

options.label: Sign
options.outcome: The ink is warm. He plays you a little tune to celebrate, and it is the most beautiful thing you have ever heard, and you know you will never hear the end of it. Answers start arriving in your head a moment before the questions do. It is not a comfortable feeling.
options.chronicle: Signed a gentleman's paper at a crossroads so the answers would come to me sooner. Now they come early. So, I suspect, will the bill.

road.hint: A shortcut through every test is still a test.

options.label: Read the small print before you decide

pass.outcome: It takes a while, because the print gets smaller as it goes, but there it is in the last line, in a hand like a scratch: and the signatory's name, in the book that is not kept by the Other Fellow. You look up. He is already smiling, a little ruefully. You tear the paper in half, and then in quarters. "Some other crossroads," he says, and there is a scorch mark on the milestone where he sat.
pass.chronicle: Read the small print on a crossroads gentleman's contract and found my name in the wrong book. I tore it up. He left a scorch mark.

fail.outcome: The print swims. He leans over helpfully and reads it to you, beautifully, every clause sounding perfectly reasonable. Then he holds out the pen again.

road.hint: The price of a bargain is always in the smallest letters.

options.label: Refuse to sign
options.outcome: "No." He folds the paper into his coat without argument. "There's always a next crossroads," he says, and goes back to tuning.
options.chronicle: Told a gentleman at a crossroads I would not sign his paper. I never did find out what was really in it.

road.hint: A no is still a no, even when you never learn what you refused.

options.label: Walk past without a word
options.outcome: He plays a few bars after you. You find you are walking in time to them for a while.

name: Something in a Copper Jar
text: A large copper jar sits in the middle of the corridor, its lead stopper stamped with a six-pointed seal and a warning in three dead languages. It is rattling. A voice from inside says, with considerable dignity: "I am aware of how this looks. Eighteen hundred years. Open it, and I will reward you as you deserve."

options.label: Open the jar
options.warning: Open it, and I will reward you as you deserve.
options.outcome: The seal scores your hands as it gives. The jinni pours out in a column of furious wind and hangs over you. "For the first hundred years I swore to make my rescuer rich," it says. "For the next, to open him the treasures of the earth. For the next, to grant him three wishes. After that I swore to kill whoever let me out."
options.chronicle: Opened a sealed copper jar because the voice inside promised a reward. It had been in there long enough to change its mind about rewards.

road.hint: A prisoner's promise can sour in the jar.

options.label: Slide coins under the stopper and bargain (150 gold)
options.outcome: You slide coins under the stopper. The jinni makes a sound of elaborate exasperation. "I cannot actually use gold in here. But I appreciate the gesture." It breathes something old and bright through the lead seal, and your mind fills like a cup.

options.label: Let it out, but first doubt that it was ever in

pass.outcome: You know the fisherman's story from the Thousand and One Nights. You lift the stopper an inch and say you don't believe a thing that size was ever in a jar this small. The jinni, offended, pours itself back in to prove it, and you slam the seal home. Then you bargain, with the jinni on the inside. It ends, as the story does, with a promise kept: it tells you where something of value lies and who must never know it.
pass.chronicle: Tricked a jinni back into its jar the way the fisherman did, by doubting it could fit. Then we bargained, with it on the inside.

fail.outcome: You try to bargain through the stopper, and it laughs at you. "In the old story," it says, "a fisherman got the better of one of us by doubting. You are not that fisherman."
fail.chronicle: Tried to bargain with a jinni in a jar. It said I was no fisherman.

road.hint: A fisherman once beat a jinni by doubting it.

options.label: Leave the jar sealed
options.outcome: "Sensible," the bottle says. "Genuinely. I have been in here a very long time and my temperament is not at its best. You made the correct call." The rattling resumes as you walk away.

name: Grey-Eyed Woman

tells: eyes the grey of storm clouds
an owl that is not quite an owl
a spear propped like a broom

text: A woman stands among the fallen columns as if the temple had been built around her. Her eyes are the grey of storm clouds before lightning, and an owl that is not quite an owl sits on her shoulder. A spear is propped against the wall beside her like a broom. The air smells faintly of olives. "You have come a long way into my house," she says. "I am curious whether your mind has sharpened to match your ambition."

options.label: Ask whether Arachne's tapestry had a single flaw

pass.outcome: Her eyes go the grey of a storm about to break. "No," she says at last. "Not one. That was the problem." The owl hoots once, as if at a joke. "Most mortals ask what lies at the bottom. You asked the one question I still think about." She touches your eyelids.
pass.chronicle: Asked a grey-eyed woman whether a certain weaver's work had any flaw. She said no, and that was the problem. I see more clearly now.

fail.outcome: "A foolish question," she says, and the owl looks away from you.
fail.chronicle: Asked a grey-eyed woman about a weaver. The owl looked away. I have been looked away from by better birds.

road.hint: Ask a proud goddess about her rival, and see what her face does.

options.label: "Grey-eyed Pallas. This was your house."
options.outcome: "It still is." She almost smiles. "Go on. I want to see how this ends."
options.chronicle: Named the grey-eyed woman to her face. She almost smiled and said she wanted to see how my story ends. So do I.

options.label: "What lies at the bottom?"
options.outcome: She tilts her head. "A question. Good." The owl blinks slowly. "At the bottom lies the thing that asked itself what lies above. Everything looks up, child. Even the abyss has ambitions."

options.label: Bow and pass
options.outcome: She inclines her head, a gesture that carries more weight than any blessing you can name. The owl watches you out of sight.

name: The Unseen Archivist
text: Nothing is there. And yet: the sound of a quill scratching on parchment. A throat cleared politely. The faint impression of a chair being occupied. "I catalog the deeds of those who descend," says a voice at desk-height, precisely where no desk is. "I have questions, if you have answers. And I pay for my interviews."

options.label: Agree to be interviewed
options.outcome: The interview is thorough. It asks about your earliest memory, your greatest fear, your theory on what lies at the dungeon's bottom, and whether you prefer mornings. It transcribes your answers with the focused energy of someone who finds all answers equally important. When it finishes, a purse of gold appears on the floor in front of you. "Excellent data," it says warmly. "Truly."
options.chronicle: Was interviewed by an archivist I could not see. My answers are now in a book somewhere.

road.hint: Someone is always writing it down.

options.label: Ask it to read you a page about the people you met
options.outcome: The quill stops. A page turns, somewhere near the back of a book you cannot see, and the voice reads, quietly:

people_lines.none: "Nobody," it says, puzzled. "You have met nobody, or saved nobody, or lost nobody yet. Come back when you have."
people_lines.after: "That is enough," it says. "The rest is for the end."

options.chronicle: The Unseen Archivist read me a page from the back of its book, about people I met on the way down.

road.hint: Someone keeps the book of what became of everyone.

options.label: Decline the interview
options.outcome: "Noted," says the voice, and you hear your refusal being noted. "That is, itself, a data point. Walk safe." The scratching of the quill follows you down the corridor for longer than seems possible, then stops all at once.

name: The Mirror Shade
text: The figure ahead looks exactly like you, or how you looked before the descent. Cleaner. Less scarred. It smiles with your face. "You have come a long way," it says, in your own voice. "I am what you left behind. I have been keeping it warm. Some of it you might want back."

options.label: Reach for what was lost
options.outcome: You press your hand to its chest. There is pain, not wound-pain, but the specific pain of remembering who you were before you knew what you know now. When you pull back, the shade is gone. But something has returned, a vigor, a readiness, the kind that only comes from knowing exactly what you are fighting for.
options.chronicle: Met myself from before the descent. I was cleaner. I did not envy me.

road.hint: Who you were is not waiting to be reclaimed.

options.label: Ask it whether you are still the one it remembers

pass.outcome: "You know what the wise said, then," it says, with your mouth. Heraclitus said no one steps into the same river twice: the water is new each time. Locke said a man is the same person as far back as his memory reaches. Others have said it is the soul, or the body, or that there is no single self at all. "I don't know which of them is right," says the shade. "You'll have to carry the question. It is lighter than what I was carrying." It hands you back something warm and goes.
pass.chronicle: Asked my own reflection whether I am still the one it remembers. It gave me Heraclitus's river and Locke's memory, and left me the question.

fail.outcome: "Of course I am," you say. The shade smiles, unconvinced. "Heraclitus would say the river is new water every time," it says. "Ask yourself again when you are not in a hurry." It dissolves like mist struck by a beam of light.
fail.chronicle: Told my reflection I am obviously the same person. It mentioned Heraclitus and went.

road.hint: No one steps into the same river twice.

options.label: Walk through it
options.outcome: It offers no resistance, you pass through cold air and a brief cascade of half-remembered smells: a specific kitchen, a specific rain. You do not look back. The shade, if it watches, says nothing.

text_variants.text: The figure ahead looks exactly like you, or how you looked before the descent. Cleaner. Less scarred. It smiles with your face. "You have come a long way," it says, in your own voice. "I am what you left behind. I have been keeping it warm. Some of it you might want back." It is holding something of yours, from a day you would rather forget.

name: Death
text: A chessboard on a rock, and at it a pale man in a black hood who is not a man. Behind you a juggler, his wife and a baby are hiding behind their painted cart, very still: the locust cult took them on the road above and dragged them down the long stair, cart and all, for an offering, and they ran. "I am Death," he says, as if apologising. "They're mine tonight. So are you, eventually. Will you play? I always offer. A knight played me once, on a beach, to buy time." He sets out the pieces. "Your years are the stake. Name what you play for."

options.label: Play for the family, staking your own years

pass.outcome: He studies the board for a long time, and knocks his king over himself, carefully, as if it mattered to get it right. "They may go." Behind you the cart creaks away down the road, and the baby laughs at something.
pass.chronicle: Played Death at chess for a juggler's family and won. He knocked over his own king, carefully. The baby laughed as the cart went.

fail.outcome: He takes your pieces one by one, and with them a little of your years. Then he stands, and goes round the cart, quite gently. The masks on the cart turn to watch him go by.
fail.chronicle: Played Death at chess for a juggler's family and lost. He took some of my years, and then them, gently. I staked what I had. It was not enough.

road.hint: A game played for someone else is never wholly lost.

options.label: Play for yourself, staking the same years

pass.outcome: "Well played." He makes a small mark in a small book. "On the way home with your Stone, I will give you back one breath I would have taken. Once."
pass.chronicle: Played Death at chess for my own life and won a breath back from him, for later. The juggler's family did not get a game.

fail.outcome: He takes your years and the family both.
fail.chronicle: Played Death at chess for my own life and lost. He took my years, and the juggler's family, who had not been asked to play.

road.hint: Some winnings are counted in other people's losses.

options.label: Offer him the family if he lets you pass
options.outcome: He looks at you for a long time, and then he nods, and goes round the cart. You do not look back. Behind you, the little bells on the cart stop ringing.
options.chronicle: Offered Death a juggler's family to let me pass. He took them. He looked at me first, for a long time, in a way I keep thinking about.

road.hint: A trade with Death always costs the other party.

options.label: Walk away
options.outcome: "Another time," he says. "There is always another time, until there isn't."

name: The Old Titan
text: A crack in the wall pulses with a slow golden light, too rhythmic to be fire, too alive to be stone, and through it you can see an eye as big as a cartwheel, very old and very tired. When you lean close you feel the heat of something enormous pressed into a space far too small for it, behind a door of bronze. A voice comes from within the crack, slow as a clock: "Smaller than I was. But not gone. I was king of the world once, traveler, before my son. Open the door a crack, and I will give you time."

options.label: Name the old king behind the bronze

pass.outcome: "Kronos," you say. The Titan who overthrew his own father with a sickle, and then, warned that a child of his would overthrow him in turn, swallowed his children one by one, until Rhea gave him a stone wrapped in swaddling clothes instead of the baby Zeus. Zeus grew up, made him spit them all out, and shut the Titans in Tartarus behind bronze doors, so far down, Hesiod says, that an anvil dropped from the earth would fall nine days and nights and land on the tenth. The eye closes. "Clever," says the voice. "My son was clever too." The air around you steadies, as if time had grudgingly agreed to wait for you.
pass.chronicle: Named the old Titan behind the bronze door: Kronos, who swallowed his children, shut in Tartarus so deep an anvil would fall nine days to reach it.

fail.outcome: You cannot place him, and the eye watches you fail with enormous patience. Later you remember Hesiod: the Titans shut in Tartarus behind bronze doors, and their old king Kronos, who swallowed his own children and was fed a stone in place of Zeus.
fail.chronicle: Met something old and enormous behind a bronze door and did not know it. It was Kronos, who once swallowed his children.

road.hint: An old king once swallowed a stone in place of his son.

options.label: Open the bronze door a crack
options.warning: Open the door a crack, and I will give you time.
options.outcome: The door moves a finger's width, and something comes through it that is not light: years. You feel them go out of you, a little at a time, into the crack, and the eye brightens as they go. You throw your weight on the door and it booms shut. "Thank you," says the voice. "I needed that." Your limbs are heavy and slow.
options.chronicle: Opened a bronze door a crack for an old Titan who promised me time. He took some of mine instead.

road.hint: An old god who offers time is usually short of it.

options.label: Offer your mana to the old Titan
options.outcome: The magic leaves you in a slow, warm exhale, drawn into the crack like breath on a cold day. "Ah. Old power," the voice says. "I am too diminished to repay you as I once could. But take this, the least I have." A warmth comes back out of the stone into your wounds.

options.label: Press on without engaging it
options.outcome: The light dims as you pass, like an eye closing. "Another time," says the voice. "I have nothing but time. Until I don't."

name: Kneeling Herald
text: A man in the black and yellow of the Locust's heralds kneels in the middle of the corridor with his hands up and his banner thrown down. "Sanctuary. I'm done with them. I know where the Destroyer is weak, and I'll tell you everything, only hide me." He keeps glancing back up the corridor. His shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.

options.label: Hide him in the side passage and hear him out
options.warning: His shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.
options.outcome: He thanks you, and weeps, and while you are watching the corridor for pursuers he puts a knife in your back and runs to fetch them.
options.chronicle: Gave sanctuary to a herald of the Locust who said he had changed sides. He had not. I should have looked at his shadow.

road.hint: A shadow that falls toward the torch belongs to no honest man.

options.label: Ask him how he got past the pickets, and keep asking

pass.outcome: He came past the eastern pickets at dusk, he says. Then it was the western ones, at the change of the watch. Then there were no pickets, because he is a herald and they let heralds through. You let him hear the three stories side by side. He hears it too. He runs, and a folded paper falls out of his sleeve: his real orders, naming the place he was to lead you, which you will now go round.
pass.chronicle: Let a herald who wanted sanctuary tell me how he got past the pickets three times. It was three different stories. He dropped his real orders running.

fail.outcome: His story holds together as far as you can follow it.
fail.chronicle: Questioned a herald about his escape and could not find the crack in it. The knife found me instead.

road.hint: A true story told three times stays the same story.

options.label: Turn him away
options.outcome: He gets up, dusts himself off, picks up his banner, and walks back the way he came without any hurry at all.
options.chronicle: Turned away a herald of the Locust who begged for sanctuary. He walked off in no hurry at all. I think I was right.

road.hint: A man fleeing for his life does not stroll.

options.label: Strike him down where he kneels
options.outcome: He is up and fighting before your blade lands, with a speed no penitent has.
options.chronicle: Struck down a kneeling herald before he could finish his story. He was quicker than any penitent. I am still not proud of how I knew.

road.hint: Being right by luck teaches nothing.

name: The Twin Flame
text: A tall flame with two tips walks the floor of a burning ditch, and the larger tip speaks in a man's voice, slow and grand. "Two of us burn in here, he and I. You are going down; so did I, once, past the pillars where no man was meant to sail. Listen, and I will tell you the short way to the bottom. My crew took it." The flame leans toward you. "Consider what you were made for. You were not made to live like beasts, but to follow virtue and knowledge."

options.label: Take his short way to the bottom
options.warning: My crew took it.
options.outcome: His short way is magnificent and wrong. It leads you along a ledge, and down a chimney, and round, and round, and some hours later you climb out of a ditch beside a tall flame with two tips, which laughs.
options.chronicle: Took a burning man's short way to the bottom. It brought me back to him, hours later, laughing.

road.hint: A grand voice in a flame once talked a whole crew into the sea.

options.label: Name the flame before you take its counsel

pass.outcome: You know this flame from Dante: Ulysses and Diomedes, burning together in one fire among the false counsellors, for the trick of the wooden horse. Ulysses told Dante how he talked his old crew out past the Pillars of Hercules into the forbidden sea with that very speech, five months out, until they saw a mountain, and a whirlwind struck the ship and the sea closed over them all. You thank him for the speech, which is a fine one, and keep your own road.
pass.chronicle: Knew the two-horned flame for Ulysses, who talked his crew past the Pillars of Hercules and drowned them. I kept the speech and my own road.

fail.outcome: You cannot place the voice, and the speech is very good, and it takes you a long moment to step back from the edge of the ditch. Only later do you remember Dante's Ulysses, burning in one flame with Diomedes, who drowned his crew with a speech like that one.
fail.chronicle: A grand voice in a flame nearly talked me into its short way. I remembered Dante's Ulysses too late to be proud of it.

road.hint: A false counsellor's speech can still be true and still drown you.

options.label: Hear his story, and go your own way
options.outcome: He tells it beautifully: the pillars, the open sea, the stars of the other sky, the mountain, the whirlwind. When he finishes you walk on the long way, and the flame watches you go with something like respect.
options.chronicle: Listened to a burning man's story of the last voyage, and went my own way.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Virtue and knowledge," the flame calls after you. "Remember."

name: Disreputable Imp
text: A small, red, deeply self-satisfied creature sits atop a crate with 'DEFINITELY FINE GOODS' stenciled on the side in handwriting that changes between letters. It points at you with a claw the size of a needle and announces: "YOU. You look like someone with gold and poor decision-making skills. Perfect. PERFECT. I have things."

options.label: Buy something from his definitely-fine crate
options.outcome: He produces something from the crate with theatrical effort, requiring both arms and one foot. "Finest quality! Mostly! The cursed ones are in the OTHER crate and I DEFINITELY didn't mix them up this time." He takes your gold and bites it experimentally. "Acceptable."
options.chronicle: Bought something from an imp's crate labelled DEFINITELY FINE GOODS. The handwriting changed between letters.

road.hint: Handwriting that changes between letters is a confession.

options.label: Look for the catch in his bargain

pass.outcome: His bargain is a ring at a tenth of its price, and you turn it over until you find the hairline of runes on the inside: whoever wears it pays later, with interest. The oldest devil's bargain there is: Marlowe's Faustus signed for twenty-four years of everything, and the bill came due at midnight. "FINE," howls the imp, and gives you an honest potion to make you go away and stop explaining things in front of the merchandise.
pass.chronicle: Found the catch in an imp's bargain: a ring that makes you pay later, with interest. Faustus got twenty-four years for his. The imp paid me to leave.

fail.outcome: It looks like a fine ring at a tenth of its price, so you put it on. It is not fine. A devil's bargain always comes due, as Faustus found when his twenty-four years ran out. You get it off again, but the cold of it stays in your fingers for a while.
fail.chronicle: Took an imp's bargain without looking for the catch. There was a catch.

road.hint: A bargain from below always comes due.

options.label: "No thank you, actually."
options.outcome: His face falls with operatic despair. "NO. No no no. Do you know how few people get this deep? Do you know how long I've been waiting?" He watches you go. "I'll be here!" he calls. "I am always here."

name: Medical Construct
text: A golem made of white stone stands in an alcove, its chest engraved with a serpent-and-staff symbol worn nearly smooth by centuries. It turns toward you with the careful movements of something built to handle fragile things. "SUBJECT ASSESSED: ALIVE. CONDITION: SUBOPTIMAL. SERVICES AVAILABLE. INDICATE REQUIREMENT."

options.label: Request wound treatment
options.outcome: It works with the impersonal efficiency of something that has been doing this for seven hundred years and finds it neither interesting nor tedious, it simply finds it correct. When it finishes, your wounds are sealed, your breathing is even, and it has left a small receipt in your pocket in a language that may not exist anymore.
options.chronicle: Paid a stone medical golem to patch me up. It assessed me as ALIVE. I appreciated the confidence.

road.hint: A healer built from stone does not flinch.

options.label: Read the symbol on its chest aloud

pass.outcome: "The rod of Asclepius," you say: one serpent on one staff, the healer's sign. Not the caduceus, with two snakes and wings, which is Hermes's, the messenger's, and which an army doctor mixed up with it in 1902; a great many signs on a great many hospitals have carried the mistake ever since. The golem's eyes brighten. "CORRECT. RARE. PATIENT ELIGIBLE FOR COURTESY TREATMENT." It sees to you for nothing.
pass.chronicle: Read the rod of Asclepius on a healing golem's chest: one serpent, one staff, not the caduceus. It treated me for nothing.

fail.outcome: "The caduceus?" "INCORRECT," says the golem, sounding tired. "CADUCEUS: TWO SERPENTS, WINGS. HERMES. MESSENGERS AND MERCHANTS. ROD OF ASCLEPIUS: ONE SERPENT. HEALING. A COMMON ERROR." Its services remain available, at the usual price.
fail.chronicle: Called a healing golem's emblem a caduceus. It corrected me: one serpent, Asclepius; two serpents and wings, Hermes.

road.hint: The healer's staff has only one serpent.

options.label: Request a restoration of drained strength
options.outcome: "DEFICIT DETECTED. RESTORING." The golem lays two cold stone palms on you and holds very still. Something that the dark took from you, piece by piece, floods back all at once.
options.chronicle: A stone golem gave me back what the drainers took. It did not say how. I did not ask.

road.hint: What a drain takes is not always gone for good.

options.label: "I am fine. Thank you."
options.outcome: It processes this for a moment. "ASSESSMENT INDICATES STATEMENT INACCURATE. HOWEVER: PATIENT AUTONOMY PROTOCOLS APPLY." It steps back into its alcove. "SAFE TRAVELS, SUBJECT." It says this with something that sounds, against all probability, like it means it.

name: Berengar the Gold
text: A towering warrior slumps against the wall, his golden armor shattered, a dozen wounds weeping light rather than blood. "I made it nearly to the bottom once," he rasps, "before the thing with a thousand mouths found me. I won't make it further. But you, you still have breath in you."

options.label: Give him bread for the road, and the words that go with it

pass.outcome: You break the bread and give it to him the old way, viaticum, the dying knight's last bread, whose name means provision for the journey. His face eases. "Then I go provisioned," he says, and presses his sword hilt to yours. "Take the edge from Berengar's blade. Let it taste whatever lies below. Say my name to it when you strike." He goes quietly, with the bread in his hand.
pass.chronicle: Gave Berengar the Gold his last bread, viaticum, provision for the journey. He gave my blade his edge and went quietly.

fail.outcome: You give him the bread but not the words; you do not know them. He eats a little anyway. "Viaticum," he says, for you. "Food for the road. Someone should know it." He goes before he can say more.
fail.chronicle: Gave a dying knight bread and could not find the words that go with it. He told me: viaticum, food for the road.

road.hint: The last bread is provision for a journey.

options.label: Sit with him a while
options.outcome: You say nothing. He says nothing. The silence between you is the companionship of people who understand what this place costs. When he finally stills, you feel something settle over you, a dying man's final wish for another's survival. You feel blessed.
options.chronicle: Sat with a dying hero who once got near the bottom. He told me what found him there.

road.hint: The last hero to come this far left a warning, if you sit long enough.

options.label: Keep moving, there is no time
options.outcome: He doesn't blame you. He just watches you go with eyes that have seen too many things walk past. You hear him whisper something as you round the corner, a name, perhaps, or a prayer.

name: Simon the Sorcerer
text: A man in a magician's robe, burned at the hem, sits on a chest that radiates the heat of the Pit, with trays of bottles and scrolls laid out before him. His feet are blackened as if they had been held in fire. "Simon, of Samaria," he says. "I sell holy things. Healing, blessing, wonders. I tried to buy them once, from a fisherman, and he would not sell. So I sell them myself now. Everything has a price."

options.label: Buy one of his healing draughts
options.outcome: He takes your coin eagerly and hands you a bottle. It is a perfectly ordinary potion, and it will work as a potion works. "A blessing," he says. It is not a blessing. It is only what it is; that has always been his trouble.
options.chronicle: Bought a potion from a damned sorcerer who calls his wares blessings. It was only a potion.

road.hint: The last shop charges what the last shop can.

options.label: Buy a scroll from him
options.outcome: He sells you a scroll sealed with wax in the shape of a coin. "Wisdom," he says. "Paid for."

options.label: Ask him who the fisherman was

pass.outcome: "Peter," you say. Simon of Samaria saw the apostles lay hands on people, and offered Peter money for the same power. "Thy money perish with thee," Peter told him, "because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." That is why buying and selling holy things is called simony, after him, and why Dante set the simonists head-down in holes of fire with their feet burning. Simon looks at his feet. Then he pushes a handful of your coins back across the tray, as if they had begun to burn.
pass.chronicle: Named the fisherman who would not sell Simon Magus the gift of God: Peter. Simony is named for him. He gave me back coin as if it burned.

fail.outcome: "A fisherman," he says bitterly. "Peter. He told me my money could perish with me, because I thought a gift could be bought. They named a sin after me for it: simony." He goes back to arranging his blessings.
fail.chronicle: Met Simon Magus, the sorcerer who tried to buy the gift of God from Peter. They named simony after him.

road.hint: A gift cannot be bought, and a sin was named for the man who tried.

options.label: Leave him to his trays
options.outcome: "Everything has a price," he calls after you, and his feet smoulder.

name: Publius Quinctilius Varus
text: A man in Roman armour stands at perfect attention over a battle map drawn on the floor in chalk that does not smudge: a forest, a road, and three marks for three legions. There is a sword wound under his breastplate that he does not seem to notice. He looks up at you with the bright, too-focused eyes of someone who has been waiting a very long time. "Soldier! Report. Where are my legions?"

options.label: Play along and give him a "report"
options.outcome: You invent a battle. He listens with furious, grateful attention, making marks on his map. "Good. Then the Nineteenth must move." He grips your arm. You walk away quicker, and feel worse.

options.label: Tell him the truth about his legions

pass.outcome: You tell him straight, as a soldier should: the Teutoburg Forest, in the ninth year of the age, the ambush on the narrow road in the rain, led by Arminius, whom he had trusted as a friend. Three legions, the Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth, lost with their eagles, and Varus fell on his own sword. In Rome, they say, Augustus beat his head against a door and cried, "Varus, give me back my legions!" Germanicus won two of the eagles back. Varus listens to the end. Then he wipes the chalk legions away with his foot, and salutes, and gives you the last thing he has to give.
pass.chronicle: Told Varus the truth about his three legions in the Teutoburg Forest. He wiped the chalk away and saluted.

fail.outcome: You tell him they were lost, and cannot say where or how, and he hears that you do not know. "Then you are no soldier of mine," he says, and turns back to the map. Three legions, lost in the Teutoburg Forest to Arminius's ambush; it is the one thing he will not hear vaguely.
fail.chronicle: Tried to tell a Roman general his legions were lost, and could not say how. He would not hear it vaguely.

road.hint: Three legions were lost in a German forest.

options.label: Salute and move on
options.outcome: He returns the salute with crisp, unbroken discipline. "At ease, soldier." You walk past his chalk army and his chalk enemy and his single chalk mark, and you do not look back, because some things deserve the dignity of an unwitnessed vigil.

name: Cassandra
text: A woman kneels in the centre of the corridor, tears streaming freely, though her face is serene: the face of someone who has made peace with being ignored. "I am Cassandra of Troy. I told them about the horse," she says. "I know what you will face. I have said so many times, to so many people, and none of them believed me until it was done."

options.label: "Tell me anyway. I will listen."

pass.outcome: You know her curse, and so you know how to listen: Apollo gave her the gift of prophecy, and when she refused him he could not take it back, so he made sure no one would ever believe her. You decide to believe her before she speaks. She speaks fast, like someone who knows the window may close. The locusts, she says: shaped like horses made ready for battle, faces like men's, hair like women's, teeth like lions', breastplates of iron, wings like the roar of chariots, and tails that sting like scorpions. "And they may not hurt any green thing," she says, "only those who do not carry God's seal on their foreheads."
pass.chronicle: Believed Cassandra before she spoke, which no one has ever done. She told me what the locusts are, the way Revelation tells it.

fail.outcome: She tells you everything. You listen, and you nod, and some part of you does not quite believe a word of it, and you can see her see that. It is not your fault. It is Apollo's curse: the god who gave her prophecy made sure no one would ever believe it.
fail.chronicle: Listened to Cassandra and could not quite believe her. That was Apollo's curse, not my choice. It felt like my choice.

road.hint: Believe her before she speaks.

options.label: Offer her food to restore her strength
options.outcome: She takes the food with both hands and eats with the careful gratitude of someone who has forgotten how it tastes. "You fed a prophet," she says softly. "The old texts say something about that. Something good." She touches your cheek, and you feel the world tilt slightly in your favor.

options.label: "Prophecy is a burden I cannot share."
options.outcome: "Yes," she says simply. "I know." She watches you go with the patient, ruined dignity of someone who has been correct about everything and helped no one. The sound of her weeping does not follow you. You almost wish it did.

name: Keeper of Last Memories
text: A robed figure sits surrounded by softly glowing motes, hundreds of them, drifting like embers from a dying fire, each one pulsing with its own quiet warmth. "Each of these," it says without turning, "is the last thought of someone who did not make it back. I keep them so they are not simply lost. You may carry one, if you choose."

options.label: Accept a fallen adventurer's last memory
options.outcome: The mote settles on your palm and dissolves. For a moment you are someone else, someone who died a little further down, who knew exactly where the shadow-thing waited, who almost made it. The knowledge that stranger died for is yours now. You feel the weight and the gift of it equally.
options.chronicle: Accepted the last memory of someone who did not make it back. It was of a kitchen, and somebody laughing.

road.hint: The last thought of the fallen is usually of home.

options.label: Leave a memory of the surface world here
options.outcome: You concentrate on something bright, a morning, a meal, a face, and it lifts gently away and joins the other motes. The Keeper watches it go. "Thank you. The collection is heavy with endings. It is good to add something that felt like a beginning." The loss settles into you strangely, like a wound that has been given proper care.

options.label: Observe the motes in silence and move on
options.outcome: You stand for a moment among the last lights of the lost. The Keeper does not press you. The motes drift around you without touching, as though they sense you are still using yourself. When you go, you feel them watching you with something that is almost hope.

name: Roland
text: A pass between black rocks, and the dead of a rear guard lying where they held it. One knight is still sitting up against a stone, blood on his temples, an ivory horn in his lap and a sword across his knees without a mark on it, and beside him a great rock split clean in two, as if a sword had been beaten against it. "Roland," he says. "Oliver told me to blow it. Three times." He holds out the horn. "Too late now for them. Blow it at the Black Gate, where they'll hear it above. So the rear guard is remembered."

options.label: Swear to blow it at the Black Gate
options.outcome: He puts it in your hands. "Oliver was right," he says. "Wisdom and courage. He had both. I had only one of them." He closes his eyes.

oath.what: Blow the Olifant at the Black Gate, so the rear guard is remembered.

thread.hint: An ivory horn is waiting to be blown at the Black Gate.

options.chronicle: Took Roland's horn and swore to blow it at the Black Gate for the rear guard. He said Oliver had been right, three times.

road.hint: A horn not blown in time can still be blown in memory.

options.label: Blow it here, now, for him
options.outcome: You blow it, and the note goes up the pass and away. Nothing answers; it is far too late for answers. Roland smiles anyway. "There," he says. "That's what it sounds like." He dies listening to the echo.
options.chronicle: Blew Roland's horn for him in his pass, far too late to bring anyone. He smiled and said that was what it sounded like.

road.hint: Some calls are made only so the caller can hear them.

options.label: Take Durendal from him
options.outcome: He tried to break it rather than let an enemy have it. He has no strength left to stop a friend. He watches you lift it. "Carry it well, then," he says, "since I couldn't break it."
options.chronicle: Took Durendal off a dying Roland. He had tried to break it on a rock so no enemy would have it. He did not have the strength to stop me.

road.hint: A sword its master tried to break is still loyal to someone.

options.label: Ask him why he didn't blow it
options.outcome: "Because a knight of France doesn't call for help against heathens," he says. "That's what I said. Oliver said a brave man who throws away his army is no wiser than a coward." He coughs. "He was right. Write that down."
