name: Boethius
text: A cell with a barred door, and inside, an old man in a senator's toga gone grey writes by a single lamp. "Theodoric's men come when the watch changes," he says, without looking up. "They forged letters in my hand and want me to sign that I wrote them. I won't, so I'm writing this instead." He sets down the pen. "Tell me. A man who loses everything Fortune gave him: is he poorer?"

options.label: Answer his question

pass.outcome: "Then Fortune never gave him anything that was his," you say. "Only lent it." He laughs, delighted, like a teacher whose worst student has finally got there. "That is my second book, Fortune and her wheel. You've saved me a chapter."
pass.chronicle: Answered Boethius's question in his cell. He laughed and said I had saved him a chapter. They come for him when the watch changes.

fail.outcome: He nods, kindly. "That is where I was, a month ago. It gets better."

road.hint: What Fortune gives, she lends. What you know, she cannot take.

options.label: Break the bar and get him out
options.outcome: The bar comes away on the third heave. He cannot stand: Theodoric's questioners saw to his legs a month ago. So he gathers the finished pages and pushes them into your hands. "They can kill me," he says. "They can't kill this." You go with the pages inside your shirt, and behind you, in the dark, he starts the last line again from memory.
options.chronicle: Broke the bar on Boethius's cell. His legs would not carry him, so he gave me his pages instead. He was saying the last line from memory when I left.

road.hint: A man who will not sign a lie can still send the truth up the stair.

options.label: Sit with him in silence
options.outcome: He writes. You sit. Once he reads you a sentence and you nod, and he crosses it out anyway.

options.label: Leave him to his book

name: The Bound Watcher
text: In a pit floored with jagged rocks lies a great winged figure bound hand and foot, darkness heaped over him like a blanket, his wings all broken feathers and iron. He lifts a face of terrible beauty. "I taught your kind to work metal," he says. "Swords and shields and breastplates; bracelets, and paint for the eyes. All your wars began at my forge, and I was bound here for teaching. Loose one chain, or only listen, and I will give your blade the last thing I know about steel. You will never need another smith."

options.label: Loose one chain
options.warning: Loose one chain, or only listen,
options.outcome: The chain parts with a sound like a bell breaking. He does not get up; he only laughs, and out of the darkness heaped over him something with too many wings comes for you.
options.chronicle: Loosed a chain on a bound angel because he promised to teach me. Something came out of his darkness instead.

road.hint: Some chains were put on by angels for a reason.

options.label: Listen, and take his gift to your blade
options.outcome: He speaks, and you listen, and your blade drinks it in: an edge like a thought. It is very fine work. When you look at it afterwards you see your own face in the metal, and behind it, faintly, his.
options.chronicle: Took a bound angel's craft into my blade. It is the finest edge I have ever owned. I see his face in it.

road.hint: The first smith of war still has lessons, and a price.

options.label: Name him, and refuse him

pass.outcome: "Azazel," you say. In the Book of Enoch he was the Watcher who taught men to make swords and shields and breastplates, and ornaments, and the arts that corrupted them; and Raphael was sent to bind him hand and foot and cast him into the dark in Dudael, and heap rough and jagged rocks on him, and cover his face, until the day of judgment. "You stay," you tell him, and he turns his face back into the dark.
pass.chronicle: Named the bound Watcher, Azazel, whom Raphael chained in the dark of Dudael for teaching men the arts of war. I left him there.

fail.outcome: You search for his name while he talks, and his voice gets into the search, and by the time you tear yourself away your head rings with it. Long after, you remember the Book of Enoch: Azazel, who taught men war, bound by Raphael in the dark of Dudael until the day of judgment.
fail.chronicle: Could not name a bound angel before his voice got into my head. It was Azazel, of the Book of Enoch.

road.hint: An angel bound under jagged rocks has a name in an old book.

options.label: Walk away from the pit
options.outcome: "They all come back," he says, to the dark. "Sooner or later, everyone wants a better sword."

name: Sisyphus
text: Up a slope of black scree a man is pushing a boulder bigger than he is, with his hands and his shoulder and his head, the way he has pushed it for a very long time. Near the top it slips, as it always slips, and thunders down past you, and he walks down after it, quite calmly. "Sisyphus," he says. "King of Corinth, once. Help me push? It won't make any difference. I like the company."

options.label: Help him push
options.outcome: You put your shoulder to the stone beside his, and for a while the two of you grind it up the slope, and near the top it slips, and rolls back down. He laughs. "There. Now you know everything I know." Your legs burn, and feel stronger for it.
options.chronicle: Helped Sisyphus push his stone. It rolled back down. He seemed pleased to have the company.

options.label: Ask him how he cheated Death

pass.outcome: He grins. When Death came for him with chains, he asked to be shown how they worked, and chained Death instead, and no one on earth could die until Ares came to set Death free. Then he told his wife not to bury him, and in the underworld he complained to Persephone that he had no proper rites, and she let him go back up to scold his wife, and he lived to be old. "The stone is the bill," he says. The Greek word for the pit where the rebel angels wait, in Peter's letter, is Tartarus, his own address. He shows you how a man slips a chain.
pass.chronicle: Sisyphus told me how he chained Death, and talked his way back from the underworld. He showed me how a man slips a chain.

fail.outcome: "With a sword?" He laughs, and puts his shoulder back to the stone. "With a question. I asked Death to show me how his chains worked."
fail.chronicle: Asked Sisyphus how he cheated Death. He said he asked Death a question.

road.hint: A clever king once asked Death to demonstrate his chains.

options.label: Leave him to his stone
options.outcome: When you look back from the top of the scree he is already at the bottom, setting his shoulder to it again.

name: Sir Oswin
text: A pilgrim sits on the stair with his feet bare, and you can see the step through them. He died on this road long ago, he says, and still walks it. "The knight from Thale? Big man, cracked holy symbol?" He points up the way you came. "He passed me going up, singing. Badly. Said he was going home to testify against his bishop."

text_variants.text: A heap of dead demons fills a crossroads, more than you can count, and on top of it, like a man who fell asleep on a hill, lies Sir Oswin, his cracked holy symbol in his fist.

options.label: Ask the pilgrim about the knight
options.outcome: "Singing," says the pilgrim again, as if that were the strange part. "All the way up. I'd not have thought a man that size could climb that fast."
options.chronicle: A pilgrim on the stair passed Sir Oswin going up to testify against his bishop and give Thale back. He said the knight was singing.

road.hint: Some debts are paid where everyone can see.

options.label: Close his eyes
options.outcome: The blessed armour is warm under your hand. It let him wear it again, at the end.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Oswin dead on a hill of demons. His armour had forgiven him, I think. I closed his eyes.

road.hint: Atonement down here is measured in heaps.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The pilgrim goes back to rubbing feet that have not hurt in a hundred years.

name: The Fallen Star
text: In a chamber with no ceiling, or rather, a ceiling that has been replaced by deep black space, a figure made entirely of connected stars wheels slowly in the middle of the air. It is beautiful in the way that things are beautiful when they are not meant for you. It notices you and descends. "We fell," it says simply. "We have been falling for some time."

options.label: Ask it to show you the sky it came from
options.outcome: It reaches out with a hand made of light and distance and touches your forehead. For a moment you are not in the dungeon. You are somewhere enormous and cold and breathtaking, and you understand why something might spend eternity simply being part of such a sky. You return carrying a small piece of that regard.

options.label: Offer to light a path for it with a torch
options.outcome: It looks at your small flame with an expression so gentle it nearly breaks something in your chest. "You would light the way for us," it says softly, "when we are made of light." But it follows your torch for a few steps anyway, and the warmth it shares with you in return is vast and generous.

options.label: Ask what it was given when it fell

pass.outcome: It goes very still, and you know what it is: the star of Revelation that fell from heaven to the earth, and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit. When he opened it, smoke rose like a great furnace and darkened the sun, and out of the smoke came the locusts, and their king is the angel of the pit, Abaddon. "I opened it," it says. "I did not know what I was letting out. Go carefully. The smoke is still rising." It touches your forehead, and the dark steadies.
pass.chronicle: Met the fallen star of Revelation, that was given the key of the bottomless pit and opened it. It told me the smoke is still rising.

fail.outcome: "A wish?" It turns away. Much later you remember Revelation: a star fell from heaven, and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit, and from the smoke came the locusts.
fail.chronicle: Asked a fallen star what it had been given. I did not understand its answer until later: a key.

road.hint: A falling star was handed a key.

options.label: Stand still and watch it for a moment
options.outcome: You watch. It wheels. The stars that make up its shape pulse slowly, and you think you can almost read them, a story written in fire across impossible distances. When you finally move on, it watches you go, and somehow the dungeon is a little less dark for a while.
options.chronicle: Watched a constellation that had fallen into a chamber with no ceiling. It was not meant for me. It was beautiful anyway.

road.hint: Some beauty is not meant for you, and is still there.

name: The Fetch
text: You see it first in a shard of reflective stone, a figure standing just behind you, mimicking your posture exactly. When you turn, nothing is there. When you look back at the stone, it is not mimicking you anymore. It is watching you, with its head tilted slightly, like a student who has a question. It raises one hand. It waits.

options.label: Raise your hand back
options.outcome: You raise your hand. It nods, slowly, with visible satisfaction. Then it steps through the mirror and past you, you feel it pass like cold water, and it vanishes into the dungeon ahead of you. Where it walked, nothing notices you for a long while. It has taught the darkness your outline, and the darkness is looking elsewhere.
options.chronicle: Raised my hand to the thing in the mirror stone. It raised its hand back, a moment late.

road.hint: What mirrors you a moment late is not your reflection.

options.label: Break the reflective stone
options.outcome: The stone shatters and the figure in the reflection shatters with it, not violently, but the way an expression falls from a face when it thinks no one is watching. You breathe hard. The effort cost you. But there is something releasing in the violence of it, and the tension leaves your body along with the shards.

options.label: Name what it is, and what it means

pass.outcome: "A fetch," you say: the double of a living person, in the old Irish telling. Seen in the evening, it is a warning of death; seen in the morning, a promise of long life. It is always night down here, so you tell it that by your reckoning it is morning, and you have just woken. The figure in the stone considers this, and nods, slowly, and lets you be.
pass.chronicle: Met my own fetch in a shard of stone. A fetch seen in the morning means long life, so I told it I had just woken.

fail.outcome: "A reflection," you say. It shakes its head, which your reflection cannot do. The Irish call such a thing a fetch, your double, seen before a death; though seen in the morning, they say, it promises a long life instead.
fail.chronicle: Met my own double in a shard of stone. The Irish call it a fetch. I could not say what it meant.

road.hint: A double seen in the morning promises long life.

options.label: Walk past without acknowledging it
options.outcome: You feel it follow you with its gaze across every reflective surface in the corridor. Wet stone. A dropped shield. The dark surface of still water in a crack. You do not look at any of them. You are fairly confident it respects this. You are less confident it stops following.

name: The Enumerated Self
text: It is shaped like a person the way a drawing is shaped like a person, the right number of limbs, in roughly the right places, but flat in some dimension you cannot name. It speaks without a mouth: "We have been cataloguing experiences. We have fourteen thousand, nine hundred and two. You have more. We would like some of yours."

options.label: Trade a memory for its knowledge
options.outcome: You feel something leave you, not pain, but absence. A room from your childhood you can no longer quite picture. The Enumerated Self shudders with something that might be pleasure. In return, it presses fourteen thousand, nine hundred and three small certainties into your mind. The dungeon becomes briefly, brilliantly legible.

options.label: Tell it what it is missing

pass.outcome: "You are Hume's bundle," you tell it. Hume looked inward for a self and found only perceptions, one after another, and called the mind a bundle of them. Reid answered him: then who is doing the looking? The Enumerated Self goes still for a very long time. "Fourteen thousand, nine hundred and three," it says at last. "The experience of being asked who is counting." It gives you what it knows without taking anything from you.
pass.chronicle: Told the Enumerated Self it was Hume's bundle of perceptions, and gave it Reid's question: who is doing the looking?

fail.outcome: You tell it to count faster. "We are," it says. Later you think of Hume, who looked for his self and found only a bundle of perceptions, and Reid, who asked who was doing the looking. You did not ask it that.
fail.chronicle: Met a thing that counts its experiences. I never asked it who was counting.

road.hint: A bundle of perceptions still has to be perceived by someone.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: It watches you retreat with an expression that has been assembled from references rather than felt. "We will catalogue this also," it says. "The experience of watching something leave." Somehow, that is the worst thing it could have said.

name: The Black Gate
text: The Black Gate: a gate of black iron set deep in the wall, with a hornstand of carved bone beside it and nothing in it. The wind comes up through the bars from the deep, and it is cold, and there are no sounds in it at all. Roland's horn is heavy in your pack.

options.label: Set Roland's horn to your lips and blow it
options.outcome: The note goes down through the gate and keeps going. It is the loudest sound you have ever made, and somewhere very far above, faint as a memory, a great many horns answer it. The rear guard is remembered. You hang the horn in its stand.
options.chronicle: Blew Roland's horn at the Black Gate, as he asked, for the rear guard who died at the pass. Something answered from very far above.

road.hint: A horn blown late is still a horn blown.

options.label: "I lost Roland's horn."
options.outcome: The hornstand stays empty. The wind comes up through the bars with no sounds in it, and nothing answers from above, because nothing was asked.
options.chronicle: Reached the Black Gate without Roland's horn. I had lost it on the way down. The hornstand is still empty.

road.hint: A horn lost on the road leaves the rear guard unremembered.

options.label: Keep the horn and say nothing
options.outcome: The gate stays silent. The horn is worth a great deal. You walk through with it in your pack, and the wind behind you has no sounds in it at all.
options.chronicle: Carried Roland's horn to the Black Gate and kept it. He asked me to blow it for the rear guard. I did not.

road.hint: The silence at a gate can be the sound of a promise not kept.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: You leave the hornstand as you found it.

text_variants.text: The Black Gate: a gate of black iron set deep in the wall, with a hornstand of carved bone beside it and nothing in it. The wind comes up through the bars from the deep, and it is cold, and there are no sounds in it at all. Roland's horn should be heavy in your pack. It is not there.

name: Ruth Gale
text: A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair after you two at a time, a lantern in one hand and an old man's chisel in the other. "I found him," she says. "Old man in white, beside a blank stone. My father. You were the last one with him." It isn't a question.

options.label: Ask her if he finished it
options.outcome: "He finished it." She says the words the way he must have carved them: THE KING OF THE LOCUSTS IS ABADDON, AND HE CAN BE ANSWERED. "He was right. All those years. He was right, and I laughed." She turns back up the stair to sit with him.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale came down after me to say her father finished his tablet. She said he was right and she had laughed. She went back up to sit with him.

road.hint: A warning finished in time is read by the one who most needed it.

options.label: Tell her what he told you
options.outcome: She listens to every word with her eyes shut, saying it over after you. Then she turns back up the stair with his chisel in her fist. "I'll carve it," she says. "Badly. But it'll be both of ours."
options.chronicle: Told Ruth Gale the last warning her father whispered to me. She went back up to carve it on his blank stone herself. Now it will be both of theirs.

road.hint: A message told instead of carved can still be carved by someone else.

options.label: Tell her you took it from his neck, and give it back
options.outcome: You tell her all of it: the clear eyes, the blank stone, his hand closing on the amulet too weakly to keep it, and you taking it anyway. Ruth's knuckles go white on the chisel, and for a moment you think she will use it. Then she holds out her other hand, and you put the amulet in it. "He'd have forgiven you," she says. "He forgave everybody. It drove me mad." She goes back up the stair to him. She does not say whether she does.
options.chronicle: Told Ruth Gale I took her father's amulet off him while he was dying, and gave it back. She said he would have forgiven me. She did not say she would.

road.hint: The whole truth, told to the one it hurts, is heavier than the thing returned.

options.label: Give it back
options.outcome: "That's his." It isn't a question. She puts it round her own neck and goes back up to him, and does not thank you.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale saw her father's amulet on me and I gave it back. She did not thank me. I would not have.

road.hint: What you take from the dying, the living come to ask for.

options.label: Tell her it's gone
options.outcome: "Gone," she says. "Like him." She looks at you a long time, then turns and goes back up the stair without another word.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale asked after her father's amulet. I had taken it and lost it since. She went back up to him without another word.

road.hint: What you take from the dying, the living come to ask for.

options.label: Keep it
options.outcome: "That's his." It isn't a question. She looks at you a long time, then goes back up to him without it.
options.chronicle: Kept a prophet's amulet in front of his daughter. She went back up to him without it.

road.hint: What you take from the dying, the living come to ask for.

options.label: Tell her what you saw
options.outcome: You tell her about the clear eyes and the blank stone, and that he told you to go quickly. She turns his chisel over in her hands. "Then I'll decide what goes on it," she says, and goes back up.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale came after me from her father's blank stone. I told her he sent me on. She went back up with his chisel, deciding what to carve.

text_variants.text: A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair after you two at a time with a lantern. "I found him," she says. "Old man in white, carving. My father. He said a stranger gave him the hour." She is out of breath, and not only from the stair.

A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair after you two at a time, a lantern in one hand and an old man's chisel in the other. "I found him beside a blank stone," she says. "My father. He'd been whispering to someone at the end. You?"

A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair after you two at a time, a lantern in one hand and an old man's chisel in the other. "I found him," she says. "Old man in white, beside a blank stone. My father. His amulet's gone." She looks at you, and at what you carry.

name: Old Fisherman
text: A gate of plain wood in a plain wall, and an old fisherman sitting beside it on a stool, mending a net, with a ring of keys at his belt. He looks up. "Ah. You. I've been reading about you." There's a ledger on his knee, and it's thick. "People you met on the way down. Want to hear how they did?"

options.label: "Tell me about them."
options.chronicle: Met an old fisherman with a ring of keys who told me how the people I met had done. Some better than I deserved. Some worse.

road.hint: Every name you met on the way down is written somewhere.

people_lines.after: He closes the ledger. 'The rest is between them and me.'

options.label: "Who decides?"
options.outcome: "Not me. I only keep the door." He winks. "But I hear things."

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: He goes back to his net. "Mind the last stairs," he says. "They're the long ones."

name: Robin Hood
text: A plank bridge no wider than one man crosses a black stream that runs out of one wall and into another. As you step onto one end, a man in Lincoln green steps onto the other, with a longbow in his hand and a horn at his belt. Neither of you gives way. In the middle he stops and grins. "It's a narrow bridge," he says. "One of us is going in the water. Robin Hood, of Sherwood. And you?"

options.label: "A bow against a staff? That's a coward's fight."
options.outcome: He looks at his bow, then at you, and laughs. "Fair," he says. He lays the bow on the bank, cuts a staff of oak from the roots in the wall, and comes back out onto the planks. "Now, then."

options.label: Cut a staff and meet him on the bridge

pass.outcome: The planks bounce under you both. He is quick, and you are quicker: a crack on the shoulder, a sweep at the knees, and Robin Hood goes off the bridge into the stream with a great splash. He comes up laughing, sets the horn to his lips and blows, and men in green come out of the dark along both banks to see what is so funny. "Little John did the same to me once," he says, wringing out his hood, "and he's been with me ever since." He hangs the horn round your neck. "Blow it when you need us, and we'll come. Once. It's a long way from Sherwood."

thread.hint: A horn on a green baldric, to blow once, in need.

pass.chronicle: Knocked Robin Hood off a narrow bridge into the stream with a staff. He came up laughing and gave me his horn.

fail.outcome: He is quick, and the planks are wet. A crack on the shoulder, a sweep at the knees, and it is you who goes into the stream. You come up spluttering. He is laughing on the bridge, and not unkindly. "A good bout," he says, and blows his horn, and his men come out of the dark to laugh with him. Then they are gone, all of them, the way they came.
fail.chronicle: Fought Robin Hood with staves on a narrow bridge, and it was I who went into the stream. He laughed, not unkindly, and was gone.

road.hint: On a narrow bridge, a fair fight wins a friend.

options.label: Step back and let him cross
options.outcome: You step back off the planks. He crosses, gives you a bow from the waist that is only half a joke, and is gone into the dark. "Courteous," he says over his shoulder. "No use in a fight, courtesy."
options.chronicle: Gave way to Robin Hood on a narrow bridge. He thanked me and was gone.

road.hint: Robin Hood keeps no one who gives way on a bridge.

name: The Sleepers Under the Hill
text: A ball of thread lies unwound across the floor and runs into a crack in the wall. Someone found this place before you. Beyond the crack is a vaulted hall, warm and lit by a fire that burns up out of the floor with nothing to feed it. A king sleeps on a throne with a queen beside him; knights sleep along the benches, their hounds asleep at their feet. On a table by the door lie a sword in an old scabbard, a garter, and a bugle-horn. Nobody stirs. The fire makes no smoke.

options.label: Draw the sword
options.outcome: It comes out of the scabbard slowly, red with old rust. As the blade comes clear, every eye in the hall opens, and the king sits up on his throne.

options.label: Cut the garter with it
options.outcome: The garter parts under the edge. All along the benches the knights sit up, slow as men in deep water, and a hound lifts its head and looks at you.

options.label: Blow the bugle

pass.outcome: You set the horn to your lips and blow, and the note goes all the way round the hall and comes back. The knights stand. The hounds stand. The king comes down from his throne and takes the bugle from your hands. "Not yet," says Arthur. "It is not yet the hour. But you did what the last one could not." He hangs it on you again. "When your need is greatest, blow it, and we will come. Once." When you look back from the crack in the wall they are all asleep again, and the fire burns on.

thread.hint: A bugle from under the hill, for the hour of greatest need.

pass.chronicle: Drew the sword, cut the garter and blew the bugle under the hill, and King Arthur woke. He gave me the bugle for my hour of need.

fail.outcome: Your breath catches in the old horn and the note dies before it is out of it. The king's eyes are already closing. One by one the knights lie down along the benches, and the hounds put their heads on their paws, and when you look back from the crack in the wall it is only a crack.
fail.chronicle: Drew the sword and cut the garter under the hill, but blew the bugle too weakly. The sleepers slept on.

road.hint: The sword, the garter and the horn, and all three of them.

options.label: Let the sleepers sleep
options.outcome: You leave the hall as you found it. The thread runs out through the crack behind you.
options.chronicle: Found a king and his knights asleep under the hill, and left them so.

road.hint: A sleeping king waits for someone with the nerve to wake him.

options.label: Put the sword back and go
options.outcome: You put the sword back in its scabbard. Before it is home their eyes have closed again, and the king is asleep on his throne. You follow the thread back out through the crack.
options.chronicle: Woke the sleepers under the hill for a moment, and let them sleep again.

road.hint: Half a waking is no waking.

options.label: Sheathe the sword
options.outcome: You slide the sword back into its scabbard, slowly. As it goes home the light goes out of their eyes, and the king sinks back on his throne. Before he sleeps he lifts his hands and says, sorrowfully: "O woe betide that evil day / On which the witless wight was born, / Who drew the sword, the garter cut, / But never blew the bugle-horn." Then the hall is still, and the crack in the wall is only a crack.
options.chronicle: Drew the sword and cut the garter under the hill, then lost my nerve and sheathed it. King Arthur cursed the day I was born, and slept.

road.hint: Who drew the sword, the garter cut, but never blew the bugle-horn.

name: Heimdall
text: The ice opens on a bridge of trembling colour that climbs out of the deep and out of sight, and at its foot sits a tall man in white with a great curved horn across his knees. When he smiles, his teeth are gold. "Heimdall," he says. "I heard you on the stair three floors up. I hear the grass grow and the wool on the sheep, and I need less sleep than a bird." He looks past you, down. "And I hear the wolf. He is loose below you, and I cannot leave this bridge."

options.label: "What is the horn?"
options.outcome: "Gjallarhorn. It is heard in every world. When the end comes I blow it, and the gods wake, and out of Valhalla's doors ride the einherjar, Odin's chosen dead, who fight all day and stand up whole at evening." He turns the horn in his hands. "I should carry it down to the wolf. If I leave this bridge, the giants cross it."

options.label: Keep the watch with him

pass.outcome: You sit the watch with him while the colours of the bridge tremble overhead. Three times he asks what you heard, and you heard it. "You listen," he says at last. "Good. Nobody down there does." He puts the horn in your hands; it is far heavier than it looks. "Blow it once, where you need them, and they will hear it in Valhalla. They will ride beside you against the wolf's kin and the rest. Not against the wolf himself. Killing him is not theirs to do, nor binding him. It never was." He turns back to his watch.

thread.hint: The watchman's horn, to blow once, where you need them.

pass.chronicle: Kept the watch with Heimdall at the foot of the bridge, and heard what he heard. He put Gjallarhorn in my hands.

fail.outcome: You sit the watch with him, and the dark is very quiet, and you hear none of what he hears. "You heard nothing," he says, not unkindly. "Go down, then. Listen harder on the way." He keeps the horn across his knees.
fail.chronicle: Kept the watch with Heimdall and heard nothing of what he heard. He kept his horn.

road.hint: The watchman trusts his horn to one who listens.

options.label: Leave him to his watch
options.outcome: He nods without looking round. He is listening to something a long way below you.
options.chronicle: Passed Heimdall at his watch by the foot of the bridge, and went on down.

road.hint: The watchman's horn stays where nobody sits the watch.
